research.plain_summary: Core-satellite keeps most of the money in a broad index fund (the core) and a smaller slice in the investor's own conviction picks (the satellites). When a pick is sold, the money goes back to the index, not to cash. The one thing the evidence says: cash has been the expensive place to wait, because shares beat cash in about three years out of four, so this structure cures "missing the move" by design. The price is that the portfolio rides every market fall in full, and most stock-pickers, professional and private, have not beaten the index with their picks.
research.how_it_works: The portfolio is split in two: a core held in a low-cost fund that simply tracks a whole market index, and a smaller satellite sleeve of individual positions chosen on fundamentals (revenue and earnings growth). The index is the resting place for all money that is not in a satellite, so the portfolio stays close to fully invested; institutions call this "equitising cash" [parking idle money in the index instead of leaving it uninvested]. Opening a satellite position means selling some index units to pay for it, and closing one means buying index units back the same day, with the technical signals deciding those switches. The main dial is the size of the satellite sleeve: institutions set it with a "risk budget" [how far they will let results stray from the index, also called tracking error], and Vanguard's published framework sizes it from four inputs: the edge expected before costs, the cost, how bumpy the active part is, and how much patience the investor has for spells of lagging. As a published example, Vanguard's Australian core-satellite model portfolios hold roughly 30% in active satellites, 69% in the index core and 1% in cash. One side effect: every satellite position is now judged against the index it was taken from, not against zero.
research.sitting_in_cash_relevance: This is the one structure that attacks the cash problem head-on, by changing the resting place of idle money from cash to the index. Under it, a technical sell signal no longer means "in the market or out"; it only means "this stock or the index". That removes the decision Sharpe's maths says is so hard to win: getting back in, which needs to be right about 7 times in 10. The question "should any money be in cash at all?" then becomes a separate, deliberate, whole-market decision instead of a side effect of selling a stock. As a rough scale (our arithmetic on the sourced long-run averages, not a forecast): US shares averaged about 6.7 points a year more than cash over 1929-2018, so a book that sits half in cash gives up roughly 3.4 points a year on average. What the structure gives up in return is the cushion: it is fully exposed in every market fall, and the evidence that extreme days cluster in downtrends (Faber, Asness) is the strongest argument that some rule for holding cash in a falling market can be worth having. No study was found that tests this exact rule (sold satellite goes to the index) for a private investor using technical entry and exit signals; the nearest evidence is institutional cash equitisation and the invest-now-versus-wait research, so the honest test is to re-run past trades with the idle cash placed in the index.

not_verified: Sharpe's original 1975 article could not be opened (the publisher's page refused access). Its method and result are taken from the 2021 open-access paper that re-tests it. The widely quoted '74% accuracy' figure was seen only in search snippets; the 2021 paper states Sharpe's conclusion as 'at least 7 times out of 10'. That paper cites the title as 'Are gains likely from market timing?'; it is usually cited as 'Likely Gains from Market Timing'.

J.P. Morgan's own Guide to Retirement slide could not be opened; the figures are from trade-press reports. Reports differ slightly for 2005-2024 (10.6% and 6.4% in one; 10.4% and 6.1% in a search snippet of another), so treat them as approximate.

S&P's own SPIVA scorecard page refused access. Only the 2025 one-year figure (79%) is confirmed, through a news report. The often-quoted long-run figure (roughly nine in ten large-company funds trailing over 15-20 years) was NOT verified in this session.

findings.claim: Waiting in cash has usually cost money, though not always. Vanguard compared investing a sum at once with drip-feeding it over three months and with staying in cash. Investing at once won about two times in three; the gap is the return given up while part of the money sat idle. In the worst outcomes the order flips: the fully invested path ended lower. The study is about a new lump sum judged after one year; it does not test repeated in-and-out switching on technical signals.
findings.numbers: MSCI World index, rolling one-year windows, 1976-2022: investing at once beat a 3-month drip-feed 68% of the time and beat cash 70% of the time; the drip-feed beat cash 69% of the time. US shares beat cash (3-month Treasury bill) 76% of the time over 1976-2022. On $100,000 all in shares, the middle outcome after one year was $111,940 invested at once versus $109,580 drip-fed (2.2% more). Worst 5% of outcomes: $82,947 invested at once versus $85,906 drip-fed. When the waiting cash earns Treasury-bill interest, investing at once still won 65% of the time; the higher the cash rate, the smaller the advantage.
findings.note: Every number seen in the Vanguard PDF text (pages 2-5, Figures 2 and 3). The headline 68% assumes no interest on the waiting cash; the 65% figure is the version with Treasury-bill interest. The paper says '76% of the time', not '76% of years'.

findings.claim: Jumping between shares and cash only pays if the calls are right far more often than a coin flip. Sharpe's 1975 study, as summarised in a 2021 open-access re-test: with one switch a year and a 2% cost per switch over 1929-1972, a timer had to be right 83% of the time to beat simply holding shares, and 74% of the time to beat a fixed shares-and-cash mix of the same risk. That is where his rule of thumb 'at least 7 times out of 10' comes from. The 2021 re-test uses a cheaper 1% switching cost and data to 2018, and finds a lower bar for the average timer, but once luck in the order of mistakes is allowed for it ends up back near Sharpe's figure.
findings.numbers: Sharpe (1929-1972, 2% per switch): 83% accuracy needed to beat buy-and-hold [just holding shares]; 74% to beat a constant mix [a fixed blend of shares and cash]. 2021 re-test (1% per switch): average timer beats buy-and-hold at 71% or better in 1929-1972 and 61% or better in 1973-2018, and beats the constant mix at 63% or better in both periods. Simulation of 10,000 timers over 1929-2018: the middle timer is ahead of the constant mix from 63%; all of them are ahead only from 72%. Shares beat cash in 68.89% of calendar years 1929-2018; in the other years shares averaged -10.80% against +4.33% for cash. Simple yearly averages 1929-2018: US shares 10.92%, cash 4.18%; worst single year for shares -43.12%.
findings.note: Read from the paper's text. Three corrections to the researcher's wording: (1) the 72% figure is measured against the fixed shares-and-cash mix, not against buy-and-hold; (2) the 2021 re-test uses a 1% switching cost, not Sharpe's 2%; (3) the '74%' figure is stated in this paper (the researcher said it was only seen in search snippets), and Sharpe's harsher 83% hurdle against buy-and-hold was left out. Sharpe's original article was not opened by me either.

findings.claim: A tiny number of days decides long-run results, and the best days sit close to the worst ones. This is the classic case against stepping out of the market: an investor who leaves after a bad day tends to miss the rebound.
findings.numbers: Dow Jones index, 1900-2006, 29,190 trading days, dividends excluded: $100 grew to $25,746 (5.3% a year). Missing the best 10 days left $9,008 (65% less, 4.3% a year). Across 15 countries and 160,278 trading days, missing the best 10 days left portfolios 50.8% smaller on average. J.P. Morgan Guide to Retirement 2026 (primary document, S&P 500 with dividends, $10,000 from 2 Jan 2006 to 31 Dec 2025): 11.0% a year fully invested ($80,619); 6.6% without the 10 best days ($35,866); 3.8% without the 20 best ($21,177); 1.6% without the 30 best. Six of the 10 best days fell within two weeks of the 10 worst days.
findings.note: Estrada figures all confirmed in the paper. The J.P. Morgan figures are replaced with the ones I read in J.P. Morgan's own current document (slide 41). The researcher's 'seven of 10' is the 2024 edition as reported by trade press (confirmed on that trade-press page); the current edition says six of 10. The researcher's 2005-2024 figures (10.6% / 6.4% / 3.7%) appear only in a MarketScreener article that does not name the J.P. Morgan document; I could not confirm them in a primary source.

findings.claim: EVIDENCE AGAINST: the 'missing the best days' argument is one-sided. Missing the worst days helps by as much or more, and both kinds of extreme day cluster when the market is already falling. So a structure that sends sale money straight back into the index during a downtrend keeps it in the zone where the wild days live (that last step is reasoning, not a tested result). The three authors read the same pattern three ways: Estrada concludes timing is a losing game, Faber concludes avoiding falling markets is worthwhile, and Asness says the effect is symmetric so it proves nothing either way.
findings.numbers: Estrada: avoiding the worst 10 days on the Dow raised the end value by 206% (to $78,781); across 15 countries by 150.4% on average. Faber, US shares Sept 1928-Dec 2010, price only (dividends excluded): 4.86% a year buy-and-hold; -7.08% without the best 1% of days; +19.09% without the worst 1%; 5.48% without both (figure from the trade-press report). Roughly 60-80% of the best and worst days came after the market had already started falling (below its 200-day average price); in the other countries studied, 76% of worst days and 67% of best days. Asness (AQR), S&P 500 monthly, Jan 1970-Dec 1996: 12.3% a year fully invested, 7.2% without the best 12 months, 18.1% without the worst 12 months.
findings.note: I found and read Faber's own paper on his website (the SSRN page refused access): 4.86%, -7.08%, 19.09%, 'price only', '60-80%', '76%' and '67%' are all in it. The 5.48% figure sits in a table image; I saw it only in the Financial Planning article. Qualifiers the page should carry: Faber's paper is a white paper from his own fund firm (Cambria), not a peer-reviewed journal; CXO's summary notes the test is 'in-sample' [uses the whole history at once, which a real-time investor could not]. Estrada's own words: 'The odds against successful market timing are just staggering.'

findings.claim: Investors as a group earn less than the funds they own because of when they buy and sell. The gap was close to zero in broad US stock index funds and widest in the jumpiest funds. That supports a calm, broad US index core, but the 'index' label alone does not protect: outside US stock funds, index-fund investors had wider gaps than active-fund investors. A 2026 academic paper also disputes how much of the gap is really bad timing.
findings.numbers: Morningstar, nearly 23,000 US funds and ETFs, 10 years to 31 Dec 2025: the average dollar earned 8.7% a year versus 9.9% for the funds, a gap of 1.2 points a year (about 12% of the total return, roughly $3.8 trillion). US stock funds: 12.8% versus 13.3%. US stock index funds: 13.7% versus 13.8% (gap 0.1). Sector funds: gap 1.2 points (sector index funds 1.5, sector ETFs 1.8). International stock funds: index 1.6 versus active 0.8. Most volatile fifth of funds: gap 2.1 points; least volatile fifth: 0.4 (the fifths in between: 1.5, 1.8, 1.3, so not a smooth staircase). ETFs: gap 1.6 points versus 1.2 for ordinary funds. Counter-evidence: a Financial Analysts Journal paper (12 May 2026) using the sample from Morningstar's 2025 edition (2015-2024) puts the true cost of bad timing at 0.10% a year. Morningstar itself says the gap is not a parable of 'dumb money'.
findings.note: All of the researcher's numbers confirmed in the Morningstar PDF (Exhibits 4, 8, 10 and the ETF table). Correction is to the conclusion: the same report says active-fund investors 'captured a slightly higher percentage' of returns than index-fund investors in most groups, 'with the notable exception of US equity'. The Fulkerson paper uses the 2025 study's sample, not the 2026 one.

findings.claim: EVIDENCE AGAINST the satellite half: most stock-pickers do not beat the index after costs, private investors who trade most do worst, and most individual shares do not even beat Treasury bills over their lives. There is some evidence FOR conviction picks: professional managers' highest-conviction holdings have beaten the market, and their stock picks beat it before costs and cash holdings are counted. The authors' own later draft puts the size of that edge well below the 2008 figure, and it is about professionals, not private investors.
findings.numbers: Against: 79% of actively managed US large-company funds trailed the S&P 500 in 2025, the fourth-worst year in the study's 25-year history (news report of S&P's scorecard; S&P's own page would not open). 66,465 US households at a discount broker, 1991-1996: average household 16.4% a year versus 17.9% for the market; the most active traders 11.4%. US shares since 1926: the best 4% of listed companies explain the whole net gain over Treasury bills; the rest together only matched bills, and the majority of individual shares earned less than one-month bills over their lives. For: fund managers' 'best ideas' beat the market by about 2.8% to 4.5% a year depending on the yardstick (April 2021 draft; the 2008 draft said 0.39% to 1.27% a month); the same draft says the vast majority of the other shares managers hold show no significant outperformance. US funds 1975-1994: the shares they held beat the market by 1.3% a year, but investors' net return trailed by 1%; of that 2.3-point gap, 0.7 came from non-share holdings and 1.6 from fees and trading costs.
findings.note: Barber-Odean, Bessembinder, Wermers and the 2008 Best Ideas abstract all confirmed on the pages fetched. Correction: the researcher quoted only the 2008 working-paper figure; I fetched the authors' April 2021 draft (Anton, Cohen, Polk) and it states 2.8-4.5% a year. It is still a working paper as far as the draft shows. The long-run S&P scorecard figure (share of funds trailing over 15-20 years) remains unverified: S&P's site returned access errors on three addresses.

findings.claim: Giving idle money index exposure is a service that large institutions buy (Russell calls it a 'cash overlay' [buying index futures so idle cash moves with the market]); the measured benefit is real but modest at their small cash levels. The counter-evidence: for skilled professional managers, holding extra cash has gone with better results, because it lets them buy opportunities without forced selling.
findings.numbers: Russell Investments: a typical multi-asset portfolio with 3.5% idle cash gives up about 0.20% a year (chart covers 1988-2017); its futures overlay added 0.19% a year to the total portfolio of one client with more than $10bn, before fees, and that figure includes the gain from carrying out decisions faster. The same document notes cash helped in falling markets such as 2000-2002. Wermers: non-share holdings cost US funds 0.7% a year, 1975-1994. Counter: actively managed share funds holding unusually high cash for their type beat low-cash peers by more than 2% a year (Simutin 2014).
findings.note: Numbers confirmed. Two wording corrections: (1) 'standard practice' is not stated anywhere I fetched; the only institutional evidence is one provider's marketing case study, quoted gross of fees; (2) the phrase 'equitising cash' does not appear in the Russell document, which says 'cash overlay'. Simutin's result is about cash above the level predicted for that fund, held by professional managers.

findings.claim: Where the idea comes from and how it is sized. The academic root is Treynor and Black (1973), whose model blends a small 'active portfolio' with a passive index fund. A 2005 pension trade article says pension funds took it up in the 1990s to spend their risk budget [allowed deviation from the index] where it might pay. Vanguard's guidance starts from the index and adds active only where the investor expects an edge after costs and can sit through lagging spells.
findings.numbers: Pension funds using core-satellite: 5% in 1995, 15% in 2000 (trade article, May 2005; it says 'research suggests' and names no source). Vanguard framework: four inputs (expected edge before costs, cost, active risk, tolerance for active risk); if the expected edge after costs is negative the answer is 100% index. Vanguard's Australian core-satellite model portfolios (target mixes, data at 31 Aug 2025), five risk levels: active 29%, 30%, 31%, 31%, 32%; index 70%, 69%, 68%, 68%, 67%; cash 1% in each.
findings.note: Treynor-Black citation confirmed on RePEc (no abstract there); the description of the model is confirmed only from Wikipedia, a secondary source. Vanguard Australia: I added up the extracted chart numbers for all five portfolios and they sum to 100 each; the active/passive labels are matched by their order in the extracted text and I could not view the chart image, so a visual check is still worthwhile. In that product the satellites are active funds chosen by a research firm (Lonsec), not individual shares, and the 1% cash is a platform minimum. It is a product brochure 'for adviser use only', an example of sizing rather than evidence that 30% is right.

findings.claim: The price of never sitting in cash: an always-invested portfolio takes market falls in full. These are the falls a core-satellite book would have ridden through with sale money returned to the index.
findings.numbers: S&P 500 index, price only: -49.1% from 24 Mar 2000 to 9 Oct 2002 (929 days); -56.8% from 9 Oct 2007 to 9 Mar 2009 (517 days); -33.9% from 19 Feb to 23 Mar 2020 (33 days); -25.4% from 3 Jan to 12 Oct 2022 (282 days). Day counts include weekends and holidays. The table lists 22 falls of 20% or more since 1928.
findings.note: All four rows and the count of 22 read directly from Table 2 of the Yardeni PDF (dated 28 Oct 2022, so nothing after that date is included).

findings.claim: (From the summary line) Shares have beaten cash roughly seven times in ten to three times in four, depending on the period measured, not a flat 'three years out of four'.
findings.numbers: 76% of the time over 1976-2022 (Vanguard, US shares versus 3-month Treasury bill). 68.89% of calendar years over 1929-2018 (Buzzacchi and Ghezzi, Table 2); in the remaining 31% of years shares averaged -10.80% while cash averaged +4.33%.
findings.note: The 76% figure is real but comes from a 47-year window. The longer record in a source the researcher already used gives a lower figure.

findings.claim: (From the cash section) As a rough scale: US shares averaged about 6.7 points a year more than cash over 1929-2018, so a book sitting half in cash gave up roughly 3.4 points a year on average. This is a backward-looking average. Vanguard's own forecast for the next ten years implies a much smaller gap over today's cash rate.
findings.numbers: 10.92% minus 4.18% = 6.74 points; half = 3.37 points (simple yearly averages, before tax and costs). Forward-looking: Vanguard's 10-year forecast for US shares is 4.2% to 6.2% a year (model run of 30 Jun 2026, lowered from 4.9%-6.9%); the 3-month US Treasury bill yielded 4.05% on 5 Oct 2026.
findings.note: Arithmetic checks out against the paper's Table 1. The qualifier is new: on Vanguard's forecast, shares are expected to beat today's bill rate by roughly 0.2 to 2.2 points a year, not 6.7. The comparison is rough (a ten-year forecast against a three-month rate that will change), and Vanguard notes valuations are poor predictors over short periods.

sources.note: 29 April 2026, paywalled. Only the opening sentence is visible: advisers favour core-satellite, 'but without structural and disciplined approaches, it can lead to a raft of unintended risks'. No figures visible; overlap, drift and cost details are NOT confirmed.

missing: The forward-looking cost of holding cash may be far smaller than the historical one. Vanguard's own model (run of 30 June 2026) forecasts US shares at 4.2% to 6.2% a year for the next ten years, lowered from 4.9%-6.9% (https://corporate.vanguard.com/content/corporatesite/us/en/corp/vemo/vemo-return-forecasts.html), while the 3-month US Treasury bill yielded 4.05% on 5 October 2026 (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DTB3). That implies a gap of roughly 0.2 to 2.2 points a year, against the 6.7-point historical average the researcher's '3.4 points a year for a half-cash book' sum is built on. It is a rough comparison (a ten-year forecast against a three-month rate), and forecasts are often wrong, but it comes from the same firm whose 1976-2022 study is the main evidence that cash is costly.

Shares have not beaten cash as often over the longer record as the 76% headline suggests. In a source the researcher already used, shares beat cash in 68.89% of calendar years from 1929 to 2018, and in the other 31% of years shares averaged -10.80% while cash averaged +4.33% (Table 2, https://mdpi-res.com/d_attachment/jrfm/jrfm-14-00250/article_deploy/jrfm-14-00250.pdf).

Sharpe's original hurdle was harsher than quoted, and the modern one is softer. The same paper reports that Sharpe needed 83% accuracy to beat simply holding shares (74% was against a fixed shares-and-cash mix), and that its own re-test used a 1% switching cost, not 2%. For 1973-2018 the average timer needed only 61%. With trading now nearly free, the 'seven in ten' rule may overstate the bar for one period and understate it for another (https://mdpi-res.com/d_attachment/jrfm/jrfm-14-00250/article_deploy/jrfm-14-00250.pdf).

The core and the satellites may be the same bet. Information technology was 40.10% of an S&P 500 index fund on 5 October 2026, with communication companies a further 9.85% (https://www.ishares.com/us/products/239726/ishares-core-sp-500-etf). Picks chosen on revenue and earnings growth tend to come from the same areas, so the structure can be less diversified than 'index plus picks' sounds. The overlap conclusion is reasoning from the sector figure.

The best evidence for conviction picks has shrunk in the authors' own hands. The April 2021 draft of 'Best Ideas' reports about 2.8% to 4.5% a year, not the 0.39% to 1.27% a month (roughly 5% to 15% a year) of the 2008 draft, and adds that 'the vast majority of the other stocks managers hold do not exhibit significant outperformance' (https://personal.lse.ac.uk/polk/research/bestideas.pdf). It covers professional fund managers, not private investors.

Private investors' own trading has been measured as a loss with complete records, not just a sample from one broker. Across every investor in Taiwan, individuals as a group lost 3.8 percentage points a year through trading, while institutions gained 1.5 (https://ideas.repec.org/a/oup/rfinst/v22y2009i2p609-632.html). This bears directly on the satellite sleeve and on the buy, add, trim, reload activity inside it.

An index core is not automatically a calm core. In the Morningstar report the researcher used, index-fund investors outside broad US shares had wider gaps than active-fund investors: international share index funds 1.6 points versus 0.8 for active; sector index funds 1.5 versus 1.2; sector ETFs 1.8. The near-zero gap applies to broad US share index funds only (Exhibit 8 and the ETF table, https://www.morningstar.com/content/cs-assets/v3/assets/blt9415ea4cc4157833/blt852a4301adc2f5db/6a7373d51f7b5ae2da78e1e8/US_Mind_the_Gap_2026.pdf).

Tax was left unresearched, and the basic US rules are easy to source. Gains on holdings kept one year or less are taxed as ordinary income, while longer holdings get rates of 0%, 15% or 20% (https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc409). A loss cannot be claimed if substantially identical shares are bought within 30 days before or after the sale (https://www.irs.gov/publications/p550). A structure that swaps between index and picks on short-term signals creates many such sales in a taxable account. Applies to US taxable accounts only.

There is published support for the worry that a single-stock sell signal is often a market-wide one: 'Correlation increases in bear markets, but not in bull markets' (Longin and Solnik, Journal of Finance 2001, https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/jfinan/v56y2001i2p649-676.html). It studies country markets rather than single shares against an index, so it supports the direction of the failure mode, not its size.

The three 'best days and worst days' authors disagree about what their own numbers mean, and the page should say so. Estrada: 'The odds against successful market timing are just staggering' (https://blog.iese.edu/jestrada/files/2012/06/BlackSwans.pdf). Faber, writing for his own fund firm in a paper that is not peer-reviewed, concludes that avoiding falling markets is 'possible, and beneficial' (https://mebfaber.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/SSRN-id1908469.pdf). Asness says the effect is symmetric and the real case against timing is that it is hard to do (https://www.aqr.com/Insights/Perspectives/So-What-If-You-Miss-the-Markets-N-Best-Days).

The J.P. Morgan figures on the page should come from the primary document, which is available and differs from the trade-press versions: $10,000 from 2 Jan 2006 to 31 Dec 2025 grew at 11.0% a year fully invested, 6.6% without the 10 best days and 3.8% without the 20 best; six (not seven) of the 10 best days fell within two weeks of the 10 worst (slide 41, https://am.jpmorgan.com/content/dam/jpm-am-aem/global/en/insights/retirement-insights/guide-to-retirement-us.pdf).

The institutional case for giving idle cash index exposure rests on one vendor's marketing case study: the 0.19% a year is quoted before fees and includes the benefit of carrying out decisions faster, and the document calls the technique a 'cash overlay', not 'equitising cash' (https://russellinvestments.com/-/media/files/us/institutions/case-studies/health-system-improved-portfolio-returns.pdf). No independent study of the practice was found by either of us.

The published Vanguard example of a roughly 30% satellite sleeve uses active funds picked by a research firm, not individual shares, and is a product brochure rather than a finding about the right size (https://fund-docs.vanguard.com/AU-Adviser_guide-Vanguard_Core-Satellite_Model_Portfolios_with_LIS.pdf). Vanguard's sizing framework says the answer is 100% index whenever the expected edge after costs is negative (https://www.vanguard.co.uk/professional/vanguard-365/investment-knowledge/portfolio-construction/active-passive-framework).

Still not verified by either of us: S&P's long-run scorecard figures (share of large-company funds trailing over 15 to 20 years), because spglobal.com refused access on three addresses; the detail of Vanguard's 2026 Australian adviser report, because the only article is paywalled (https://www.financialstandard.com.au/news/core-satellite-models-can-only-be-effective-with-purpose-vanguard-179812344); Schwab's market-timing study, whose page returned an authorisation error; and what Interactive Brokers currently pays on idle cash, whose rates page returned 403. Web search was unavailable to me (the session's search allowance was already spent), so replacement addresses could only be tried directly.
failure_modes_checked: Deep market falls. The structure is close to 100% in shares by design, so it would have taken the full -49.1% of 2000-2002 and -56.8% of 2007-2009 (S&P 500, price only) [yardeni2022]. Russell's own case study says idle cash helped in 2000-2002 [russell2018], and in Vanguard's worst 5% of one-year outcomes the fully invested path ended lower than the drip-feed path ($82,947 versus $85,906 on $100,000) [vanguard2023]. All confirmed.

When the picks are the weak part. If the satellites lag the index, the whole structure does worse than simply holding the index, and the larger the sleeve the larger the shortfall. 79% of professional large-company funds lagged in 2025 (news report of S&P's scorecard; S&P's own page would not open) [spiva2025_news]; the most active private traders earned 11.4% a year against 17.9% for the market [barber_odean2000]; in Taiwan private investors as a group lost 3.8 points a year to their trading [barber_lee_liu_odean2009]; 96% of US shares together only matched Treasury bills [bessembinder2018]. The best evidence for conviction picks is smaller than first quoted: about 2.8% to 4.5% a year for professionals' best ideas, with no significant edge in their other holdings [best_ideas2021].

When a sell signal on one stock is really a signal about the whole market. Roughly 60-80% of the biggest up and down days came once the market was already below its 200-day average [faber2011_ssrn], and markets move together more closely in falling markets than in rising ones [longin_solnik2001, a study of country markets]. Moving sale money straight into the index at that moment may swap one falling holding for another. This last step is still reasoning from the evidence, not a tested result; no study of this exact rule was found.

Behaviour under stress. The jumpier the fund, the bigger the gap between what the fund earned and what its investors earned: 2.1 points a year in the most volatile fifth versus 0.4 in the calmest, and wider in easy-to-trade ETFs (1.6) than in ordinary funds (1.2) [morningstar2026]. Two qualifiers: an academic re-check puts the part that is truly bad timing at only 0.10% a year [fulkerson2026], and index funds outside broad US shares showed wider gaps than active funds, so a sector or theme fund used as the 'core' would not get the benefit.

Cash is not always dead weight. Professional managers holding unusually high cash beat low-cash peers by more than 2% a year [simutin2014], and the advantage of being invested shrinks as the interest paid on cash rises [vanguard2023]. Today that matters: the 3-month Treasury bill yielded 4.05% on 5 Oct 2026 [fred_dtb3], while Vanguard's ten-year forecast for US shares is 4.2% to 6.2% a year [vanguard_vcmm2026]. Cash also beat shares in about 31% of calendar years from 1929 to 2018 [buzzacchi2021].

Doubling up, and satellites without a clear job. Information technology companies were 40.10% of an S&P 500 index fund on 5 Oct 2026 [ishares_ivv], so satellites chosen for fast revenue and earnings growth are likely to add to what the core already holds most of. That overlap point is reasoning from the sector figure, not a tested result. Vanguard's 2026 review of Australian adviser portfolios is reported to warn of 'a raft of unintended risks' when core-satellite is run without discipline, but the article is paywalled and none of its detail (overlap, drift, cost, number of satellites) could be confirmed [financialstandard2026].

Switching costs and tax. Sharpe assumed 2% per switch and the 2021 re-test 1% [buzzacchi2021]; trading is far cheaper now, but in a taxable US account every move between core and satellite is a sale. Gains on holdings kept one year or less are taxed as ordinary income rather than at the lower long-term rates [irs_tc409], and a loss cannot be claimed if the same share is bought back within 30 days [irs_p550]. These are US rules and apply only to taxable accounts; no study was found that measures this drag for a core-satellite book run on technical signals.

research.plain_summary: Stay in a broad index fund by default and step aside into Treasury bills [interest-paying cash] only when the index drops below its own 10-month (about 200-day) average price. Over a century this roughly matched buy-and-hold returns while about halving the worst losses, and it was invested 70-80% of the time. The one thing the evidence says: it is insurance, not a return booster. It paid off in 1929, 2000 and 2008, but since 2009 fast rebounds have made it sell low and buy back higher, and a real fund running a version of it has trailed the S&P 500 by about five points a year since 2015.
research.how_it_works: The default position is fully invested in a broad index fund (for example an S&P 500 fund); cash is the exception, not the resting state. On a fixed schedule (the best-known version checks once, on the last trading day of each month) you compare the index price with its moving average [the average closing price over the last 10 months, or roughly 200 trading days]. If the price is above the average you stay in; if it is below you sell and hold Treasury bills [short-term US government IOUs that pay interest] until the price closes back above the average, at which point you must buy back in, even if that is at a higher price than you sold. An optional second lock adds market breadth [a count of how many individual stocks or industries are themselves in uptrends]: you leave only if the index is below its average AND most of its parts are also in downtrends, which makes exits rarer. The rule cannot spot tops or bottoms; it reacts after the fact, so in real bear markets it has typically sold a little below the peak and bought back well above the low, and it pays for that protection through many small whipsaws [selling on a dip and then having to buy back higher].
research.sitting_in_cash_relevance:
This structure attacks the cash problem by flipping the default. Instead of 'in cash until I find a reason to buy', it is 'fully invested in the index unless one written rule says out', and the same rule forces the buy-back, so there is no decision to hesitate over. The evidence on how much cash that leaves: historically these rules were out only about 20-30% of the time [S1, S7, S15], and about 18% of months since 2017 on our own arithmetic [S23]; with a breadth second lock the one available test shows under 8% of the time out [S15]. So as a home for money that would otherwise wait on the sidelines, it sharply limits cash time and removes the judgment call that causes missed moves.

The uncomfortable part, which the page should say plainly: over the last decade even that modest time out was expensive. Nine of the last ten exits were bought back higher [S23], and the live fund that follows a 200-day rule trailed the S&P 500 by about five points a year from 2015 to mid-2026 [S9]. In other words the evidence suggests the 'always invested' half of this structure is what fixes missed opportunities; the 'exit rule' half is insurance against a 1929-, 2000- or 2008-style collapse and has cost more than it has paid since 2009.

Where the evidence points on design choices (for the page to present, not as instructions): check monthly rather than daily [S3]; a buffer or smoothing cuts false signals [S16, S7]; a breadth lock makes exits rarer but allows a deeper worst loss [S15]; taxes matter a great deal outside a tax-sheltered account [S1, S22].

Fit with Alan's standing rule: this is a pure 'when' rule applied to the whole market. It has no 'what' in it, so it does not replace his fundamentals-based stock selection; it would sit underneath it as the place idle money lives while he waits for stock ideas.

Faber's results table (Figure 7) is an image our text extraction could not read. The volatility (12.0% vs 17.9%), Sharpe (0.55 vs 0.32) and maximum drawdown (-50.3% vs -83.5%) figures are CXO Advisory's transcription. The paper's own text gives 42.24% for the rule's 1929-32 loss; we could not reconcile that with the -50.3% maximum and suggest checking the PDF by eye before publishing either number.

Siegel's 'Stocks for the Long Run' was not read directly. The 1886-2012 figures (9.7% / 9.4% / 8.1%) are as reported by Ben Carlson (S7); more precise versions (9.73% / 9.39% / 8.11%) appeared only in search-result snippets of a Validea blog page that now redirects. Our own arithmetic on FRED data (key finding 7) has not been independently checked. It uses the price index only (no dividends on either side), month-end closes, no trading costs or taxes, and Treasury-bill interest from a monthly average rate. It covers only Aug 2017-Sep 2026 because the free FRED series holds ten years. It should be recomputed with total-return data before the page relies on the 7.2% vs 13.1% figures.

Pacer's exact triggers (five consecutive business days above/below the 200-day average; 100% Treasury bills when the average itself is falling) were seen only in a search snippet, not on a page we opened; the SEC filing confirms only the three exposure states and the 200-business-day average. The exact dates of the fund's switches in 2020 and 2023 were not found.

Goulding, Harvey and Mazzoleni (S12) and both AQR papers (S13, S14) were read as abstract or summary pages only; no figures for how much more frequent trend breaks became were obtained. A statement that the SG Trend Index Sharpe ratio fell to 0.05 in 2010-2018 from 0.28 since 2000 appeared only in a search snippet and is not used.

No independent, peer-reviewed, out-of-sample test was found of the exact combination in the brief: S&P 500 below its 200-day average AND weak breadth measured as percent of stocks above their 200-day average or the advance/decline line. The only breadth-as-exit-filter test found is VanEck's vendor backtest (industry-level breadth, fitted 150/400-day settings, six signals, ends Aug 2019, so it has not been shown through 2020, 2022, 2023, 2025 or 2026).

Wayne Whaley's 2010 Dow Award study of breadth thrusts ('Planes, Trains and Automobiles') could not be read; the CMT Association page is only a video landing page. Thrust thresholds seen in search snippets are not used.

The US wash-sale rule (a loss is not deductible if substantially identical shares are bought within 30 days before or after the sale; relevant when the rule exits at a loss and re-enters within a month, which happened several times above) is stated from general knowledge. Gannon and Blum (2006) after-tax figures (10.62% to 6.72% to 6.27%) are as quoted by Faber; the original was not read and reflects older US tax rates.

findings.claim: FOR: In Faber's back-test [a rule replayed on past prices, not real money] of the S&P 500 from 1901 to 2012, the once-a-month 10-month-average rule returned slightly more than buy-and-hold and cut the worst losses by roughly 40-50%. That is before taxes and trading costs, and the rule still lagged the index in about half of all calendar years.
findings.numbers: Faber 2013 update, paper text: compounded return 10.18% a year (rule) vs 9.32% (buy-and-hold); invested 'approximately 70% of the time' with 'less than one round-trip trade per year'; 1929-32 loss 42.24% vs 83.66%; 2000-02 loss 16.52% vs 44.73% (rule exited October 2000); rule exited 31 Dec 2007 and avoided the 50.95% fall of 2008-09. CXO Advisory's transcription of the paper's table: volatility [how bumpy the ride is] 12.0% vs 17.9%, Sharpe ratio [return per unit of bumpiness] 0.55 vs 0.32, and WORST LOSS OVER THE WHOLE PERIOD -50.3% vs -83.5%. Across five asset classes returns were on average 60% lower and volatility 30% higher when a market was below its 10-month average. 'Taxes, commissions, and slippage are excluded.'
findings.note: Every number in the researcher's version was found on the pages cited (Faber PDF pp. 22-26 and 38, text extracted from the fetched PDF; CXO page fetched). One wording fix: 'roughly halved the worst losses' holds for the 1929-32 episode in the paper's text (42.24% vs 83.66%), but the paper's summary table, as transcribed by CXO, gives the rule's worst loss over the full 112 years as -50.3% against -83.5%, a cut of about 40%. A reader should not be told the rule's worst loss was about 42%; the table says about 50%. The table itself is an image I could not read, so the -50.3% figure rests on CXO's transcription.

findings.claim: FOR, with a catch (independent academic test): UK academics found that on the S&P 500 from July 1988 to June 2011 a 200-day-average rule checked only at month-end beat buy-and-hold after trading costs, that checking once a month did better than checking every day, and that bolting on stop-losses [automatic sell orders after a set percentage fall] added nothing. The catch, from the same paper's tables: the same 200-day rule checked DAILY earned less than buy-and-hold, and over the longer 1952-2011 period the 10-month rule earned about the same return as buy-and-hold. The gain was a smoother ride, not more money.
findings.numbers: Clare, Seaton, Smith, Thomas (Journal of Asset Management 2013), 0.2% cost per buy and per sell. Jul 1988-Jun 2011: buy-and-hold 9.49% a year, volatility 18.16%, Sharpe 0.31; 200-day rule checked at month-end 10.66%, volatility 11.89%, Sharpe 0.58; 200-day rule checked daily 7.68%, Sharpe 0.34. Sharpe range for daily-checked moving-average rules -0.79 to 0.54; for month-end rules 0.06 to 0.59. Jan 1952-Jun 2011: buy-and-hold 10.54%, volatility 14.65%, Sharpe 0.39; 10-month rule 10.50%, volatility 10.57%, Sharpe 0.54; 12-month rule 11.01%, Sharpe 0.58 (the best of nine lengths tested). The 1988-2011 sample ends right after two roughly 50% bear markets.
findings.note: All of the researcher's numbers match Tables 1-3 of the accepted version (text extracted from the fetched PDF). Corrected for selective quoting: the researcher cited only the 12-month rule ('over 11.00%', Sharpe 0.58), which is the best-performing length in Table 3. The 10-month rule, the one this structure actually uses, returned 10.50% against 10.54% for buy-and-hold in the same table, and the daily-checked 200-day rule returned 7.68% against 9.49%. The stop-loss conclusion is the authors' own wording: 'a change of trend is the best stop loss'.

findings.claim: TIME OUT OF THE MARKET: historically these rules have been out of the market roughly a fifth to a third of the time. In one vendor back-test, a rule that exits on breadth alone [it sells only when most of the market's industries are in downtrends, and ignores the index's own average] was out under a tenth of the time.
findings.numbers: Faber: invested 'approximately 70% of the time', 'less than one round-trip trade per year' (S&P 500, 1901-2012). Carlson: S&P 500 about two-thirds of the time above and one-third below its 200-day average since 1928. Zakamulin as summarised by CXO: timing rules 'are in cash about a third of the time' (1860-2009). VanEck: 50-day/200-day crossover rule invested 78.20% of the time, breadth rule 92.50%, May 1991-Aug 2019. Own arithmetic on FRED data, which I recomputed independently and reproduced: the 10-month rule was out 20 of 110 months (18.2%), Aug 2017-Sep 2026.
findings.note: Numbers all confirmed on fetched pages, and the FRED arithmetic reproduces exactly. The correction is to the label 'second lock'. VanEck did not test 'index below its average AND weak breadth'. It tested a breadth-only exit (sell when 13 or more of 24 industries are bearish) as a replacement for the index-level rule. Nobody has shown what a true two-condition lock would have done.

findings.claim: AGAINST (long run): once realistic trading costs and honest out-of-sample testing [testing on data the rule was not tuned on] are applied, most of the return edge disappears. What survives is lower risk, and the benefit comes from a handful of big bear markets separated by decades of lagging.
findings.numbers: Siegel as reported by Carlson: Dow Jones Industrials, 1886-2012, 200-day rule with a 1% band: 9.7% a year vs 9.4% buy-and-hold, falling to 8.1% once transaction costs are included. Zakamulin as summarised by CXO Advisory (post dated 23 April 2014): data Jan 1926-Dec 2012, out-of-sample 1930-2012, 0.5% one-way cost on stock indexes: only three of eight rule/index combinations beat buy-and-hold, MEASURED BY SHARPE RATIO [risk-adjusted return, not raw return]; the S&P moving-average rule improved net Sharpe by 10%; stock timing 'underperform[ed] buy-and-hold throughout the 25-year period from 1975 through 1999'; outperformance driven by 1930-31, 1973-74, 2001-02 and 2007-08. Zakamulin 2015 as summarised by CXO (S&P Composite Jan 1860-Dec 2009, 0.25% one-way cost): mean returns of the timing rules were lower than buy-and-hold, Sharpe ratios generally higher; over 5- or 10-year horizons the rules were 'about equally likely to outperform and underperform' (CXO adds that the average win was bigger than the average loss, and longer horizons improved the odds). Zakamulin's abstract: performance 'is highly overstated, to say the least'.
findings.note: Each figure was seen on a fetched page, but all of them are second-hand: Siegel's book and Zakamulin's full papers were not read by either of us (SSRN returns 403). Two precision points to carry onto the page: the '3 of 8' count is on Sharpe ratio, not on return; and CXO's summary of the 2015 paper includes two points in the rule's favour (bigger average win than loss, better odds over longer horizons) that the researcher left out. The Wikipedia line (S8) that the 200-day rule 'does not improve returns nor reduce risk' for the Dow conflicts with Faber's reading of the same book, which says risk-adjusted returns stayed higher after costs; do not lean on S8.

findings.claim: AGAINST (real money, the strongest evidence): a live fund that runs a version of a 200-day rule on the S&P 500 (Pacer Trendpilot US Large Cap, ticker PTLC) has trailed simply holding the S&P 500 by about five percentage points a year over its eleven years. It did help in the 2022 decline, but by far less than it had given up elsewhere.
findings.numbers: Pacer fact sheet, data as of 30 Jun 2026: launched 11 Jun 2015, total expenses 0.60%. Annualised, fund NAV vs S&P 500: since launch 8.99% vs 14.11%; 10 years 11.18% vs 15.51%; 5 years 10.21% vs 13.41%; 1 year 16.02% vs 22.32%; 2026 year-to-date 4.82% vs 10.21%. Its index before fees 9.13% since launch, so fees explain very little of the gap. SEC annual reports (fiscal years end 30 April), fund vs S&P 500: May 2021-Apr 2022 +3.48% vs +0.21% (four switches between 25 Feb and 28 Apr 2022); May 2022-Apr 2023 +4.20% vs +2.66% (in Treasury bills 28 Apr 2022 to 26 Jan 2023). Over those two years together the fund gained about 7.8% vs 2.9% for the index (my arithmetic from the two filings).
findings.note: Fact-sheet numbers confirmed line by line (text extracted from the fetched PDF). The 2022 claim is confirmed and strengthened by a second SEC filing the researcher did not cite (fiscal 2023, source N3). One caution for the page: this fund is not the simple once-a-month rule. It moves between three positions (100% stocks, 50/50, 100% Treasury bills) on business-day signals, so it is evidence about 'a version of' the rule. The exact trigger wording (five consecutive business days) is shown only as an image on the fact sheet and is not in the SEC filing text I could read, so it stays unverified.

findings.claim: WHY IT HAS STRUGGLED SINCE 2009: the rule is wrong most of the times it sells, and researchers tie the weak recent record to more frequent sharp reversals and fewer long declines, not to the idea being permanently broken. Note that the two academic explanations come from studies of funds that follow trends across many markets at once, not of a single stock-index in/out rule.
findings.numbers: VanEck: S&P 500, Jul 1955-Aug 2019, 50-day/200-day crossover rule made 36 exits and only 20% of them beat staying invested; 9.40% vs 10.12% a year; worst loss -25.21% vs -50.95% (VanEck used price-only returns before 1988 and total returns after, so the return comparison is rough). Hill: S&P 500, Jan 1994-Jan 2019, 'some 180' crossings of the 200-day average (about 7 a year), 90 completed signals, 20 winners averaging +13.69% and 70 losers averaging -1.32%. Carlson: 150 crossings since 1997 (written May 2018) but only 11 corrections of 10% or worse. Maggiulli: 'going back to 1950, the 200-Day MA strategy outperformed Buy & Hold up until after the GFC'; 1950-2024 median one-year S&P 500 return 12.8% when the rule was out vs 9.4% when in. Goulding, Harvey and Mazzoleni (Financial Analysts Journal 80(1)): 'an increase in the frequency of trend breaks' after 2008. AQR (Journal of Portfolio Management 2020): lower returns 'due to fewer large moves across markets', with 'little evidence to suggest this is a permanent structural change'. Neither academic page gives figures.
findings.note: Every figure and quotation was found on the fetched page. Two qualifiers added to the claim: the academic papers are about multi-market trend funds, and VanEck's long-run return comparison mixes price-only and dividend-included data.

findings.claim: V-SHAPED RECOVERIES, OWN ARITHMETIC (not a published study, but independently reproduced by the fact-checker from the same public data): applying the month-end 10-month rule to free FRED data shows that in the last nine years 9 of 10 exits were bought back at a higher price than they were sold. The only exit bought back lower was 2022.
findings.numbers: S&P 500 price index (no dividends), month-end closes, Aug 2017-Sep 2026 (110 months). Exit month to re-entry month, re-entry price vs exit price: Oct 2018 to Nov 2018 +1.8%; Dec 2018 to Feb 2019 +11.1%; May 2019 to Jun 2019 +6.9%; Feb 2020 to May 2020 +3.0%; Feb 2022 to Mar 2022 +3.6%; Apr 2022 to Nov 2022 -1.3%; Dec 2022 to Jan 2023 +6.2%; Oct 2023 to Nov 2023 +8.9%; Mar 2025 to May 2025 +5.3%; Mar 2026 to Apr 2026 +10.4%. Result: 7.2% a year for the rule (with Treasury-bill interest while out) vs 13.1% a year for holding, both before dividends, costs and taxes. On daily data: 56 crossings of the 200-day average (about 6 a year) and 18.8% of days closed below it, 24 Jul 2017-5 Oct 2026. End-Sep 2026 close 7,651.54 vs 10-month average 7,230.78, so the rule reads 'in'.
findings.note: I downloaded both FRED series myself and recomputed everything from scratch in memory: 20 of 110 months out, the same ten exit/re-entry pairs to the decimal, 7.16% vs 13.13% a year, 56 crossings, 18.76% of days below. It all matches. Limits that must stay on the page: nine years only, one real bear market in the window, price index without dividends (including them would widen the gap slightly, because the holder collects every dividend and the rule misses some), no costs or taxes.

findings.claim: BREADTH INSTEAD OF THE INDEX AVERAGE: the only test found of exiting on breadth [selling only when most of the market's industries are themselves in downtrends] halved the number of exits and kept the investor in the market far more, at the price of a deeper worst loss. It tested breadth as a replacement for the index rule, not as a second lock on top of it, and it is a vendor back-test with fitted settings and only six signals, so treat it as a hypothesis, not proof.
findings.numbers: VanEck (Schassler and Schafer, Nov 2019), S&P 500, 31 May 1991-31 Aug 2019. Breadth rule (sell when 13 or more of the 24 S&P 500 industries are bearish, using 150-day and 400-day averages 'selected using a proprietary statistical process'; signal must persist five trading days): 10.95% a year, worst loss -28.67%, invested 92.50% of the time, 6 exits of which 50% helped. 50-day/200-day crossover: 9.74%, -16.30%, 78.20%, 12 exits of which 25% helped. Buy-and-hold: 9.62%, -50.95%. Test ends Aug 2019. Related: Zaremba and co-authors (Economic Modelling 97, 2021) find breadth predicts returns across 64 countries, 1973-2018, and say it 'may be employed for equity allocation and market timing' but that frequent rebalancing 'can lead to higher transaction costs that may affect profitability'. Breadth thrusts [sudden bursts where almost all stocks rise together]: Hill counts 'just 8 signals' in 40 years, and the NY Composite made a new low after the October 2015 signal. Smoothing: using a 5-day average instead of the daily close cut signals from 90 to 34 over 1994-2019 (Hill).
findings.note: All numbers confirmed in the fetched VanEck PDF and the Hill and Zaremba pages. Corrected for framing: the researcher described this as 'exit only when most of the market's parts are ALSO in downtrends', implying two conditions. VanEck's rule has one condition (breadth) and is compared against the crossover rule, not combined with it. The exact two-lock design in the brief remains untested in anything either of us found. Also softened: the Zaremba abstract does mention market timing as a possible use, so 'not an exit filter' overstated it; it is still not a test of an exit rule on one index.

findings.claim: TAXES AND FRICTIONS: the published results leave taxes out. In an ordinary taxable account each exit of a core position realises its accumulated gains, and US gains on positions held a year or less are taxed at ordinary-income rates. Faber's own estimate is that the extra tax drag from the higher trading is real but modest, because the rule's losing trades tend to be short and its winning trades long. Commissions on a liquid index fund are small by comparison; the bigger hidden cost is buying back higher. A US wash-sale rule [a loss cannot be deducted if you rebuy the same thing within 30 days] can also bite when the rule sells at a loss and re-enters a month later.
findings.numbers: Faber: 'Taxes, commissions, and slippage are excluded'; a normal rebalanced portfolio turns over [share of the portfolio traded per year] about 20%, 'the system has a turnover of almost 70%'; citing Gannon and Blum (2006) for a top-bracket US investor in the S&P 500 since 1961: 10.62% before tax, 6.72% after tax at 20% turnover, 6.27% at 70% turnover ('an additional haircut of less than 50 basis points' [under half a percentage point a year]); 'the system results in a high number of short-term capital losses, and a large percentage of long-term capital gains'; 'the obvious solution for individuals is to trade the system in a tax-deferred account'. IRS Topic 409 (tax years beginning in 2025): more than one year is long-term, taxed at 0%, 15% or 20%; 'net short-term capital gains are subject to taxation as ordinary income at graduated tax rates'. IRS Publication 550 (2025): 'A wash sale occurs when you sell or trade stock or securities at a loss and within 30 days before or after the sale you buy substantially identical stock or securities'; the disallowed loss is added to the cost of the new shares. Siegel via Carlson: costs took 1.6 points a year (9.7% down to 8.1%), Dow 1886-2012. Clare and co-authors assume 0.20% per trade; Zakamulin 0.25% to 0.5%.
findings.note: Quotations and figures confirmed in the Faber PDF (pp. 22, 35-36), IRS Topic 409 and IRS Publication 550. Two corrections. First, the researcher left out Faber's own qualifier that short trades are mostly losses and long trades mostly gains, and that the Gannon and Blum figures put the extra tax cost of 70% turnover at under half a point a year; without that, the paragraph overstates the tax penalty. Faber's turnover figure is quoted in his section on the five-asset-class system, not the S&P-only test, and the Gannon and Blum numbers use older US tax rates and were not read in the original. Second, the wash-sale rule, which the researcher listed as unverified, is now confirmed from the IRS page. Tax treatment depends on Alan's country and account type, which are unknown.

missing: Real money in a fast crash made things worse, not better. SEC filing for the year to 30 April 2020: the Pacer fund moved to 50/50 on 12 March 2020 and to 100% Treasury bills on 13 March 2020, after most of the COVID fall, and returned -10.71% for the year while the S&P 500 returned +0.86%. https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1616668/000139834420013455/fp0054195_ncsr.htm

It then missed part of the rebound. SEC filing for the year to 30 April 2021: the fund did not return to stocks until 2 June 2020 and returned +36.86% against +45.98% for the S&P 500. Compounding the two filed years (my arithmetic): about +22% for the fund vs +47% for the index. https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1616668/000139834421014146/fp0066631_ncsr.htm

The one bear market since launch paid back only a little. SEC filing for the year to 30 April 2023: the fund sat in Treasury bills from 28 April 2022 to 26 January 2023 and returned +4.20% vs +2.66%. Combined with the prior year (+3.48% vs +0.21%), the 2022 protection was worth roughly five points in total, against about 25 points lost around the 2020 crash. https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1616668/000139834423012671/fp0083941-3_ncsr.htm

More live whipsaws on file. Year to April 2024: +19.96% vs +22.66%, including a one-week trip to 50/50 (1 to 8 November 2023). https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1616668/000139834424012449/fp0087829-4_ncsr.htm  Year to April 2019: +8.65% vs +13.49% after sitting out the late-2018 dip. https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1616668/000139834419011668/fp0042510_ncsr.htm  Across the six filed years May 2018 to April 2024 the fund compounded at about 9.4% a year vs about 13.2% for the S&P 500 (my arithmetic from the six filings).

The supportive academic paper is less supportive than quoted. In Clare and co-authors' own tables the 200-day rule checked daily earned 7.68% a year against 9.49% for buy-and-hold (1988-2011, after 0.2% costs), and over 1952-2011 the 10-month rule earned 10.50% against 10.54%. The researcher quoted only the best-performing 12-month setting. The benefit shown is lower volatility (10.57% vs 14.65%), not higher return. https://openaccess.city.ac.uk/17842/8/BLACKBOX%20%20%20SSRN-id2126476.pdf

Faber's own paper softens the tax objection and also contradicts the Wikipedia line on Siegel. On taxes: the system 'results in a high number of short-term capital losses, and a large percentage of long-term capital gains', and the cited extra drag from higher turnover is under half a point a year. On Siegel: Faber reports that on the Dow timing kept a higher risk-adjusted return even after all costs, and on the Nasdaq since 1972 beat buy-and-hold by over 4 points a year. https://mebfaber.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/SSRN-id962461.pdf

The breadth evidence is thinner than presented. VanEck's breadth rule replaces the index rule rather than adding a second lock; its settings were chosen by 'a proprietary statistical process'; and its long-run crossover comparison uses price-only returns before 1988. No test of the actual two-condition design was found. https://www.vaneck.com/globalassets/home/us/insights/blogs/guided-allocation/market-breadth-whitepaper_2019.11.pdf

The comparison with 100% stocks flatters the rule. Zakamulin's long-run study (as summarised by CXO) attributes the lower risk to the rules being 'in cash about a third of the time', with lower average returns than buy-and-hold. https://www.cxoadvisory.com/technical-trading/market-timing-with-moving-averages-over-the-very-long-run  A vendor study that uses the fairer yardstick of half stocks, half Treasury bills still finds a benefit before costs, but also shows the rule losing its entire lead over buy-and-hold for twenty years, 1942-1962. https://blog.thinknewfound.com/2018/03/protect-participate-managing-drawdowns-with-trend-following/

Small changes in the settings can change the outcome a great deal. In a related monthly trend-switching strategy, moving the look-back from 10 months to 9 months cut the ten-year total return from 146.1% to 43.1%, and in 2010 the two versions returned +12.2% and -9.31%. This is a different strategy from the plain 10-month rule, so treat it as a warning about fragility, not a measurement of it. https://blog.thinknewfound.com/2019/01/fragility-case-study-dual-momentum-gem/

Evidence that the 'be invested by default' half does the work on its own. Vanguard found that putting money to work immediately beat phasing it in 68% of the time and beat staying in cash 70% of the time over one-year periods (MSCI World, 1976-2022). This bears directly on Alan's complaint about sitting in cash and needs no exit rule at all. https://corporate.vanguard.com/content/dam/corp/research/pdf/cost_averaging_invest_now_or_temporarily_hold_your_cash.pdf

US wash-sale rule, now confirmed at source: a loss is not deductible if substantially identical shares are bought within 30 days before or after the sale; the loss is added to the cost of the new shares instead. Six of the ten exits in the FRED arithmetic re-entered the following month. https://www.irs.gov/publications/p550

Limits of this check, to be stated on the page: the web-search allowance was already used up in this session, so I could only fetch addresses I already knew and could not search for newer contrary studies. Not reachable: SSRN (403), the Pacer product page (403), a Morningstar article on tactical funds (403), and Pacer's 2025 and 2026 annual reports (too large to load), so the fund's switch dates for March-May 2025 and March-April 2026 and its exact five-day trigger wording remain unverified. Faber's results table is an image, so the -50.3% worst-loss figure rests on CXO's transcription. Siegel's book and Zakamulin's full papers were not read by anyone; their numbers are second-hand.
failure_modes_checked: V-shaped recoveries (confirmed, and worse in real money than the researcher showed): the rule sells after the fall and buys back higher. Reproduced arithmetic on FRED data: 9 of the 10 month-end exits between 2018 and 2026 were re-entered at a higher price, including Dec 2018 to Feb 2019 (+11.1%), Oct 2023 to Nov 2023 (+8.9%) and Mar 2026 to Apr 2026 (+10.4%) [S23]. Live fund: PTLC went to Treasury bills on 12-13 March 2020 and back to stocks on 2 June 2020; over the two fiscal years May 2019 to April 2021 it gained about 22% while the S&P 500 gained about 47% (my compounding of the filed annual figures) [N1, N2]. Academic work on multi-market trend funds links post-2008 weakness to more frequent turning points [S12].

Long, calm bull markets (confirmed): there is nothing to dodge, so every exit is a cost. Stock timing lagged buy-and-hold throughout 1975-1999 [S5]; Faber notes the rule lagged in a 1990s-style bull market and in roughly half of all years [S1]; a separate back-test shows the rule giving up its entire lead over the 20 years 1942-1962 [N7]; the live Pacer fund returned 8.99% vs 14.11% a year from June 2015 to June 2026 [S9].

Choppy, sideways markets (confirmed): repeated crossings of the average produce a string of small losses. Faber's FAQ: a market that oscillates 'can be a poor market for trendfollowers' because of whipsaws [selling on a dip and having to buy back higher] [S1]; Hill counted 70 losing signals out of 90 on the daily 200-day rule, 1994-2019 [S16]; VanEck found only 20% of 36 exits beat staying invested, 1955-2019 [S15]. Real-money example: PTLC went half to cash on 1 November 2023 and back on 8 November 2023 [N4].

Crashes that are too fast (confirmed and strengthened): a slow average cannot react to a one-day or three-week collapse, and can make the result worse than doing nothing. VanEck: no protection on Black Monday, 19 October 1987 [S15]. Pacer wrote in April 2020 that its large-cap fund was 'slower to move' in 'one of the fastest selloffs in market history' [S11]; the SEC filing shows it sold on 12-13 March 2020 after most of the fall, and for the fiscal year to April 2020 it lost 10.71% while the S&P 500 gained 0.86% [N1].
Late at both ends even when it works (confirmed): in 2007-09 the month-end signal sold '6% or so below the peak' and bought back 'roughly 20% off the lows' [S20].

The payoff arrives rarely, so patience runs out first (confirmed): gains are concentrated in 1930-31, 1973-74, 2001-02 and 2007-08 [S5]; over five- or ten-year windows the rule was about as likely to trail as to beat the market on a risk-adjusted basis [S6]; after the 2000 exit it took about 18 months before the exit was clearly right [S19]. Carlson: 'an insurance strategy where sometimes you're forced to pay the premium without the protection' and 'You have to follow the rules for it to work' [S20].

Back-test flattery and fragile settings (confirmed and extended): Zakamulin argues published results contain 'a considerable data-mining bias' [choosing the settings that happened to work in the past] and ignore frictions [S4]. Faber says the model 'was published only as a simple example' and his firm does not run client money with those exact parameters [S21]. In Clare's tables the 12-month rule looks better than the 10-month rule and the daily-checked 200-day rule actually trails buy-and-hold [S3]. In a related monthly switching strategy, a 9-month instead of a 10-month look-back changed the ten-year result from +146% to +43% [N8].

Taxes in an ordinary taxable account (confirmed, with a qualifier): published results exclude them [S1]; exits realise gains, and US gains on holdings of a year or less are taxed as ordinary income [S22]; a loss on an exit followed by a re-entry within 30 days can fall under the US wash-sale rule [S26]. Qualifier from Faber himself: the rule's short trades are mostly losses and its long trades mostly gains, and the extra tax drag he cites is under half a point a year [S1]. Applies to US taxable accounts only; Alan's tax position is unknown.

Breadth trade-off (confirmed, re-labelled): in VanEck's test a breadth-only exit had fewer false exits but a deeper worst loss (-28.67% vs -16.30% for the plain crossover rule) [S15]. It was tested as a replacement for the index rule, not as a second lock; the two-lock version has no published test that either of us found. Breadth-thrust signals are too rare to rely on (8 in 40 years) and have failed (new low after the October 2015 signal) [S17].

Not every index responds the same way (confirmed in part): Hill reports the 200-day approach 'tested pretty good' on the Nasdaq 100 but 'did not fare well at all' on the Dow Industrials and Russell 2000 [S16]. For Siegel's Dow and Nasdaq results use Faber's and Carlson's accounts (Dow: 9.7% before costs, 8.1% after, vs 9.4% buy-and-hold; Nasdaq since 1972: timing ahead by over 4 points a year after costs) [S1, S7] rather than the Wikipedia sentence, which contradicts Faber on the risk point [S8].

Wrong yardstick (added by fact-checker): a rule that sits in cash a fifth to a third of the time will always look calmer than 100% stocks. The fair comparison is a fixed mix with the same average exposure, for example roughly half to two-thirds stocks and the rest in Treasury bills [S6, N7]. None of the headline comparisons on the page use that yardstick.

research.plain_summary: Dual momentum is a once-a-month, three-fund rule: own US stocks or foreign stocks, whichever did better over the past 12 months, and switch to a bond fund if stocks are doing worse than Treasury bills [short-term government debt, the stand-in for cash]. The author's backtest [rule run on past prices, not real money] for 1974-2013 looked superb: about 17% a year with a worst fall near 23%. The one thing the evidence says: since the book came out in 2014 the plain rule has made roughly 8% a year against roughly 14% for holding the S&P 500, and it did not soften the 2020 or 2022 falls.
research.how_it_works: On the last trading day of each month you look up three numbers: the past-12-month total return [price change plus dividends] of a US stock fund (S&P 500), of a non-US stock fund, and of Treasury bills. Relative momentum [which of the two is ahead]: pick the stock fund with the higher 12-month return. Absolute momentum [is it beating cash at all]: if that return is below the Treasury-bill return, hold a broad bond fund instead. All the money sits in one fund at a time and nothing happens until the next month-end check; this three-fund version is called GEM (Global Equities Momentum) and comes from Gary Antonacci's 2014 book. His 2012 paper runs the same two-step test on four pairs (US vs foreign stocks, high-yield vs safer corporate bonds, two kinds of property funds, gold vs long Treasury bonds) with a quarter of the money in each. Sector-rotation versions rank stock sectors the same way and hold the top few.
research.sitting_in_cash_relevance:
It attacks the cash habit directly: the rule has no "wait in cash" state. It always holds one of three funds, and its fallback is a bond fund rather than cash. In the 1974-2013 backtest it was in stocks 70% of the time [qi-book]; in this session's cross-check it was in stocks about 88% of months from January 2014 to September 2026 [own-check]. As a discipline for getting idle money invested without a fresh decision each time, it does what it says.

What it does not fix is missing moves. Its documented weak spot is exactly the fast rebound: it was in bonds for January-February 2019 (S&P +11.5%), April-May 2020 (+18.1%) and the first four months of 2023 (+9.2%), and since 2014 it has trailed buy-and-hold by about five points a year [own-check] [q4f].

It also sits outside Alan's standing rule. It chooses WHAT by price trend among index funds, not by revenue and earnings growth, and its WHEN is one all-or-nothing switch a month.

Read as a structure rather than an instruction, the evidence leaves two usable ideas. First, a rules-based default home for money that would otherwise sit idle, checked once a month. Second, if such a rule is used, spreading it across several lookbacks or several trading days [tranches], which the critics show reduces the luck without changing the idea [newfound] [resolve] [as-tranche]. A sector version stayed about 98% invested since 2014 in one unaudited check, but that is a single result [own-check]. None of this is a personal recommendation.
