Antonacci's 2012 paper itself was not read. Its abstract wording comes from a search listing, and its own tables (return, Sharpe ratio and drawdown per pair and for the four-pair composite) are not confirmed here.
Antonacci's 2014 book was not read directly. The 1974-2013 figures come from three secondary pages that agree with each other (CXO Advisory, Quant Investing, Ben Carlson).

Antonacci's own post-2014 track record, his 'Extended Backtest' figures for 1950-2018, his own sector model (Dual Momentum Sector Rotation), and any written reply to the Newfound and ReSolve critiques could not be read. Whether and how he has changed his recommended models is known only from a podcast host's one-line summary.

Allocate Smartly's tracked performance numbers for Antonacci's 'Traditional Dual Momentum' are members-only and were not seen. Only its public blog posts were read, and none gives GEM-specific return figures.
Newfound's 43.1% vs 146.1% comparison: the start and end dates of that test are not stated in the text that could be read.

ReSolve's summary gives no separate result for the 2012-2018 out-of-sample stretch and no day-of-month test; the day-of-month evidence for GEM here rests on this session's own calculation plus general (not GEM-specific) Allocate Smartly and Newfound material and one forum post.

All figures labelled 'own cross-check' are a quick, unaudited calculation made in this session from Yahoo Finance adjusted prices: one data vendor, no trading costs, taxes or slippage, trades assumed at the closing price on the signal day. The sector-rotation check is a single setting marked at month-end only, so its worst-fall figure is understated and its result could be luck.

Quant for Free, PortfolioDB and StrategyIndex are anonymous or commercial re-tests with undisclosed methods. The first two agree with the own cross-check; StrategyIndex's 12.3% a year for 2016-2026 does not, and the gap was not resolved.
The TuringTrader commentary concerns a different Antonacci rule (five asset classes with a beat-cash test), not the three-fund GEM rule.
Faber's sector paper was not opened; its figures come from Quantpedia's summary. The publication year Quantpedia shows (2013) differs from the 2010 working-paper date in the search listing.

findings.claim: The claimed backtest is the whole sales case. In Antonacci's book (published late 2014) the three-fund rule (GEM) about doubled the return of a world stock index, with a worst fall nearly two-thirds smaller, on little more than one trade a year. A commercial tracker still shows strong 57-year numbers, but its two deepest falls both came after the book was published.
findings.numbers: 1974-2013 (40 years), index data, before fees, trading costs and taxes. GEM: 17.43% a year, volatility [how much returns bounce around] 12.64%, Sharpe ratio [return per unit of bumpiness; higher is better] 0.87, worst peak-to-trough fall 22.7%. World stock index (MSCI ACWI): 8.85% a year, volatility 15.56%, worst fall 60.21% (as restated by Quant Investing; CXO's one-line summary shows 9.55% for the index; the book itself was not read). Time spent: 41% S&P 500, 29% non-US stocks, 30% bonds; 1.35 switches a year. PortfolioDB (57-year backtest, last updated Aug 2026; monthly data; index or simulated fund data before the ETFs existed; before taxes and trading costs): 14.53% a year vs 9.5% for a US 60/40 mix [60% stocks, 40% bonds, held always]; worst fall -21.65% vs -29.7%. That -21.65% ran Dec 2021 to Oct 2023 (recovered Jun 2024) and the second-worst, -19.5%, was Jan-Mar 2020. PortfolioDB's latest 10-year figure: 9.64% a year vs 9.3% for 60/40.
findings.note: Book figures seen on CXO (quoting pages 94 and 103: 17.43%, 12.64%, 0.87, 22.7%, 'almost doubling', 'maximum drawdown drops by nearly two-thirds'), Quant Investing (8.85%, 15.56%, 60.21%, 41/29/30, 1.35) and Carlson (1.35, 41/29/30). Two corrections. (1) 'Method not disclosed' is too strong: PortfolioDB has a methodology page saying everything is computed from monthly returns, earlier years may use index data or simulated ETF equivalents, and all returns are before taxes and transaction costs; what is missing is the specific data source for this portfolio. The 1970 start is inferred from '57 yr backtest' and the earliest listed drawdown (Feb 1970). (2) The researcher left out that PortfolioDB's headline worst fall is itself a post-publication event. The two secondary sources disagree on the world-index return (8.85% vs 9.55%); 'about doubled' holds either way.

findings.claim: The 2012 paper is broader than GEM. It runs the two-step test on four pairs of assets with a quarter of the money in each, and when a pair's winner is not beating cash it falls back to Treasury bills [short-term government debt, the stand-in for cash], not to a bond fund as GEM does. Its abstract says both tests can raise returns but the beat-cash test 'does far more to lessen volatility and drawdown', and that combining the two works best. Results are gross [before costs], and an outside reviewer flagged data-snooping risk [a rule can fit the past simply because many rules were tried].
findings.numbers: Monthly data, January 1974 (or earliest available) to December 2011. Pairs: US vs foreign stocks; high-yield vs intermediate credit bonds; equity vs mortgage REITs [property funds]; gold vs long Treasury bonds. 12-month lookback [how far back the rule looks], re-checked monthly. 1.2 to 1.6 switches a year per pair. Matching ETFs cost about 0.25% a year, before trading costs. Paper posted on SSRN 19 April 2012; later published in Journal of Management & Entrepreneurship, vol. 2 no. 1 (March 2017), pages 27-55. Allocate Smartly's replication (Nov 2016) uses SPY/EFA, LQD/HYG, VNQ/REM and GLD/TLT at 25% each, moves a module to cash when it fails the test, and is tested from 1985 net of costs; its public text gives no return figures. The paper's own return, Sharpe and drawdown tables were not opened.
findings.note: Abstract is now confirmed, not just 'seen in a search listing': read word for word on the Crossref record and on an archived copy of the SSRN page (the live SSRN page returns 403). CXO page confirms dates, pairs, switches, 0.25%, 'Reported returns are gross, not net' and the data-snooping caution, and states the rule 'substitut[es] Treasury bills (T-bills) for each pairwise winner that has not outperformed T-bills'. The researcher's 'how it works' text says the paper runs 'the same two-step test' as GEM, which hides that the fallback asset differs (bills in the paper, a bond fund in GEM). CXO calls the April 2012 version 'Risk Premia Harvesting Through Momentum'; the SSRN title is '...Through Dual Momentum'.

findings.claim: The best independent stress test supports the idea but not the exact recipe. Across 1,226 versions of the rule, the published 12-month version came out above the middle but not special, and a statistical test could not tell its edge over its neighbours from luck.
findings.numbers: 1950 to September 2018, index data, hypothetical, gross of taxes and transaction costs (ReSolve Asset Management, posted April 2019). Compound return: published version 14.9% a year (80.8th percentile of all versions); median version 14.1%; weakest 5% of versions 12.4%; best 5% 15.7%. Sharpe 0.90 published vs 0.83 median. Average of the five worst falls: 16.5% published vs 17.4% median. In a block-bootstrap test [history reshuffled many times] the published version beat the other 1,225 only 61% of the time. An ensemble [money spread across all versions at once] made 14.2% a year with Sharpe 0.93 and average worst falls of 13.2%, at an estimated 0.5% a year in extra tax cost, which a noise filter that cut trades by over 50% almost removed.
findings.note: Every number read in the page's own Table 1 and text (raw page text, not a summary). The 1,226 versions are 324 lookback combinations (18 x 18) plus moving-average and multi-market trend variants. ReSolve's section heading is 'Nothing special about the Original specification'. Note the ensemble's edge is in stability (falls, Sharpe), not in return: 14.2% is below the published version's 14.9%.

findings.claim: Strongest critique, part one: fragility. Because the rule puts 100% in one fund on one setting, near-identical settings give wildly different results, and late 2018 showed the problem live.
findings.numbers: Newfound Research (14 Jan 2019), lookbacks of 6 to 12 months: the 9-month version returned 43.1% in total over the test window while the 10-month version returned 146.1%. Newfound's text does not state the window; Antonacci's reply says it was only about 10 years of data. In 2010 alone the 10-month version made +12.2% and the 9-month version -9.31%. In Q4 2018 the rule kept followers 'mostly aggressively positioned' and signalled a defensive shift at the start of January 2019, when the S&P 500 was already down 14% (it had been down over 19% on 24 December). Allocate Smartly (23 Jan 2019): by its scorecard the version spread across seven lookbacks had beaten the original in end wealth and in risk-adjusted terms over the 6+ years since the paper, 'at the cost of higher turnover and a bit less tax efficiency', and December 2018 'scared a lot of investors away'.
findings.note: All figures and quotes read on the Newfound and Allocate Smartly pages. Returns are backtested and hypothetical, gross of fees except ETF expense ratios (Newfound's own disclaimer). The '10 years' window comes from Antonacci's written reply (archived copy), which the researcher had not been able to read; see 'missing' for his counter-argument.

findings.claim: Strongest evidence against: the out-of-sample record [the years after publication, which the rule could not have been tuned to]. Since 2014 the plain rule has trailed simply holding the S&P 500 by about five points a year, slightly trailed a plain 60/40 mix, and has not delivered the smaller worst fall the backtest promised.
findings.numbers: Quant for Free re-test (31 Jul 2026), ETFs SPY/VEU/AGG/BIL, 2014-2026: GEM 8.4% a year, Sharpe 0.70, worst fall -20%; SPY 13.6%, 0.94, -24%; 60/40 9.1%, 0.95, -20%. Same source, 2008-2026: GEM 9.1%, Sharpe 0.74, -20% vs SPY 11.6%, 0.77, -42% vs 60/40 8.3%, 0.84, -27%; the 2008 crash is where the protection worked. Independent re-run by the fact-checker from a different data vendor (monthly total returns, SPY/VEU/BND/BIL, no costs, Jan 2014-Sep 2026): GEM 8.4% a year vs SPY 13.6% vs 60/40 9.0%; $100 became about $279 vs $511 vs $300; worst fall on month-end numbers GEM -21.4%, SPY -23.9%, 60/40 -20.1%. Four rule and fund variants gave 8.3% to 8.6% a year. NOT re-derived: the researcher's daily-price figures (GEM -33.7%, SPY -33.7%, 60/40 -21.5%). What is confirmed is that the rule sat in US stocks all through February and March 2020 (PortfolioDB shows a -19.5% month-end fall Jan-Mar 2020, the same as the index), so its within-month fall must have matched the index's. Ben Carlson wrote in July 2015: 'Since 2009 this strategy has underperformed the S&P 500 by wide margin.'
findings.note: Quant for Free tables and wording read on the page ('a gap of more than five points a year'; drawdown protection 'quietly disappeared'). The researcher's own-check monthly figures (8.4% / 13.6% / about 9%; $278 / $511 / $300; -21.6% / -23.9% / -20.0%) are reproduced to within rounding by my re-run using lazyportfolioetf.com monthly returns with VEU in place of ACWX and BND in place of AGG. The daily drawdown numbers need daily prices; Yahoo returned HTTP 429 to me and I found no other free daily source, so they stay the researcher's unaudited figures. Quant for Free is a pseudonymous site (byline 'ridingyo').

findings.claim: Episode by episode the pattern repeats: the 12-month signal leaves stocks after the fall and comes back after the bounce [a whipsaw: sell low, buy back higher], and in 2022 its shelter, the bond fund, fell too.
findings.numbers: Calendar years, GEM vs S&P 500 ETF, fact-checker's independent re-run with PortfolioDB's figure in brackets: 2015 -6.7% (-6.9%) vs +1.3%; 2016 +6.9% (+6.4%) vs +12.0%; 2018 -8.0% (-7.9%) vs -4.6%; 2019 +18.9% (+18%) vs +31.2%; 2020 +3.7% (+2.5%) vs +18.4%; 2022 -16.9% (-17%) vs -18.2%; 2023 +7.0% (+6.8%) vs +26.2%; 2024 +24.9% (+25%) vs +24.9%. What happened: held US stocks through Q4 2018 (S&P -13.5%), then sat in bonds for Jan-Feb 2019 while the S&P rose 11.5%. Held stocks through Q1 2020 (S&P -19.4%), then sat in bonds for Apr-May 2020 while the S&P rose 18.1%. In 2022 stayed in US stocks to the end of May (-12.8%), then held the bond fund, which lost 4.7% over Jun-Dec (about -13% for the full year), and was still in bonds for Jan-Apr 2023 while the S&P rose 9.2%. Allocate Smartly on 2022: strategies that move to bonds regardless 'were trapped in bonds all the way down'.
findings.note: Holdings and episode returns reproduced month by month in my own re-run (different data vendor, VEU and BND as stand-ins); they match the researcher's figures to within a few tenths of a point, except 2020 (+3.7% with BND vs the researcher's +2.6% with AGG and PortfolioDB's +2.5%), a bond-fund pricing difference in April 2020. PortfolioDB yearly figures read on its page. Antonacci's own reply puts the Q4 2018 loss of the 12-month model at 13.6%, 'the same amount as the S&P index'. Free Float on 2020: 'The strategy got into bonds just when the equity markets were recovering and stayed there until well-after.' All figures are before costs and taxes.

findings.claim: Strongest critique, part two: timing luck [results that depend on which day of the month you happen to trade]. For rules of this kind in general, the trading day matters and the traditional month-end day has recently stopped being a favourable one. The GEM-specific size of the effect since 2014 rests only on the researcher's own unaudited calculation.
findings.numbers: Seen on source pages (general, not GEM-specific): Allocate Smartly (30 May 2024), 76 tactical strategies back to 1970: month-end trading historically added about 0.5% a year for the average strategy, but cost about 1% a year over the latest three years and about 2% in the latest year ('we shouldn't overreact... a year or even three is a short period'). Newfound: gaps 'often exceeding 100 basis points [1 percentage point] annualized' from rebalance date alone in US stock factor strategies, and calendar-year differences above 40% in one index replication. The standard remedy is tranching [splitting the money across several trading days or settings]. NOT reproduced by the fact-checker: the researcher's own test of 20 trading days (7.0% to 11.6% a year; calendar 2020 from -7.1% to +15.5%; 2018 from -12.4% to +0.9%; 2023 from +6.7% to +18.4%). Reproduced approximately: changing the lookback from 6 to 12 months at month-end gave 7.7% to 9.8% a year in my re-run (researcher: 7.7% to 10.1%); none reached SPY's 13.6%.
findings.note: The day-of-month test needs daily prices; Yahoo returned HTTP 429 to me, so those ranges could not be checked and should be printed, if at all, as the researcher's own unaudited figures. PortfolioDB's GEM page shows a 'Timing Sensitivity' reading of 25.6pp / 16.5pp but does not define it, so I did not use it. The QuantConnect forum quote ('day-2 shows the largest historical premium, day-17 is the worst performer', user Tony Walker) is real but is forum-grade and gives no figures. Allocate Smartly's tranching page contains no GEM numbers. The web search tool was out of quota this session, so I could not look for a published GEM-specific day-of-month study.

findings.claim: It trades rarely on average but in bursts, and every trade moves all of the money.
findings.numbers: Book backtest 1974-2013: 1.35 switches a year. Antonacci's 1950-2018 extension: 1.5 a year. 2012 paper: 1.2 to 1.6 a year per asset pair. Quant for Free, 2008-2026: 30 switches in 18 years (about 1.7 a year), in US stocks about two-thirds of the time. Fact-checker's re-run, Jan 2014-Sep 2026: 23 switches (about 1.8 a year), none in 2014, 2024 or the first nine months of 2026, five each in 2023 and 2025; months held: 104 US stocks, 30 non-US stocks, 19 bonds out of 153 (researcher, using a different non-US fund: 106 / 28 / 19). The most it can trade is 12 times a year. Each switch sells 100% of the holding, so in a taxable account every switch can realise a gain; Antonacci says about 70% of the 12-month rule's trades would have been long-term gains.
findings.note: 1.35 seen on Quant Investing and Carlson; 1.2-1.6 on CXO; 30 switches and 'two-thirds' on Quant for Free; 'only twelve potential rebalances a year (and often much less)' on Newfound; 'Generates taxable events on every switch in taxable accounts' on PortfolioDB. Switch counts by year reproduced in my re-run with VEU as the non-US fund (with EFA the count is 22, including two in 2026).

findings.claim: Sector-rotation versions (rank stock sectors by 12-month return, hold the top few, with or without the beat-cash test) have long-history support for higher return but not for smaller crashes, their record since 2010 is mixed, and Antonacci himself advises against them.
findings.numbers: Faber's study as summarised by Quantpedia: top 3 of 10 US sectors by 12-month momentum, monthly, 1928-2009: 13.94% a year (nearly 4 points above buy-and-hold), volatility 18.38% ('same as US equity index'), Sharpe 0.54, worst fall -46.29%. Faber's own abstract: more return 'with equity-like risk'; adding a trend filter lowers volatility and drawdown. CXO Advisory, 2002 to part-2015, top 5 of 40 Fidelity sector funds by 240-day return, held only if that return is positive (empty slots in cash): 10.8% a year vs 6.1% for SPY (Sharpe 0.56 vs 0.32), but no better than SPY with a plain 10-month moving-average rule (8.7% a year, Sharpe 0.67). StockViz (Oct 2021) on sector ETFs: 'it worked before 2010 and stopped working after that' (no rules or figures given). Antonacci, as reported by Robot Wealth: in his backtests back to 1974 sector rotation beat the S&P 500 but trailed GEM. Fact-checker's re-run, Jan 2014-Sep 2026, nine original sector SPDR ETFs, top 3 by 12-month return with the Treasury-bill test: 12.2% a year (13.1% without the test) vs SPY 13.6%; worst fall on month-end numbers -15.8% vs -23.9%; +5.8% in 2022 vs -18.2%; in bonds about 2% of the time; about 8 new positions a year. Holding only the single top sector: 10.8% a year, worst fall -28.5%. One setting, month-end numbers, no costs: exactly the kind of single result the timing-luck research warns about.
findings.note: The Robot Wealth sentence was WRONG and is replaced. Robot Wealth (Kris Longmore, 28 Apr 2017) did not test US stock sectors against GEM. Its own 'Dual Momentum Sector Rotation' is a global mix of eight stock, bond and gold ETFs (top three by 6-month return), which the author preferred to the paper's module approach while admitting 'the parameters that I used are among the best parameter sets'. The 'trailed GEM' statement on that page describes Antonacci's backtests ('sector rotation outperformed GEM only intermittently... with GEM coming out well on top over time') and the page adds 'Gary explicitly advises against a sector rotation model'. Quantpedia, CXO and StockViz figures read on their pages. The researcher's own sector cross-check (12.1% / 13.1% / -15.8% / +5.8% / 2% / about 8; single sector 10.8% and -28.5%) is reproduced by my re-run from a different data vendor.

findings.claim: How the rule works (wording fix for the page). The published rule first tests US stocks: if the S&P 500's 12-month return is below the Treasury-bill return, hold the bond fund, whatever non-US stocks are doing. Only if US stocks pass does it pick whichever of US or non-US stocks has the higher 12-month return. The researcher's wording (pick the leader first, then test the leader against bills) is a common simplification.
findings.numbers: Fact-checker's re-run, Jan 2014-Sep 2026: published order 8.6% a year, simplified order 8.4% (VEU as the non-US fund); 8.3% vs 8.4% with EFA. The two orders differ in only a handful of months.
findings.note: Antonacci's own post: 'When the trend of stocks is up according to absolute momentum applied to the S&P 500, we use relative strength to determine if we will be in U.S. or non-U.S. stocks. When the trend of stocks is down, we invest in bonds.' Robot Wealth and Quant for Free describe the same order. It does not change any conclusion, but the page should describe the rule as published.

findings.claim: Cash-habit numbers in the summary: the rule was in stocks about 70% of the time in the 1974-2013 backtest and about 88% of months from January 2014 to September 2026; it was in bonds for January-February 2019 (S&P +11.5%), April-May 2020 (+18.1%) and January-April 2023 (+9.2%).
findings.numbers: Book backtest: 41% US + 29% non-US = 70% in stocks, 30% in bonds. Fact-checker's re-run: 134 of 153 months in stocks (88%), 19 in bonds (12%).
findings.note: 70% from Quant Investing and Carlson. The 88% figure and the three missed rebounds are reproduced in my re-run from a different data vendor.

findings.claim: What the author now does (previously listed as not verified). Antonacci describes GEM as the simple public version for do-it-yourself investors; the models he licenses to advisers add 'multiple criteria for deciding when to be in stocks or bonds', more assets and several lookbacks. A 2024 podcast host says his focus has moved to channel breakouts [buying when price breaks above a recent range], with dual momentum used to rotate between models.
findings.numbers: Antonacci's own table, January 1970 to August 2020, hypothetical: public GEM 15.6% a year, Sharpe 0.91, worst month-end fall -19.8%, 26 months to recover; 60/40 8.9% and -29.7%.
findings.note: Read on archived copies of his site (the live site returns 403): the proprietary-models page (archived Sep 2020) and his January 2019 reply ('I use multiple lookback periods with both equities and bonds. But I do not indiscriminately choose them.'). Podcast notes confirm only the host's summary; Antonacci's words there were not transcribed. His proprietary model figures are unaudited marketing numbers and should not be relied on.

missing: The author's own reply to the fragility critique was left out (the researcher could not open it; an archived copy loads). Antonacci, 17 Jan 2019: Newfound's lookback comparison used 'only 10 years of past data'; over 1950-2018 (hypothetical index data) the 12-month rule made 15.5% a year with a worst fall of -17.8%, against 14.3% and -17.7% for a blend of 3, 6, 9 and 12-month lookbacks, with the same Sharpe ratio (0.95); the blend made 35% more trades; about 70% of the 12-month rule's trades would have been long-term gains; in Q4 2018 the 12-month rule lost 13.6% versus 12.3% for Newfound's seven-lookback blend. He concedes 'specification risk exists, and we can reduce it by using multiple lookback periods' and says he uses several lookbacks in the models he licenses. His suggested fix for a do-it-yourself investor is different: hold a fixed bond slice beside the rule (he cites 70% rule / 30% bonds from his book). https://web.archive.org/web/20230128193207/https://www.optimalmomentum.com/whither-fragility-dual-momentum-gem/

Antonacci's own extended backtest (also now readable via an archived copy) cuts both ways. For 1950-2018, hypothetical: GEM 15.8% a year, worst fall -17.8%, 1.5 trades a year, against the S&P 500 at 11.4% and -51.0%; in the 2007-09 bear market GEM lost 13.1% against 50.9%. But his own bull-market table shows the rule lagging badly in three of eight bull markets: Mar 2009-Dec 2017 S&P 500 +338.7% vs GEM +142.3%; Oct 1974-Dec 1980 +198.3% vs +103.3%; Jul 1962-Nov 1968 +143.7% vs +58.0%. So the post-2009 lag was visible in the author's own numbers, and a long lag in a steady bull market is normal for this rule, not new. The same post shows mixing the rule 50/50 with a fixed stock-and-bond portfolio: 13.0% a year with a worst fall of -28.1%. https://web.archive.org/web/20220516221903/https://www.optimalmomentum.com/extended-backtest-of-global-equities-momentum/

The author no longer presents the plain rule as his best work. His site calls GEM the simple public model for do-it-yourself investors and markets 'enhanced' licensed models with 'multiple criteria for deciding when to be in stocks or bonds and a wider selection of investable assets'. His table for Jan 1970-Aug 2020 gives public GEM 15.6% a year with a worst month-end fall of -19.8% and 26 months to recover. (His figures for the licensed models are unaudited marketing numbers.) https://web.archive.org/web/20200923060317/https://www.optimalmomentum.com/dual-momentum-proprietary-models/

The tracker the researcher cites for strong long-run numbers also shows the damage is recent: on PortfolioDB the two deepest falls in the rule's 57-year record are both after the book (-21.6% from Dec 2021 to Oct 2023, recovered Jun 2024; -19.5% in Jan-Mar 2020), the longest drawdown is 37 months, and the latest 10-year return is 9.64% a year against 9.3% for a US 60/40 mix and against the rule's own 15.1% long-run 10-year average. https://www.portfoliodb.com/portfolios/gem-dual-momentum

The academic footing of the beat-cash test [called time-series or absolute momentum] is contested, which the researcher did not mention. Huang, Li, Wang and Zhou (Journal of Financial Economics, 2020) find 'little evidence' of it asset by asset, 'both in- and out-of-sample', and that a strategy built on it performs 'virtually the same' as one that needs no predictability at all: 'Overall, the evidence on TSM is weak.' https://web.archive.org/web/20220305135803/https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3165284

Evidence on the other side that was also left out: AQR's long-history study builds a trend-following strategy back to 1880 and finds it 'consistently profitable' over 110 years, and a 2020 AQR paper blames the weak 2010s on unusually small market moves, finding 'little evidence to suggest this is a permanent structural change'. Important limit: both study many-market futures strategies that can also bet on falls, not a three-fund, stocks-or-bonds switch, so they support the general idea of trend following more than this recipe. https://www.aqr.com/Insights/Research/Journal-Article/A-Century-of-Evidence-on-Trend-Following-Investing and https://www.aqr.com/Insights/Research/Journal-Article/You-Cant-Always-Trend-When-You-Want

Real-money base rate for the whole category: Morningstar (Amy Arnott, Sep 2021) found tactical allocation funds [funds that shift between stocks, bonds and cash on signals] 'have fallen behind more static asset allocation funds for every trailing period' and 'haven't achieved significantly better downside protection, either'. These are costly managed funds, not a do-it-yourself three-ETF rule, but it is the nearest live-money evidence and none was cited. https://www.morningstar.com/funds/tactical-asset-allocation-dont-try-this-home

Rule wording: the published rule applies the beat-cash test to US stocks only and then chooses between US and non-US stocks; the researcher's description (pick the leader, then test the leader) is a simplification. Faber's own abstract says the sector ranking alone gives higher returns 'with equity-like risk' and that it is the added trend filter that lowers volatility and drawdown; and Antonacci 'explicitly advises against a sector rotation model' because in his backtests back to 1974 it beat the S&P 500 but trailed GEM. https://web.archive.org/web/20220106065925/https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1585517 and https://robotwealth.com/dual-momentum-review/

Confirmed by an independent re-run and by three outside write-ups [newfound] [freefloat] [turingtrader] [checker-recompute]

The bond fund lost about 13% in 2022 and the rule finished the year at about -17% against -18.2% for the S&P 500, so there was almost no protection. Faster variants are not a free fix: a version using 1, 3 and 6-month lookbacks looked excellent on a short history (from 1990), was flagged for possible overfitting, and its 30-year sustainable withdrawal estimate fell from about 9.0% to about 6.6% once 20 more years of history were added [as-adm] [as-adm-redux]

A related Antonacci rule (five asset classes at 20% each, each held only if it beats Treasury bills; from the book's appendix, not GEM) shows the same weakness on another tracker: 'only little benefits in late 2018 or spring 2020', and it has 'continuously trailed its benchmark' since 2012. Figures are behind a paywall [turingtrader]

research.plain_summary: Volatility-targeted sizing means letting how jumpy something is decide how much of it you hold: smaller positions in wild stocks, bigger in calm ones, and, optionally, less total exposure when the whole market gets rough. The one thing the evidence says: it reliably makes the ride smoother, but it does not reliably make more money. The famous study showing extra return leaned on borrowed money and some hindsight; a later test on 103 strategies found it helped about half the time. It answers "how much", not "what" or "when", and at the whole-portfolio level it holds more cash in rough markets, not less.
research.how_it_works: There are two versions. Version one works per position: measure how far each stock typically moves in a day (ATR, average true range [the average daily price swing, gaps included]) and put fewer dollars into the jumpy names, so a normal bad day costs about the same in every holding. The Turtle rule sized each "unit" so one average daily swing equalled 1% of the account; Van Tharp's percent-risk rule sizes so that being stopped out costs a fixed slice (his example: 1%) of the account. Version two works on the whole portfolio: choose how bumpy an account you will tolerate (a volatility target [the usual size of yearly swings], for example 10%), then each week or month set total exposure to roughly target divided by recent volatility, so exposure falls when markets turn rough and rises when they calm. Both lean on one well-documented fact: volatility clusters [rough stretches tend to follow rough stretches], so last month's jumpiness forecasts next month's jumpiness fairly well while saying little about next month's return. In the academic tests the "scale up" side used leverage [borrowed money, such as margin]; without borrowing, the rule can only move between fully invested and partly in cash. Neither version picks stocks or times entries; it only sets the amount.
research.sitting_in_cash_relevance:
This structure does not, by itself, get anyone out of cash, and one half of it does the opposite. The two versions need to be kept apart.

Per-position risk sizing (ATR or inverse-volatility) changes how invested money is split, not how much is invested. Its link to the cash problem is indirect and is reasoning rather than tested evidence: it turns "should I buy this jumpy name or wait?" into "buy it, but small", so an all-or-nothing decision becomes a size decision. It also sits comfortably beside the fundamentals-pick-what, technicals-pick-when rule, because it answers a third question, how much. The evidence for it is a modest smoothing benefit (volatility 14.6% vs 17.2% for equal weight on 1,000 US stocks, 1969-2011) with no dependable return gain and a real cost in growth-led markets [S7].

Portfolio-level volatility targeting is an exposure dial. Without margin it can only move between fully invested and partly in cash, so in rough markets it holds MORE cash, and it tends to be lightest exactly when rebounds happen [S1, S2]. Its only help with the cash problem is in calm, rising markets, where the rule says to be fully invested: in the no-leverage version tested over 1926-2015 the dial sat at 0.93 or higher in half of all months and at the 100% cap in at least a quarter of them [S1]. That figure comes from a back-test whose scaling constant was set with hindsight, which is one of the criticisms in S3 and S4.

So: if the cash is being held during quiet uptrends out of hesitation, a mechanical dial removes the hesitation. If the cash is being held after sell-offs, this structure would have held it too. The evidence supports it as a way to make the ride steadier and position risk even, not as a way to capture more of the moves being missed.

not_verified: Moreira and Muir figures are from the 2016 NBER working-paper PDF, not the typeset 2017 Journal of Finance article; published numbers may differ slightly.

The buy-and-hold market's average excess return for 1926-2015 is not printed in the Moreira-Muir table that gives 5.61% for the no-leverage version. My own arithmetic from the paper's Sharpe ratios (0.42 vs 0.52 at equal volatility, with 9.47% for the managed version) implies roughly 7.6% a year, which would put the no-leverage version below buy-and-hold in raw return. That is an inference, not a figure from the paper.
The Harvey et al. SSRN page (abstract_id=3175538) returned HTTP 403; the Duke-hosted copy of the published article was used instead.

Harvey et al. tables are stored in a shifted font; I decoded them by shifting character codes. The decoded Sharpe (0.40, 0.48-0.51) and vol-of-vol (4.6%, 1.8%) figures match the paper's prose, but the tail figures (-11.4%/-9.0%, +11.8%/+7.3%), the bond Sharpe ratios (0.25 vs 0.04-0.09) and the balanced-portfolio row come only from the decoded tables. They are also stated at a 10% volatility level, so real-world stock-market swings would be larger.

For S4, S5, S6, S10, S11, S12, S13 and S14 only the abstract or publisher summary page was read, not the full paper. Sample periods, exact market lists and any figures beyond those quoted were not checked. The Bongaerts et al. sample period was not visible on the pages read.

The Anderson, Bianchi, Goldberg full text (cdar.berkeley.edu PDF) would not load (DNS error), so no return or Sharpe figures for risk parity vs 60/40 are given. The 1926-2010 data period appeared only in a search snippet.
The often-quoted Barroso and Santa-Clara Sharpe figures (about 0.53 rising to about 0.97) were not on the abstract page and are not asserted here.

Clare, Motson, Thomas is a working paper sponsored by AON Hewitt, not a peer-reviewed article. The p-value of about 6% for inverse-volatility vs equal-weight was read from an extracted table whose layout was partly scrambled.
The Turtle rules were read from a third-party mirror (oxfordstrat.com) of the 2003 OriginalTurtles.org PDF, not from the original site.

Van Tharp's separate 'percent volatility' (ATR-based) model and a claimed comparison of about 21% vs 23% annualised returns for percent-risk vs percent-volatility sizing appeared only in forum search results. The book 'Trade Your Way to Financial Freedom' was not read and those claims are not asserted.

No peer-reviewed study was found that tests ATR or percent-risk sizing on a concentrated portfolio of individually picked growth stocks. The evidence here is on indexes, factor portfolios, asset classes and a 1,000-stock basket; applying it to a 10-30 name portfolio is extrapolation.
The statement that risk-based sizing makes it psychologically easier to get invested is reasoning, not a sourced finding.
No source was fetched on how volatility-target funds behaved in the 2020 crash and rebound, so that episode is not cited.
Cboe, Vanguard and Interactive Brokers pages were not consulted for this topic. Details of the S&P 500 Risk Control indices appeared only in search snippets and are not used.
Nothing here was tested on Scintilla data or on any actual holdings; no files were created or changed.

findings.claim: The best-known case FOR it: cutting exposure to the US stock market after volatile months and raising it after calm ones gave a better return per unit of risk over 1926-2015. The test relied on leverage [borrowed money] in calm periods, and the authors set its scaling constant using the whole 90-year sample.
findings.numbers: US stock market, monthly, 1926-2015 (NBER working paper 22208, April 2016, revised June 2016): alpha [return not explained by simply holding the market] 4.86% a year (standard error 1.56), beta 0.61; Sharpe ratio [return per unit of bumpiness] 0.42 buy-and-hold vs 0.52 managed; $1 grew to about $20,000 vs about $4,000 for buy-and-hold at the same overall volatility (nominal, log-scale chart). Exposure used: median 0.93x, 75th percentile 1.59x, 90th 2.64x, 99th 6.39x. Break-even trading cost 56 basis points [0.56%]. By 30-year thirds the alpha was 8.11% (1926-1955), 2.06% with standard error 2.82, i.e. not distinguishable from zero (1956-1985), and 4.22% (1986-2015).
findings.note: Read the 57-page PDF directly. Every number matches: alpha and beta in Table 1, 'Original Sharpe 0.42' in Table 2, managed Sharpe and weight percentiles in Table 5, 56bps in Table 4, the $20,000/$4,000 sentence on p.8 of the text. Footnote 5 confirms the scaling constant c is computed from the full sample (the authors say this does not affect the Sharpe ratio). The weak middle-third result is in Table 2 Panel B and was not mentioned by the researcher. Figures are from the working paper, not the typeset Journal of Finance version (Wiley returned HTTP 403).

findings.claim: RETURN versus SMOOTHNESS, from the same paper: remove the borrowing and the rule still looks good on a risk-adjusted basis, but its raw return drops sharply, because all it can then do is step down toward cash. The authors write that after the autumn-2008 falls their strategy 'cashed out almost completely and returned to the market only as the spike in volatility receded'.
findings.numbers: Same data, 1926-2015. Capped at 100% invested (no leverage): average excess return [return above T-bills] 5.61% a year vs 9.47% uncapped; alpha 2.12% vs 4.86%; Sharpe ratio unchanged at 0.52; exposure median 0.93x and at the 1.0x cap from the 75th percentile up. Capped at 1.5x (the paper's 'standard margin requirement'): 7.18% a year, alpha 3.10%, Sharpe 0.53. Derived by the fact-checker, not printed in the paper: alpha 4.86 and beta 0.61 with a 9.47% managed return imply buy-and-hold earned about 7.6% a year, so the no-leverage version (5.61%) earned LESS raw return than simply holding the market, at lower volatility.
findings.note: Table 4 gives E[R] 9.47%, 5.61%, 7.18% and Table 5 gives alpha 2.12/3.10, Sharpe 0.52/0.53 and the weight percentiles (0.93, 1, 1, 1). The paper's own words: 'Sharpe ratios do not change but of course the leverage constrained have lower alphas because risk weights are, on average, lower.' The 2008 quote is on p.2 of the text. The 7.6% buy-and-hold figure is arithmetic from printed numbers ((9.47-4.86)/0.61) and should be labelled as derived.

findings.claim: A wider study by Duke and Man Group researchers found the return-per-risk gain only in stocks and credit. Its clearest effect across assets was steadier volatility and fewer extreme months in BOTH directions; worst months were milder for 'almost all' assets, but not for US bonds over 1963-2017, where they were slightly worse. Results are shown after the fact at a fixed 10% volatility, using a scaling constant chosen with hindsight.
findings.numbers: US equities 1927-2017, scaled and unscaled both set to 10% yearly volatility: Sharpe 0.40 unscaled vs 0.48-0.51 scaled; vol of vol [how much the bumpiness itself varies] 4.6% vs 1.8% (20-day half-life); average of the worst 1% of one-month returns -11.4% vs -9.0%; average of the best 1% +11.8% vs +7.3% (so 4.5 points were shaved off the best months to save 2.4 points on the worst); turnover 2.39 round-trips a year at a 20-day half-life; average exposure 52% unscaled vs 70% scaled to reach the same 10% volatility. Sharpe did not improve in the middle sub-period (text says 1957-1987, the data table says 1958-1987). US bonds 1963-2017: Sharpe fell from 0.25 to 0.04-0.09 net of costs (0.05-0.09 gross), and the worst-1% average went from -8.4% to between -8.6% and -9.5%. Balanced 60/40 portfolio (in risk terms, S&P 500 and 10-year Treasury futures) 1988-2017: Sharpe 0.80 unscaled, 0.87 with asset-level scaling, 0.91 gross / 0.90 net with asset- and portfolio-level scaling; worst-1% average -9.7% to -7.3%.
findings.note: Read the Duke-hosted PDF and decoded the shifted-font tables myself (Exhibits 1, 5, 11, 16); the equity Sharpe and vol-of-vol figures also appear in plain prose. The researcher's numbers are right. Correction: 'the smoothing effect appeared in every asset class ... milder worst months' is too strong. The paper says vol of vol and mean shortfall improve 'for almost all assets', and its own Exhibit 11 shows the US bond left tail got worse. The paper also states the constant k is 'chosen such that ex post, over the full sample period, the target volatility is realized'. A later study (S6 full text) says its opposite tail-risk result is 'at odds with Harvey et al.' and blames this ex post scaling.

findings.claim: The strongest evidence AGAINST: across 103 stock strategies the volatility-managed version beat the plain version only about half the time, and a real-time investor who mixed the managed and plain versions using only past data usually ended up worse off than one who simply held the plain strategy. Momentum-type strategies were the main exception.
findings.numbers: 103 US equity strategies (the 9 factors from the original paper plus 94 anomaly portfolios): managed version had the higher Sharpe ratio in 53 cases, the plain version in 50; only 8 differences were statistically significant, concentrated in momentum-related strategies. In hindsight regressions 77 of 103 showed positive alpha (23 significantly positive, 3 significantly negative), but the real-time combination earned a lower certainty-equivalent return [the guaranteed return an investor would accept in place of the risky one] in 72 of 103 cases. For the stock market itself, real-time Sharpe 0.42 for the combination vs 0.46 for the plain market. Out of sample, managed momentum, profitability (ROE) and betting-against-beta still gave 'large utility gains'.
findings.note: Read the published JFE PDF (pp. 95-117). All figures are in the introduction, word for word. Nuance worth keeping: the real-time test compares (managed + plain + cash) against (plain + cash) for an investor with risk aversion 5 and a 5x leverage cap; it is not a test of a no-leverage retail account. The authors attribute the failure to 'structural instability' in the regressions.

findings.claim: Other critics traced much of the paper gain to hindsight and trading costs. The debate is not closed: a 2024 Journal of Finance paper argues a more elaborate version, timing nine long-short factors at once, does survive both objections. That version is an institutional construction, not something a long-only private account can copy.
findings.numbers: Liu, Tang, Zhou (2019): once look-ahead bias [using information not known at the time] is corrected, maximum drawdown [worst peak-to-trough fall] is 68%-93% 'in almost all cases' and the strategy 'outperforms the market only during the financial crisis period'. Barroso and Detzel (2021): after transaction costs, volatility management of factors besides the market 'generally produces zero abnormal returns and significantly reduces Sharpe ratios'; the managed market portfolio is robust to costs but 'only provides superior performance when sentiment is high'. DeMiguel, Martin-Utrera, Uppal (2024): conditional multifactor portfolio has an out-of-sample, net-of-costs Sharpe ratio 13% higher than the unconditional one (significant at the 1% level); traded one at a time, 4 of the 9 managed factors had a negative net-of-cost average return.
findings.note: Liu et al. and Barroso-Detzel confirmed from abstract pages only (WUSTL profile page; RePEc, quoted verbatim). For DeMiguel et al. I also read the open-access full text on the LBS repository, which supplies the 13% and 4-of-9 figures the researcher could not see.

findings.claim: It helps most on momentum-style strategies and when the dial is only turned at extremes. Plain, always-on volatility targeting did not reliably reduce drawdowns or bad months across world stock markets, and it overshot its own volatility target.
findings.numbers: Bongaerts, Kang, van Dijk (2020), 10 largest equity markets, strategy period 1982-2019, net of costs. Conventional targeting: Sharpe higher in 8 of 10 markets but by only 0.04 on average and significant only in the US; maximum drawdown INCREASED in the UK, Canada, Australia and Hong Kong (by 4.0 to 34.4 percentage points); average of the worst 1% of months got WORSE in 8 of 10 markets including the US; realised volatility ran above target (1.16x US, 1.31x UK, 1.57x Hong Kong); turnover 1.8-2.6 a year. 'Conditional' version (adjusts only in very high or very low volatility states, with exposure capped at 200% in calm states): maximum drawdown down by 6.6 percentage points on average, in every market except the UK; turnover 1.4 vs 2.1. Applied to momentum across six regions (1995-2019) it more than doubled the Sharpe ratio (from 0.12, +0.23) and cut maximum drawdown BY 20.1 percentage points FROM 54.1%, i.e. to roughly 34%, not to 20.1%. Barroso and Santa-Clara (2015): managing momentum's risk 'virtually eliminates crashes and nearly doubles the Sharpe ratio'.
findings.note: WRONG NUMBER CAUGHT. The CFA Institute summary page the researcher cited says drawdowns fall 'from 54.1% to 20.1%'. The article itself (full text fetched from the Erasmus repository) says 'reduced maximum drawdowns, by an average of 20.1% (from 54.1%)' and Table 3 Panel C lists the reduction as -20.1. The summary page is a misprint. Also added from the full text: the expected-shortfall result, the overshoot, the 200% exposure cap (the 'conditional' version still borrows in calm markets), and the sample dates the researcher could not see. Barroso-Santa-Clara quote confirmed on the RePEc abstract page.

findings.claim: For sizing individual stocks, one long-run index study found inverse-volatility weights [smaller positions in jumpier names] gave a slightly higher return with less bumpiness than equal-dollar weights. The edge over equal weight was statistically thin, the worst fall was still close to half, and it lagged badly in the 1990s when the largest companies led. The same study found that randomly chosen weights also beat the standard index, so the gain is not clear evidence that volatility weighting itself is clever.
findings.numbers: 1,000 largest US stocks, returns 1969-2011, weights reset once a year from the past five years of monthly volatility (working paper): inverse-volatility 11.4% a year, volatility 14.6%, Sharpe 0.45, maximum drawdown -45.7%; equal-weight 11.0%, 17.2%, 0.39, -50.2%; market-cap weight 9.4%, 15.3%, 0.32, -48.5%. Sharpe gap inverse-volatility vs equal-weight: p-value 6.0% (short of the usual 95% bar); vs market-cap: p-value 2% (passes). By decade: 1990s inverse-volatility 13.2% a year vs equal-weight 15.0% and cap-weight 17.6%; 2000s 6.9% vs 6.2% and 0.4%. With a simple trend rule added (hold the index only when above its 10-month average, otherwise T-bills): cap-weight Sharpe 0.46 and maximum drawdown -23.3%; inverse-volatility Sharpe 0.46 and -21.8%.
findings.note: Read the City Research Online PDF (Tables 2, 3 and 6). All of the researcher's numbers match, including the 6.0% p-value. Corrections: (1) 'the one direct long-run comparison' overclaims; it is one study that was read. (2) This is slow index weighting on 1,000 stocks using 5-year standard deviation, not ATR sizing of a concentrated portfolio. (3) 'Growth-led decade' is the researcher's label; the paper calls the 1990s 'the Market-cap decade'. (4) Left out: the paper's headline is that ten million random 'monkey' weightings also mostly beat cap-weighting ('it is not so much that these alternative indices are well designed'), and that a simple trend filter roughly halved every scheme's drawdown and erased the Sharpe gap between inverse-volatility and cap-weight. Working paper sponsored by AON Hewitt, not peer reviewed.

findings.claim: At the asset-class level (risk parity [each asset class given an equal share of the risk]), supportive results exist but depend heavily on the dates chosen and on borrowing and trading costs. A separate study found simple volatility-based weights beat equal weighting when allocating across groups of stocks.
findings.numbers: Anderson, Bianchi, Goldberg (2012), 1926-2010, four strategies (value-weighted, 60/40, unlevered and levered risk parity): start and end dates materially change the result even over decades; transaction costs can reverse the ranking, especially with leverage; a statistically significant return premium does not guarantee outperformance over reasonable horizons; risk parity does relatively better 'in turbulent periods than in bull markets'. Asness, Frazzini, Pedersen (2012): 'Empirical evidence dating back to 1926 shows that RP portfolios have outperformed traditional portfolios over the long term, but we must ask ourselves whether this evidence alone is conclusive.' Kirby and Ostdiek (2012): volatility-timing and reward-to-risk-timing weights 'outperform naive diversification even in the presence of high transaction costs'. No return figures were visible on the pages read.
findings.note: All three confirmed from publisher or abstract pages only (CFA Institute and RePEc; AQR; Cambridge). Correction: Kirby and Ostdiek is not an asset-class or risk-parity study. Cederburg et al. (S3, footnote 1) describe it as 'volatility-timing strategies for portfolio allocations across multiple stock portfolios', so it belongs with stock-weighting evidence. The 1926-2010 period, which the researcher saw only in a search snippet, is confirmed on the RePEc abstract page. The Berkeley full text still fails to load (DNS error).

findings.claim: The practitioner version (Turtle units, Van Tharp percent-risk) is a rule for making every position able to hurt you by the same amount. Neither document offers an independent test showing it adds return; they present it as risk control. The Turtle document itself records a day when the rule and its position caps did not prevent very large losses.
findings.numbers: Turtle rules (published 2003, describing 1980s leveraged futures trading): N = 20-day exponential moving average of the true range ('now more commonly known as the ATR'); one Unit sized so a 1N move equals 1% of account equity; stop placed 2N from entry so 'no trade could incur more than 2% risk'; caps of 4 Units per market, 6 in closely correlated markets, 10 in loosely correlated markets, 12 per direction; notional account cut 20% for each 10% lost. The day after the October 1987 crash, with the Turtles 'loaded long in interest rate futures', 'in some cases, 20% to 40% of account equity was lost in a single day'. Van Tharp Institute: 'percent risk' sizing risks a constant percentage of current equity per trade (example 1%); R is the initial risk per share set by the stop (example: buy at $50, stop at $47, R = $3). The same document warns losses can exceed 1R 'when the market gaps against you'.
findings.note: Read both PDFs in full. All quoted rules and the 1987 passage match. Wording tightened: 'not a tested source of extra return' is the researcher's inference from absence of evidence, not a finding in either source. The Turtle document says the 1987 losses 'would have been correspondingly higher without the maximum position limits', so it presents the episode as an overnight gap through the stops on leveraged, correlated positions, not as a failure caused by calm markets. The Van Tharp PDF is a free promotional report for a paid game and book; its only numbers are from a simulated 60-draw 'marble game' (40.1% return, 12.3% drawdown at 1% risk), not from market data.

missing: The page's headline that this 'reliably makes the ride smoother' needs a qualifier. Tested on 10 stock markets over 1982-2019 without after-the-fact scaling and net of costs, plain volatility targeting made the average of the worst 1% of months WORSE in 8 of 10 markets, including the US, and ran above its own volatility target (1.16x US, 1.31x UK, 1.57x Hong Kong). The authors write that this 'is at odds with Harvey et al. (2018)' and that 'a possible reason is their ex post scaling'. The researcher cited only the summary page and missed this. https://repub.eur.nl/pub/130215/Bongaerts-Kang-van-Dijk-Conditional-volatility-targeting-2020-FAJ.pdf

A number on the cited CFA Institute summary page is a misprint that the researcher repeated: momentum's maximum drawdown was cut BY 20.1 percentage points FROM 54.1% (to roughly 34%), not 'from 54.1% to 20.1%'. The same full text shows the 'conditional' version still borrows, with exposure capped at 200% in calm states; a no-leverage variant was tested only for momentum. https://repub.eur.nl/pub/130215/Bongaerts-Kang-van-Dijk-Conditional-volatility-targeting-2020-FAJ.pdf

The stock-weighting study's own headline undercuts reading it as proof that volatility weighting is clever: ten million randomly weighted portfolios also mostly beat the cap-weighted index, and the authors conclude 'it is not so much that these alternative indices are well designed'. Inverse-volatility did beat most of the random portfolios on Sharpe ratio, but the gap over equal weight was not significant. https://openaccess.city.ac.uk/id/eprint/16844/1/Heuristic%20and%20Optimised%20Weighting%20Schemes.pdf

In that same study a simple timing rule did far more for the worst fall than the weighting scheme did. Holding each index only when it was above its 10-month average (otherwise T-bills) cut cap-weight's maximum drawdown from 48.5% to 23.3% and inverse-volatility's from 45.7% to 21.8%, and left both with the same Sharpe ratio of 0.46. This bears directly on the fundamentals-pick-what, technicals-pick-when rule: in this test the 'when' rule, not the 'how much' rule, did the heavy lifting, and it did so by sitting in cash part of the time. https://openaccess.city.ac.uk/id/eprint/16844/1/Heuristic%20and%20Optimised%20Weighting%20Schemes.pdf

Harvey et al.'s tables contain exceptions to their own summary that the researcher did not report: for US bonds 1963-2017 the worst 1% of months was slightly WORSE with scaling (-8.4% unscaled vs -8.6% to -9.5% scaled); for US stocks the cut to the best months (4.5 points) was almost twice the gain on the worst months (2.4 points); and every figure is shown after rescaling to 10% volatility with a constant chosen using the full sample. https://people.duke.edu/~charvey/Research/Published_Papers/P135_The_impact_of.pdf

The original supportive paper's own sub-period table shows the effect was not steady: alpha was 8.11% a year in 1926-1955, 2.06% with a standard error of 2.82 (statistically indistinguishable from zero) in 1956-1985, and 4.22% in 1986-2015. The authors say results 'rely on a large degree of variation in volatility to work'. https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w22208/w22208.pdf

Real-world behaviour in the 2020 crash, which the researcher said was not sourced: the European Central Bank's May 2020 Financial Stability Review estimates up to USD 2 trillion globally in volatility-based strategies, notes that calm markets had let risk-parity funds lever positions 'by up to twice the amount of assets under management', and that in a stylised model 'assets worth nearly 225% of the portfolio's capital had to be sold' in March 2020, leaving 'a cash share of nearly 25%'. It concludes these strategies 'probably contributed' to March price moves. It does not measure the cost of missing the rebound. https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/financial-stability-publications/fsr/focus/2020/html/ecb.fsrbox202005_02~f6616db9be.en.html

A qualifier in the structure's favour that was left out: two of the critics' own co-authors later found that scaling by DOWNSIDE volatility [bumpiness on down days only] 'exhibit[s] significantly better performance than strategies scaled by total volatility', including in real-time tests, and that using fixed weights 'significantly improves' real-time results. So the weak real-time record applies to the plain version, not necessarily to every variant. Abstract only. https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/jbfina/v131y2021ics0378426621001576.html

The original authors' reply to the 'long-term investors should just ride it out' objection was left out: they estimate 'a long-term investor who ignores variation in volatility gives up the equivalent of 2.4% of wealth per year'. This is a model-based estimate from the proponents themselves. Abstract only. https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/jfinec/v131y2019i3p507-527.html

Evidence that qualifies the worry about underweighting jumpy stocks: across the whole US market, 'stocks with high idiosyncratic volatility ... have abysmally low average returns'. This is an average over all stocks, not over hand-picked growth names, so it does not settle the question for a concentrated portfolio, but it means 'jumpier means more upside' is not what the broad data show. Abstract only. https://www.nber.org/papers/w10852

The 2024 rescue of the idea is narrower than 'the debate is not closed' suggests: it times nine long-short factors together, optimised for trading costs, and gains a 13% higher Sharpe ratio; traded one at a time, 4 of the 9 managed factors lose money after costs. It says nothing about a long-only account of individual stocks. https://lbsresearch.london.edu/id/eprint/3716/1/The%20Journal%20of%20Finance%20-%202024%20-%20DeMIGUEL%20-%20A%20Multifactor%20Perspective%20on%20Volatility%E2%80%90Managed%20Portfolios.pdf

Caveats on the two practitioner sources: the Turtle rules were for leveraged futures (up to 12 one-percent Units per direction), and the Van Tharp document is promotional material whose own text warns that losses can exceed the planned amount 'when the market gaps against you and goes through your get me out price'. Stop-based sizing caps the planned loss, not the actual one. https://vantharp.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/06/A_Short_Lesson_on_R_and_R-multiple.pdf

Still not found by either researcher or fact-checker: any peer-reviewed test of ATR or percent-risk sizing on a concentrated portfolio of individually picked growth stocks. The web search allowance for this session ran out before a further search could be made, so absence here is not proof that none exists. Closest evidence read is the 1,000-stock index study. https://openaccess.city.ac.uk/id/eprint/16844/1/Heuristic%20and%20Optimised%20Weighting%20Schemes.pdf
failure_modes_checked: It misses the snap-back. Volatility is highest just after a fall, so the rule is at its smallest exposure when the rebound arrives. The original authors say their strategy 'cashed out almost completely' after autumn 2008 and returned 'only as the spike in volatility receded' [S1]. In the 1927-2017 US test at a 10% volatility level, the average of the best 1% of months shrank from +11.8% to +7.3%, a bigger cut than the 2.4 points saved on the worst 1% [S2]. Confirmed.

Without borrowing it lowers raw return. Capped at 100% invested, average excess return was 5.61% a year against 9.47% for the leveraged version [S1]. The paper's own alpha and beta imply plain buy-and-hold earned about 7.6% (fact-checker's arithmetic, not a printed figure), so the no-leverage version gave a smoother ride for less money. Confirmed.

It does not hold up in real time for most strategies. Managed beat unmanaged in only 53 of 103 cases, and the real-time mix was worse in 72 of 103 [S3]; one study reports look-ahead bias and drawdowns of 68%-93% once it is corrected (abstract only) [S4]. Exceptions that did hold up out of sample: momentum, profitability and betting-against-beta [S3]. Confirmed, with the exception added.

Trading costs eat it. After costs, volatility-managing factors other than the market gave about zero extra return and lower Sharpe ratios [S5]; the simple US equity version traded about 2.4 round-trips of exposure a year [S2], and conventional targeting ran turnover of 2.1 a year on average across 10 markets, 1.8-2.6 by market [S6F]. Confirmed.

Calm before the storm. The rule is at its largest size when things have been quiet, so a sudden shock lands on a full position. The original authors note their strategy's losses are 'concentrated' in low-volatility times such as the 1960s [S1]. The Turtle example needs softer wording: 'in some cases' Turtles lost 20%-40% of equity in one day after the October 1987 crash on leveraged, correlated interest-rate futures positions when prices gapped overnight; the document does not say markets had been calm beforehand and adds that losses would have been higher without the position caps [S8]. Partly confirmed; Turtle wording corrected.

Low volatility is not the same as safe. In US bonds, 1960-1980 had 'both negative returns and low volatility', so the rule held large positions through a long bear market and the Sharpe ratio over 1963-2017 fell from 0.25 to 0.04-0.09 [S2]. Confirmed.

It does not reliably cut the worst fall or the worst months. Conventional volatility targeting increased maximum drawdown in 4 of 10 equity markets (UK, Canada, Australia, Hong Kong) and made the average of the worst 1% of months worse in 8 of 10, including the US [S6F]; inverse-volatility stock weighting still fell 45.7% at worst versus 50.2% for equal weight [S7]. Confirmed and strengthened. Note the US-only, hindsight-scaled test in S2 shows the opposite for US stocks.

It overshoots its own target when run without hindsight. Realised volatility came in above target in most markets (1.16x in the US, 1.31x in the UK, 1.57x in Hong Kong), which the authors call 'the main driver of the increased drawdown and/or tail risk' [S6F]. New, added by the fact-checker.

It leans away from the biggest winners of some decades. Inverse-volatility weighting earned 13.2% a year in the 1990s against 17.6% for the cap-weighted market and 15.0% for equal weight [S7]. Numbers confirmed. The follow-on sentence that 'the jumpiest names are often the highest-conviction ones' for a growth picker is the researcher's reasoning, not a sourced finding; across the whole market, the jumpiest stocks have had 'abysmally low average returns' [S18].

It works only where falls and volatility arrive together. The Sharpe benefit was confined to stocks and credit and was 'negligible' for bonds, currencies and commodities, and it did not appear in the middle (1957-1987) sub-period even for US stocks [S2]. Across 10 stock markets the link between last month's volatility and next month's return averaged only -0.02 [S6F]. Confirmed.

Results depend on the dates chosen. For risk parity over 1926-2010, start and end dates changed the verdict even over decades, and transaction costs could reverse the ranking, especially with leverage [S13]. Confirmed from the summary and abstract pages only.

Everyone sells at once. A central-bank review of March 2020 found volatility-targeting and risk-parity funds had built leverage of up to twice assets while markets were calm and then, in a stylised model, had to sell assets worth nearly 225% of capital as volatility jumped, ending about 25% in cash [S15]. New, added by the fact-checker; it is a model estimate, not measured fund flows.

research.plain_summary: Level-based scaling in means splitting a purchase into parts and buying each part only if price falls to a level chosen beforehand: a support line (a price where earlier falls stopped) or the 21-day or 50-day moving average (the average close of the last 21 or 50 trading days). The one thing the evidence says: money that waits for a lower price has ended up behind money invested straight away about two times in three, and sixty years of "buy the dip" rules did not beat simply holding. So levels look more useful for pacing buys than for deciding whether to be invested.
research.how_it_works: Fundamentals choose the stock and the total amount to own; the question here is only how the money goes in. Instead of buying everything today (lump sum) or in equal slices on fixed dates (dollar-cost averaging), the amount is cut into parts and each part is tied to a price decided in advance, for example one part at the 21-day moving average, one at the 50-day, one at the last support line. Each part is normally a limit order (an instruction to buy only at that price or cheaper); Interactive Brokers' own wording is that a limit order protects the price "but it does not guarantee a fill". If price drops to a level, that part is bought; if price never drops that far, that part simply stays in cash. So the structure has two possible endings: a rising market leaves you under-invested, and a falling market fills every part on the way down. The design choice that matters most is therefore what happens to the unfilled parts: whether there is a deadline or a "buy anyway" rule.
research.sitting_in_cash_relevance:
Taken on its own, this structure does not cure the cash problem and can deepen it, because it turns waiting into a rule. The plain answer to "how often has waiting for a lower price meant missing the move": about two times in three for a wait of three to twelve months (66-68% across the US, UK, Australia and global stocks), roughly nine times in ten for a three-year wait, with stocks higher a year later in about 76% of all 12-month periods and 81% of the time after a record high. Those figures come from calendar-based waiting; no published figure was found for an order resting specifically at the 21-day or 50-day line (see not_verified).

What the structure does offer is real but narrower: a decision made in advance so that buying actually happens when a drop comes, and a softer landing if the start is unlucky (in the US study a loss in the first year 17.6% of the time instead of 22.4%, and a smaller one).

The versions that fit the evidence share two features: some of the money goes in at the start, and the unfilled parts have a time limit after which they are bought anyway. Vanguard's conclusion is that the waiting window should be short, such as three months, and that having any plan for the cash matters far more than which plan.

On the standing rule (fundamentals choose what, technicals choose when): the research gives better support to "when" rules that own a stock while it is above its moving average than to "when" rules that wait for it to fall back to that average. Used that way, levels set the order and size of the buys rather than deciding whether the money is ever invested. This is a description of structures and evidence, not a personal instruction.
