not_verified: No published study was found that measures the exact thing asked: how often a buy order resting at the 21-day or 50-day moving average, or at a support line, gets filled versus left behind, for an index or for individual growth stocks. The 'about two times in three' figure is for calendar-based waiting (3 to 12 months) and is the nearest evidence, not a direct measurement of level-based orders.

An own check on daily S&P 500 prices was attempted to fill that gap, but the free data sources tried in this session (Stooq, Yahoo, FRED) refused or timed out, and no daily price history was found in the local project folder. No self-computed number is reported. Scintilla's own price data could answer it directly.

AQR's dip rules trigger on a percentage fall from a recent price and sell again after a set holding period; they are not a test of buying at moving-average or support levels and then holding a fundamentally chosen stock. AQR's footnote says a staged 'double down' version would be in line with its results, but that version was not shown.

Osler's support and resistance test is on currencies within the trading day in 1996-1998. No equivalent test was verified for daily stock charts, and Osler did not test whether trading the levels was profitable.

Constantinides 1979: the conclusion was not seen on any fetched page (Cambridge and RePEc show only the opening extract; JSTOR would not load). The usual description, that a fixed pre-set schedule is suboptimal because it ignores information arriving along the way, is from memory and is not used as a finding.
George and Hwang 2004 was not fetched; the 52-week-high result is reported only as cited inside Avramov et al.
Brock, Lakonishok and LeBaron: only the abstract was read. The often-quoted figures of roughly +12% a year after buy signals and -7% after sell signals were not seen on the page and are not used.

Lo, Mamaysky and Wang: only the NBER abstract was read; the statement that the paper shows information content rather than trading profit goes beyond the abstract's wording ('may have some practical value').
Two earlier dip-buying studies cited by AQR (Ning 2018, S&P Global 'Buying the Dip'; Bonini et al. 2023) could not be read: the S&P Global page returned Access Denied.
A search summary attributed to AQR the statement that stocks spend far more time near highs than in deep falls; that sentence was not found in the AQR PDF and is not used.
Schwab's figure for the worst-timing investor ($151,343) is derived from the page's statement that she finished $19,212 below the immediate investor; the page text read did not print that total.
Maggiulli's piece does not state whether the waiting cash earned interest, and the exact data source for the index series was not confirmed.
Sullivan, Timmermann and White was read in its October 1998 working-paper version, with 4 of 57 pages unreadable; the published 1999 Journal of Finance text was not compared line by line.
Avramov, Kaplanski and Subrahmanyam was read as a working paper; the year 2018 is taken from the file name, and the later journal version was not checked.

Vanguard, Schwab, Dimensional and AQR all sell investment products and these are their own calculations, not peer-reviewed research. All figures are historical index results before taxes and, in most cases, before trading costs; none is a forecast.

findings.claim: Holding money back to buy later has lost to investing at once about two times in three. Vanguard compared putting the whole amount in immediately with splitting it into three equal monthly parts and checked who had more money after one year. The whole-amount approach was ahead 68% of the time; staying in cash lost to investing 70% of the time. Even when the waiting cash earned Treasury-bill interest (short-term US government bills, i.e. cash), investing at once still won 65% of the time.
findings.numbers: MSCI World Index (global stocks), 1976-2022, rolling one-year periods, 100% stocks: lump sum ahead of 3-month cost averaging 68% of the time; lump sum beats cash 70%; cost averaging beats cash 69%. Middle outcome on $100,000 after one year: $111,940 lump sum vs $109,580 averaged in (2.2% more). For a 60% stock / 40% bond mix: $109,360 vs $107,453 (1.8% more). By market, 3-part split: US 66.4% (Russell 3000, 1979-2022), UK 68.1% (1986-2022), Canada 67.2% (1985-2022), Europe 66.5% (1998-2022), Australia 67.5% (1992-2022), emerging markets 61.6% (1988-2022). A 6-part split raised the US figure to 73.7%, but not everywhere: Europe 65.4%, emerging markets 61.8%.
findings.note: Read all 11 pages of the Vanguard PDF. Every figure matches Figures 2, 3 and 6 and the text on page 5. Two qualifiers seen on the page that the claim leaves out: (1) the 68% base case assumes 'no interest earned on any uninvested portion', and Vanguard adds that 'as cash interest increases, LS's advantage diminishes'; (2) the longer split did not raise the lump-sum win rate in Europe (66.5% to 65.4%) or emerging markets (61.6% to 61.8%). Also note this is a calendar schedule on broad indexes that always finishes investing, not money waiting for a lower price on a single stock.

findings.claim: The longer the wait, the worse the odds. Vanguard's earlier study spread the money in over 6 to 36 months. A 12-month spread lost to investing at once in about two-thirds of periods in the US, UK and Australia; a 36-month spread lost in roughly 90% of US ten-year spans. Vanguard's own words: delaying investment is itself a form of market-timing, something few investors succeed at.
findings.numbers: US 1926-2011, 60% stocks / 40% bonds, rolling 10-year periods, 12-month spread: lump sum ahead 67% of the time (UK 1976-2011: 67%; Australia 1984-2011: 66%). Average ending value on $1,000,000: $2,450,264 lump sum vs $2,395,824 spread in (2.3% more; UK 2.2%, Australia 1.3%). 36-month spread: lump sum ahead in approximately 90% of US 10-year spans. Return per unit of risk (Sharpe ratio) in the first 12 months, US 60/40: 0.81 lump sum vs 0.72 spread in. For 100% stocks: US 66%, UK 68%, Australia 62%.
findings.note: Read all 8 pages (third-party host carrying Vanguard's own document, imprint ICRDCA 072012). All figures match Figures 1, 2 and 4 and the text on pages 2-4, including the market-timing sentence word for word. In this study the waiting cash did earn interest (held in 'cash instruments'). Wording caution for the page: the 90% figure is for money drip-fed over 36 months, not for money sitting in cash for three years and then invested.

findings.claim: STRONGEST EVIDENCE AGAINST: "buy the dip" rules have not beaten simply holding. AQR built 196 versions (wait for a fall of 5%, 10%, 15% or 20% over one week to one year, buy, hold one month to five years, otherwise sit in cash) and ran them on the S&P 500 for 60 years. On average they earned less than holding and less per unit of risk taken; the handful that looked good are about what luck alone would produce when 196 rules are tried. AQR's explanation: buying a fall over weeks or months is betting against momentum (the tendency of recent direction to continue). A footnote says a staged version (buy after a 5% drop, more after another 5%) would behave like a blend of the 5% and 10% rules, and that investors on a fixed buying schedule should not deviate from it to wait for dips. Caveat: these rules trigger on a percentage drop, not on a moving-average or support line, and they sell again after the holding period.
findings.numbers: S&P 500 price index (dividends not counted), 1 Jan 1965 - 30 Sep 2025, 196 rules, no fees or trading costs deducted. Holding beat the average dip rule by 1.1% a year in plain return (0.6% vs the better-quartile rule, 1.7% vs the worse-quartile rule). Average Sharpe ratio (return per unit of risk) 0.04 lower than holding, about 16% worse; over 60% of the 196 rules were worse. From Oct 1989 (data including dividends): 0.27 lower, 47% worse. Return after allowing for time in the market (alpha) averaged +0.5% a year, positive but not reliable: only 16 of 196 rules (8%) passed the usual statistical test and none passed once adjusted for having tried 196 rules (threshold about 3.52).
findings.note: Read all 22 pages of the AQR PDF. Every number matches: Exhibit 2 (4 depths x 7 lengths x 7 holds), page 5 and footnote 10 (1.1% / 0.6% / 1.7%), page 5 (0.04, 16%, over 60%; 0.27, 47%), page 7 and footnote 15 (0.5%, 16 of 196, 3.52), footnote 8 (staged version), footnote 13 (fixed schedule). Two details to print: the 1965-2025 test uses price returns without dividends (footnote 5), and the average alpha is slightly positive, just not distinguishable from luck.

findings.claim: Buying weakness leaves you holding through the long declines, which is where following the trend did better. In the four S&P 500 falls deeper than 20% since 2000, the average dip-buying rule lost about 18%. That is less than half of the 40% lost by simply holding, because the rule is partly in cash, but over the same falls an index of trend-following funds (funds that buy what is rising and cut what is falling) gained about 29%. The same test on seven very large US growth stocks (Google, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia, Tesla) also found dip-buying gave a worse return per unit of risk than holding them. Caveats: AQR runs trend-following funds, so it is an interested party; the trend index is after fees while the dip rules are before costs; and trend-following lost a little in the very short crash of Feb-Mar 2020.
findings.numbers: S&P 500 falls deeper than 20%, 2000 - Sep 2025, average of the four: S&P 500 -40.2%, average dip rule -18.4%, SG Trend Index +28.6%. Oct 2007-Mar 2009: -55.3% / -34.0% / +31.7%. Sep 2000-Oct 2002: -47.4% / -14.7% / +51.4%. Feb-Mar 2020: -33.8% / -17.3% / -2.4%. Jan-Oct 2022: -24.5% / -7.7% / +33.9%. Alpha (return NOT explained by simply being in the stock market), 2000-2025: trend index 4.7% a year vs 0.3% for the average dip rule; the trend index's own return above cash was 4.0% a year. Seven-stock test: May 2012 - Sep 2025, compared on Sharpe ratio.
findings.note: All drawdown figures match Exhibit 7 exactly. Correction: the researcher wrote 'extra return over holding stocks ... 4.7% a year'. AQR's 4.7% is alpha to equities (return unexplained by market exposure), not a return 4.7% higher than stocks; the trend index earned 4.0% a year above cash (page 9). Also added the context that the dip rule lost less than half as much as buy-and-hold in those falls. The seven-stock appendix (Exhibit A1) compares Sharpe ratios and says alphas are 'indistinguishable from zero'. Confirmed separately on AQR's own fund page that it runs a trend-following managed futures fund.

findings.claim: Even a perfect dip-buyer gains little, and a slightly imperfect one loses. Schwab gave five imaginary investors $2,000 a year for 20 years: the one who bought at each year's exact low finished only about 9% ahead of the one who invested on the first trading day of each year, and the one who never bought finished with less than a third. A separate analysis by Nick Maggiulli found that saving up cash and buying only at exact market bottoms, with perfect foresight, still lost to plain monthly buying in more than 70% of 40-year periods, and missing the bottom by two months turned that into a loss 97% of the time.
findings.numbers: Schwab, S&P 500, 2005-2024, $2,000 a year: perfect timing $186,077; invest on first trading day $170,555; twelve monthly parts $166,591; worst timing (each year's high) $151,343 (derived: stated as $19,212 below investing immediately, and as $103,986 above cash-only, both give $151,343); cash only $47,357. Same ranking in 70 of 80 rolling 20-year periods back to 1926. Schwab: the market rose in 75.6% of 1,177 rolling 12-month periods, 1926-2024. Maggiulli, US stocks with dividends, inflation-adjusted, $100 a month, 40-year periods 1920-1979: perfect bottom-buying underperformed monthly buying over 70% of the time; 97% of the time if two months late.
findings.note: Schwab: the fetch tool was served an error page, so the page was read by a direct request; article dated July 18, 2025, by Schwab Center for Financial Research. All dollar figures, 70 of 80, and 75.6% (footnote 3) seen on the page. 186,077 / 170,555 = 9.1% ahead; 47,357 / 170,555 = 28%. Maggiulli page loaded normally; 'over 70%' and '97%' are direct quotes. Both tests are about regular new savings, not a one-off pile of cash, and the Schwab page itself notes one stretch (1962-1981) when investing immediately ranked fourth of five. Maggiulli is a blog post, not peer-reviewed, and does not state its data source or whether waiting cash earned interest.

findings.claim: The limit-order problem is real and documented, but the research is not one-sided. A buy order resting below the market fills when the price falls to it, which can be because of bad news, and does not fill when good news sends the price away. Handa and Schwartz name exactly these two risks. Linnainmaa, using every individual investor's trades in Finland, found that much of individuals' apparent bad timing (poor returns after trading, losses around earnings, buying what is falling) arises mechanically because limit orders suffer from adverse selection (they tend to be filled by people who know more). Evidence the other way: Handa and Schwartz's own tests found limit orders did better than market orders for traders with well-balanced portfolios, and Harris and Hasbrouck found New York Stock Exchange limit orders placed at or better than the current quote did better than paying the market price even after a penalty for orders that never filled. That favourable evidence is about orders at or near today's price, not orders parked well below it.
findings.numbers: No single percentage in the abstracts. Linnainmaa: all individual investors in Finland, Journal of Finance 65(4), 2010. Handa and Schwartz: Journal of Finance 51(5), 1996. Harris and Hasbrouck: New York Stock Exchange SuperDOT orders, JFQA 31(2), 1996. Interactive Brokers: a limit order 'does not guarantee a fill'.
findings.note: All four pages loaded and the abstracts say what is claimed. Small correction: the researcher attributed the favourable result to 'patient traders' via Harris and Hasbrouck; their abstract does not restrict it that way (it reports measures for both must-trade and passive traders). The 'well-balanced portfolios' wording, and the finding that a network of buy and sell limit orders 'is profitable', come from Handa and Schwartz's own abstract, which the researcher's finding understated. Interactive Brokers page: fetch tool got 403; read by direct request; exact sentence seen: 'The Limit order ensures that if the order fills, it will not fill at a price less favorable than your limit price, but it does not guarantee a fill.'

findings.claim: Support levels do hold more often than chance, but the edge is small, very short-lived in how it was measured, and the best test is in currencies within the day, not stocks. Osler at the New York Fed checked support and resistance levels that six firms published daily. A 'bounce' meant only that, fifteen minutes after touching the level, the price was still on the right side of it. That happened more often at published levels than at randomly chosen levels, and the levels stayed useful for at least five business days. But the edge shrank when markets became more volatile, the firms' own 'strength' ratings were not useful, levels that several firms agreed on were no better, and Osler did not test whether trading on them made money. Lo, Mamaysky and Wang found that several chart patterns in US stocks carry some extra information and 'may have some practical value', which is not the same as a proven profit.
findings.numbers: Osler: dollar-mark, dollar-yen, dollar-pound, one-minute quotes 9am-4pm New York, Jan 1996 - Mar 1998, six firms. Bounce rate 60.8% at published levels vs 56.2% at arbitrary levels (edge 4.6 points; 4.2 for the mark, 5.6 yen, 4.0 pound). Five days after publication the bounce rate was 1.7 points lower. In the more volatile second half the edge was no longer statistically significant in half the cases. 96% of published levels ended in 0 or 5 (round numbers). Lo, Mamaysky, Wang: US stocks 1962-1996.
findings.note: Read all 16 pages of the Osler article. Every number matches (Table 8 and pages 61-63). Correction: the researcher wrote that prices 'stopped and turned'; the paper's definition (page 59) is that the trend 'was interrupted if the bid (ask) price exceeded (fell short of) the support (resistance) level fifteen minutes later' (thirty minutes as an alternative). 'Nobody tested' narrowed to 'Osler did not test': the paper calls profitability 'an appropriate subject for future research'. Data are indicative quotes, not trade prices. Lo-Mamaysky-Wang: NBER abstract read; the 'not a proven profit' gloss is the researcher's reading, not the abstract's words.

findings.claim: On moving averages, the published tests are of owning while price is ABOVE the average; none of them tests waiting for price to fall back to it, so the comparison is an inference rather than a measured result. Brock, Lakonishok and LeBaron found that moving-average buy signals on the Dow (price above its average) were followed by higher and calmer returns than sell signals, and returns after sell signals were negative. Avramov, Kaplanski and Subrahmanyam found, across thousands of US stocks, that the further a stock's 21-day average sits above its 200-day average, the higher its later return compared with other stocks, with no fading for several months (the effect was gone at 13 to 24 months). Dimensional found the S&P 500 was higher a year after a record high 81% of the time. Evidence against leaning on any of this: Sullivan, Timmermann and White re-tested on the following ten years and found scant evidence that such rules still had value.
findings.numbers: Brock et al.: Dow Jones index 1897-1986. Avramov et al.: US stocks June 1977 - Oct 2015, 8,367 firms; buying the most stretched-up tenth and selling short the most stretched-down tenth returned more than 13% a year, more than 12% after risk adjustment, before the investor's own costs. Dimensional: S&P 500 monthly closes 1926-2022; 30% of months ended at a new high; index higher one year later 81% of the time and five years later 86%; average return after a new high almost 14% over the next year and more than 10% a year over five. Sullivan et al.: Dow 1987-1996, the best rule as of 1986 (a five-day moving-average rule from their wider set of 7,846 rules) returned 2.8% a year with p-value 0.322 (not distinguishable from luck); the best of Brock's own 26 rules returned 8.6% a year in 1987-1996 with a luck-adjusted p-value of 0.154.
findings.note: Brock abstract page, Dimensional page and the Sullivan-Timmermann-White working paper (read in full) all confirm the figures. Avramov et al.: read pages 1-13 and the reference list by text extraction; 21-day vs 200-day, June 1977 - Oct 2015, 8,367 firms, 'in excess of 12% per year' and 'do not decay even after several months' all seen. Corrections: (1) the headline 'not waiting for price to fall back' is the researcher's inference; no fetched paper tests a pullback entry. (2) 'Stretched-up stocks tended to keep going rather than come back to the line' overstates: the paper ranks stocks against each other in a long-short portfolio; it does not say an individual stock will not revisit its average, and it reports the effect 'is insignificant for the 13-24-month horizon'. (3) The 2.8% / 0.322 result is for the five-day moving-average rule chosen from the authors' own 7,846-rule universe, not one of Brock's 26 rules. Sullivan et al. also found Brock's result held up in-sample (1897-1986) after the luck adjustment, against a benchmark of being out of the market.

findings.claim: EVIDENCE FOR going in gradually: it softens a bad start, it can suit investors who are both cautious and feel losses sharply, and it beats never investing. Vanguard found that in the worst 5% of one-year outcomes the averaged-in investor finished ahead, and that averaging in beat staying in cash 69% of the time. In its model, a moderately or very cautious investor who feels a loss about two and a half times as much as an equal gain preferred averaging in, though only by a hair; an adventurous investor with the same loss aversion still preferred investing at once. Its conclusion: having a plan for the cash is the most important part, the choice between the two makes only a marginal difference compared with staying in cash for good, and the waiting period should be kept short, such as three months. Separately, Brennan, Li and Torous found that for individual stocks added to an existing portfolio, uninformed investors who bought gradually were better off, in a world where share prices tend to swing back.
findings.numbers: Vanguard 2023, MSCI World 1976-2022, $100,000, 100% stocks, worst 5% of one-year outcomes: $85,906 averaged in vs $82,947 lump sum (lump sum is still ahead at the 25th percentile: $102,070 vs $101,531). Loss aversion set at 2.50; certainty-equivalent return (the sure return an investor would accept instead) for the moderately conservative investor: 1.0100 lump sum vs 1.0102 averaging in; adventurous: 1.0321 vs 1.0296. Vanguard 2012, US 1926-2011, 1,021 rolling 12-month periods on $1,000,000: lump sum lost money in 229 periods (22.4%) with an average loss of $84,001; the 12-month spread lost in 180 periods (17.6%) with an average loss of $56,947. Brennan, Li, Torous: Review of Finance 9(4), 2005, no figure in the abstract.
findings.note: All dollar and period figures match (Vanguard 2023 Figure 3 and conclusion; Vanguard 2012 page 6). Correction: the researcher wrote that 'an investor with strong loss aversion ... rationally prefers averaging in'. Figure 5b shows that with loss aversion of 2.50 the adventurous persona still prefers lump sum; only the moderately conservative and very conservative personas prefer averaging in, and for the moderately conservative one the margin is 1.0102 vs 1.0100. Brennan-Li-Torous abstract confirmed word for word; note that Vanguard 2023's footnote 1 lists the same paper among literature 'generally in favor of lump-sum investing', so the two sources characterise it differently.

sources.title: Buy the dip?
sources.authors: Stefano Bonini; Thomas Shohfi; Majeed Simaan
sources.note: Added by the fact-checker. University research-portal page loads with the abstract; European Financial Management 30(4), pp. 2033-2070, September 2024. This is one of the two earlier studies AQR cites that the researcher could not read. The SSRN version returned 403.

missing: US evidence that cuts against the 'resting orders get picked off' reading: Kelley and Tetlock (Journal of Finance, 2013), using about one-third of US self-directed retail trading, found that net buying through passive (limit) orders followed price falls and was followed by higher returns over the next month 'with no evidence of return reversal', 'consistent with traders providing liquidity and benefitting from the reversal of transitory price movements'. Linnainmaa's adverse-selection result is from Finland. https://business.columbia.edu/sites/default/files-efs/pubfiles/4471/Kelley_Tetlock_JF_12_How_Wise_Are_Crowds_with_Appendix.pdf (publication details: https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/jfinan/v68y2013i3p1229-1265.html)

Individual stocks have tended to snap back over about one month, which is roughly the horizon of a pullback to a 21-day average: Jegadeesh (Journal of Finance, 1990) found 'the negative first-order serial correlation in monthly stock returns is highly significant', with positive correlation at longer lags (strongest at twelve months), and a 2.49% per month gap between extreme portfolios over 1934-87. This qualifies 'buying weakness fights momentum', which AQR tested on the index. Caveats: old sample, long-short portfolios, before trading costs. https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/jfinan/v45y1990i3p881-98.html

A peer-reviewed dip-buying study that AQR cites but the researcher could not read gives a more mixed verdict: Bonini, Shohfi and Simaan (European Financial Management, 2024) find buy-the-dip 'does not necessarily maximize investors' real terminal wealth and is sensitive to market conditions at the beginning year of investment', but 'under certain conditions, BTD may improve risk-adjusted performance over a passive investment policy or a classical dollar-cost averaging approach', subject to estimation risk. https://researchwith.stevens.edu/en/publications/buy-the-dip/

Qualifiers inside AQR's own paper that soften the headline: the average dip rule's alpha was positive (+0.5% a year), just not reliably different from zero; in the four big falls it lost less than half as much as holding (-18.4% vs -40.2%); swapping 20% of a 60/40 portfolio into the average dip rule gave a slightly higher Sharpe ratio (0.46 vs 0.45), lower volatility (8.8% vs 9.3%) and a slightly lower return (4.0% vs 4.2% above cash); dips measured over five years did better (Sharpe 0.21, alpha 0.8%, t-statistic 1.0); and the 1965-2025 test uses the price index without dividends. https://www.aqr.com/-/media/AQR/Documents/Alternative-Thinking/AQR-Alternative-Thinking---Hold-the-Dip.pdf?sc_lang=en

The momentum evidence the researcher leans on has faded in recent data by its own source: Avramov, Kaplanski and Subrahmanyam report that 'over the 2001-2015 period, the momentum, 52-week high price, and trend effects all disappear (t=0.70, -1.26, and 0.45)'; only their moving-average-distance measure stayed significant (t = 2.80), and it 'is insignificant for the 13-24-month horizon'. The result is a long-short ranking across 8,367 stocks, so it does not say whether any one stock will or will not come back to its average. https://anderson-review.ucla.edu/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/Avramov-Kaplanski-Subra_2018_SSRN-id3111334.pdf

Sullivan, Timmermann and White is less one-sided than presented: for 1897-1986 they find Brock's results 'appear to be robust to data-snooping'; the benchmark was being out of the market, not holding stocks; the Dow data ignore dividends; with a one-day delay in acting on signals the best rule's 100-year return fell from 17.2% to 7.8% a year and its Sharpe-ratio test was no longer significant (p = 0.26); and on S&P 500 futures 1984-1996 no rule beat the benchmark after the luck adjustment (p = 0.908). The authors offer 'markets have become more efficient' as one explanation. https://www.fmg.ac.uk/sites/default/files/2020-11/dp303.pdf

Vanguard 2023 qualifiers left out: the 68% base case assumes waiting cash earns nothing and 'as cash interest increases, LS's advantage diminishes'; in Europe and emerging markets a longer split did not raise the lump-sum win rate (Europe 66.5% to 65.4%, emerging markets 61.6% to 61.8%); and Vanguard says the choice between the two 'will make only a marginal difference compared with permanently keeping a cash allocation'. All tests are on broad indexes, not single growth stocks. https://corporate.vanguard.com/content/dam/corp/research/pdf/cost_averaging_invest_now_or_temporarily_hold_your_cash.pdf

Osler's 'bounce' is a fifteen-minute measure on indicative quotes, not trades, and 96% of the published levels ended in 0 or 5, so part of what was measured is a round-number effect in currencies. That makes it weak support for daily-chart support lines on stocks. https://www.newyorkfed.org/medialibrary/media/research/epr/00v06n2/0007osle.html

The limit-order papers cited as the 'problem' also report favourable results: Handa and Schwartz's tests 'suggest that trading via limit orders dominates trading via market orders for market participants with relatively well-balanced portfolios, and that placing a network of buy and sell limit orders as a pure trading strategy is profitable'. https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/jfinan/v51y1996i5p1835-61.html

Schwab's own page gives reasons for buying gradually that the researcher did not carry over (it 'prevents procrastination' and 'minimizes regret'), notes one 20-year stretch (1962-1981) when investing immediately ranked fourth of five, and warns 'there's always a chance we could enter another period like the 1960s through early 1980s'. Its test, like Maggiulli's, is about regular new savings rather than a one-off cash pile. https://www.schwab.com/learn/story/does-market-timing-work
failure_modes_checked: The market runs away: orders parked below the price never fill and the cash stays cash. The nearest measured figure is for calendar-based buying, which always finishes investing: spreading money in over 3 to 12 months ended up behind investing at once about two times in three, and stocks rose in roughly three of every four 12-month periods (75.6%, 1926-2024). A level-based plan with no deadline has no such guarantee of ever being invested. [vanguard-2023] [vanguard-2012] [schwab-2025]

The longer the wait, the worse it has been: money drip-fed over 36 months lost to investing at once in roughly 90% of US ten-year spans, and Vanguard notes that many investors hold too much cash by indefinitely deferring the decision. [vanguard-2012] [vanguard-2023]

You can get filled when you least want to be: resting buy orders fill on the way down, sometimes on bad news, and dip-buying rules stayed invested through long declines. In the four S&P 500 falls deeper than 20% since 2000 the average dip rule lost about 18% (holding throughout lost about 40%; a trend-following index gained about 29%). Evidence on individuals' resting orders is mixed: bad in Finnish data, favourable in US data. [aqr-2025] [linnainmaa-2010] [handa-schwartz-1996] [kelley-tetlock-2013]

It can fight momentum: AQR's explanation for the weak results is that buying a market fall over weeks or months sits on the opposite side of the trend. Qualifier: this is tested on the S&P 500 and seven mega-cap stocks; one older study found individual stocks tend to snap back over about a month, and one paper found plain momentum effects faded in 2001-2015. [aqr-2025] [jegadeesh-1990] [aks-2018]

The level is weaker than it looks: the measured edge for published support levels is about 61% versus 56% for random levels, in currencies, where 'held' meant only that price was still on the right side fifteen minutes later; the edge weakened when volatility rose, and the publishers' own strength ratings carried no useful information. No equivalent test on daily stock charts was found. [osler-2000]

Hindsight tuning: among 196 dip rules, 16 looked statistically good and none survived the adjustment for having tried 196; moving-average rules that worked on the Dow for 90 years showed scant evidence of value in the following ten. A level fitted to the past chart of one stock is exposed to the same trap. [aqr-2025] [stw-1999]
A limit order (an instruction to buy only at a set price or cheaper) does not guarantee a fill, so a plan that looks fully specified can leave an unknown share of the money uninvested. [ibkr-limit]

research.plain_summary: You are paid a fee for promising to buy a stock at a lower price you pick (cash-secured put), or to sell shares you own at a higher price (covered call). Run every month on the S&P 500 from mid-1986 to end-2018, the put version earned 9.54% a year against 9.80% for the index, with two-thirds of the swings and a worst fall of 32.7% against 50.9%. The one thing the evidence says: this is a calmer, capped way of holding stocks, not a way to catch rallies. From 2013 to 2025 it earned about half the market's yearly return.
research.how_it_works: Cash-secured put: you promise to buy 100 shares at a price you choose (the "strike" [the agreed price]) any time up to a set date, and the other side pays you a fee up front (the "premium"); you keep enough cash set aside to pay for the shares. If the price stays above your level the promise lapses and you keep the fee; if it falls below, you must buy at your level even when the market price is far lower. Covered call: the mirror image on shares you already own - you are paid a fee for promising to sell 100 shares at a higher price, and if the stock runs past that price your gain stops there. The two yardsticks that measure this, Cboe's PUT and BXM indexes, do it mechanically on the S&P 500 once a month (around the third Friday) with the strike set at the current price ("at the money"), holding Treasury bills (PUT) or the index itself (BXM); both are paper indexes before costs and taxes. Economically the two are the same trade: stock-like downside, capped upside, plus a fee. The fee has been worth having on average because option buyers have paid for bigger swings than later happened (the VIX [the swing size option prices were charging for] averaged 19.3 against 15.1 actually delivered, 1990-2018).
research.sitting_in_cash_relevance: It directly attacks the 'cash earns nothing while I wait' half of the problem: the same cash sits in Treasury bills and also collects a fee, and in flat or choppy years that has beaten simply owning the market (2011, 2015; PUT averaged +1.67% in flat months against -0.08% for the S&P 500). It does much less for the 'I miss the moves' half. The put index caught only about a third of the market's up months (up-beta 0.34) while taking about three-quarters of the down months (down-beta 0.75); after the March 2020 low the S&P 500 rose 67.9% by year-end and the put index 40.6%. If a chosen stock never dips to the level, the investor keeps a small fee and still owns nothing. Fit with Alan's rule: fundamentals can still pick WHAT (which names to make the promise on) and technicals can pick WHEN and WHERE (the strike at a support level acts as a paid limit order; a covered call at resistance acts as a paid trim order). The difference from his current reload and trim orders is that these are binding: he must buy on a drop even if the drop came from a broken earnings story, and a covered call sells the whole 100-share lot on a breakout rather than letting a winner run. The evidence describes it as a smoother, capped form of stock exposure, not a substitute for being invested.

Israelov and Nielsen 2015: only the abstract page was read. The sample period behind the 'Sharpe near 1.0 / 10% of risk / 25% of risk' figures and any BXM return figures inside the paper were not checked.

The since-1986 BXM figures after January 2012 (about 8.50% a year to end-2018, 8.48% to end-2025) and PUT figures after December 2018 (9.58% to end-2025) are OUR arithmetic - a published starting value carried forward with Cboe's index files - not numbers any source publishes. The same goes for every calendar-year, crash, rebound and 2013-2025 figure taken from S2-BXM / S2-PUT / S2-SPX. Cross-checks that passed: the method reproduces Cboe's published PUT 9.40% to Aug 2023 and the published -32.7% PUT month-end drawdown.

The S&P 500 'with dividends' comparisons for 2019-2025 use Damodaran's yearly series, which differs slightly from S&P's official total-return index (for example 2008: -36.55% here vs the 'down 37%' quoted in S4). The roughly 11.1% a year S&P figure for 30 Jun 1986 - 31 Dec 2025 mixes Bondarenko's value to 2018 with Damodaran's later years.

The Cboe/Solaka post (S3) quotes the S&P 500 at 9.91% a year for 1 Jul 1986 - 31 Aug 2023 without saying whether dividends are included. Our total-return chain gives about 10.5% for that period, so that comparison probably flatters PUT by about half a point; the PUT figure itself checks out.

A dividend.com article quoted in search results gives BXM since June 1986 as 8.5% a year vs 11.2% for the S&P 500 total return, volatility 10.7% vs 15.2%, max drawdown -35.8% vs -50.9%, beta 0.62. The page returned 403. Our own arithmetic matches the 8.5% and the -35.8%, but the 10.7% volatility, the beta and the end date are unverified. No fetched source gives BXM volatility since 1986 beyond the 11.4% to January 2012.

Daily-return volatility is much higher than the monthly figures the studies use (3 Jan 2007 - 5 Oct 2026, our calculation: BXM 14.3%, PUT 13.9%, S&P price index 19.7%). A model fed daily data should not be compared to the 9.95% / 11.4% monthly-based figures.
Wilshire's 2016 and 2019 full studies (gated) were not opened; only the 2016 press release was read.

Single stocks: from memory, the research literature (Driessen, Maenhout and Vilkov 2009; Carr and Wu 2009; Bakshi and Kapadia 2003) finds the 'overpriced insurance' effect is large for index options and small or absent on average for individual stocks. The abstracts fetched do not say this plainly, so it is unverified here. Nothing in this research measures out-of-the-money puts on individual growth stocks at chart support levels.
Interactive Brokers documentation could not be opened (403), so IBKR's specific cash, margin and permission rules for cash-secured puts and covered calls are not verified. Vanguard was not searched.

Tax points are US federal only, from IRS Publication 550 (2025 edition) sentences. State tax, wash-sale interactions, the 'special year-end rule', and the different treatment of broad index options (Section 1256, from memory) were not checked. This is not tax advice.

The Ennis Knupp table of PUT vs S&P returns in up, flat and down months was read from flattened PDF text; the column mapping (share of months, PUT return, monthly deviation, S&P return, correlation) is very likely right but was not checked against the page image.
The two Options Industry Council pages and several Cboe pages were read through an automatic page summariser, so their wording is paraphrased rather than quoted.
2026 figures run only to 5 October 2026 (year to date: BXM +11.8%, PUT +10.7%, S&P price index +13.6%) and may be revised.

Housekeeping: no project files were created, edited or deleted, no git writes, no orders. The fetch tool itself cached four downloaded PDFs in the session's own tool-results folder; those are harness cache files, not project files.

findings.claim: MODEL CHECK, PUT index: selling one-month puts on the S&P 500 every month, with the cash in Treasury bills, earned about the same as owning the S&P 500 over 32.5 years, with about two-thirds of the swings and a shallower worst fall. Add one caveat the researcher left out: the PUT index only went live in 2007, so everything before that is a reconstruction (a back-test [a what-would-have-happened calculation]) that assumes each put was sold at the bid price.
findings.numbers: Cboe S&P 500 PutWrite Index (PUT) vs S&P 500 total return [dividends included], 30 Jun 1986 - 31 Dec 2018, month-end data, before costs and taxes: compound yearly return 9.54% vs 9.80%; volatility [size of the swings, annualised] 9.95% vs 14.93%; maximum drawdown [worst fall from a peak] -32.7% vs -50.9%; longest time under water 40 vs 73 months; $1 grew to $19.35 vs $20.85; Sharpe ratio [return per unit of swing] 0.65 vs 0.49; beta [move per 1% market move] 0.56. Guest post on Cboe Insights (by a manager who sells the strategy), 1 Jul 1986 - 31 Aug 2023: PUT 9.40% a year, volatility 10.26%, max drawdown -32.66%. Our arithmetic from Cboe's public index file (recomputed independently): 9.58% a year for 30 Jun 1986 - 31 Dec 2025; the same method gives 9.396% to 31 Aug 2023, matching the published 9.40%. On DAILY closes the PUT worst fall is -37.1% (19 May 2008 - 9 Mar 2009).
findings.note: Every published number seen in the Bondarenko PDF (Exhibits 4, 6, 10, 27) and on the Solaka page. I re-downloaded PUT_History.csv and reproduced 9.58%, 9.396% and the -37.09% daily drawdown; month-end drawdown from the file is -32.66% (end-May 2008 to end-Feb 2009). Bondarenko's Exhibit 1 lists PUT as launched 2007 with price history from 30 Jun 1986, and the paper's disclaimer says the data are back-tested and ignore costs and taxes; Cboe paid for the research.

findings.claim: MODEL CHECK, BXM index: the covered-call version tied the S&P 500 for its first 25 years with less swing, then fell well behind in the long bull market that followed.
findings.numbers: Cboe S&P 500 BuyWrite Index (BXM) vs S&P 500 total return. 1 Jun 1988 - 31 Mar 2004: 12.39% vs 12.20% a year, about two-thirds of the volatility (Ibbotson). 1 Jun 1988 - 31 Aug 2006: 11.77% vs 11.67%; volatility 9.29% vs 13.89% (Callan). 30 Jun 1986 - 31 Jan 2012: 9.17% vs 9.17%; volatility 11.4% vs 15.9%; $1 grew to $9.43 vs $9.44 (Hewitt EnnisKnupp). Our arithmetic (that $9.43 carried forward with Cboe's BXM file, recomputed independently): 8.50% a year for 30 Jun 1986 - 31 Dec 2018 against the S&P's 9.80%, and 8.48% a year to 31 Dec 2025 against about 11.1% for the S&P 500 with dividends. BXM maximum drawdown: -35.8% on month-end values (end-May 2008 to end-Feb 2009), -40.1% on daily closes (26 Dec 2007 - 9 Mar 2009). Month-end volatility Dec 2006 - Sep 2026 (our calculation): BXM 10.96%, PUT 10.74% (from Jan 2007), S&P 500 price index 15.40%.
findings.note: All three consultant figures seen in the PDFs. Recomputed from BXM_History.csv: 8.505% and 8.484%; month-end drawdown -35.81%, daily -40.14%; volatilities 10.96 / 10.74 / 15.40. The 11.1% S&P figure (11.06%) chains Bondarenko's $20.85 at end-2018 with Damodaran's 2019-2025 yearly returns - a mix of two series, as the researcher disclosed. All three consultant studies state that Cboe gave financial support (the researcher flagged this for Ibbotson and Hewitt but not Callan).

findings.claim: CORRECTED WORDING: in the years asked about, option-selling took roughly a quarter to a half off the loss in down years, and gave up about half or more of the gain in most big up years - but not all of them. In 2021 and 2024 it kept roughly three-quarters of the market's gain.
findings.numbers: Calendar-year returns, BXM / PUT / S&P 500 with dividends: 2008: -28.7% / -26.8% / -36.55%. 2013: +13.3% / +12.3% / +32.15%. 2019: +15.7% / +13.5% / +31.21%. 2020: -2.8% / +2.1% / +18.02%. 2021 (not in the original list): +20.5% / +21.8% / +28.47%. 2022: -11.4% / -7.7% / -18.04%. 2023: +11.8% / +14.3% / +26.06%. 2024: +20.1% / +17.8% / +24.88%. 2025: +8.9% / +9.2% / +17.78%. Over the 18 calendar years 2008-2025, BXM beat the S&P 500 in 4 years (2008, 2011, 2015, 2022) and PUT in 5 (those plus 2009). BXM and PUT are our arithmetic from Cboe's daily files (last close of each year); S&P figures are Damodaran's 'includes dividends' series.
findings.note: Every number reproduced from the Cboe files and the Damodaran page. The original wording ('softened the down years a little and gave up half or more of the big up years') does not fit all the years: in 2022 PUT lost under half of what the market lost (-7.7% vs -18.04%), and in 2024 BXM kept about 80% of the gain (+20.1% vs +24.88%). BXM in 2009 was +25.91% against Damodaran's +25.94% - a near tie that would flip using S&P's official total-return figure, so '4 years' for BXM is sensitive to the data source.

findings.claim: CORRECTED WORDING - STRONGEST EVIDENCE AGAINST (1): in a fast crash you take most of the fall (about 85-90% of it in 2020), and then the cap costs you roughly 40-47% of the rebound - so you needed many more months to get back to where you started.
findings.numbers: Covid crash, daily closes 19 Feb - 23 Mar 2020: S&P 500 price index -33.9%, BXM -30.2%, PUT -28.9%. Month of March 2020: BXM -14.9% and PUT -13.4%, both WORSE than the S&P 500 price index at -12.5%. Rebound 23 Mar - 31 Dec 2020: S&P +67.9%, PUT +40.6%, BXM +36.3% (so the sellers kept about 53-60% of the rebound, not a small fraction). Back to the 19 Feb 2020 level: S&P 18 Aug 2020, PUT 7 Jan 2021, BXM 22 Mar 2021. Other falls: 3 Jan - 12 Oct 2022 S&P -25.4% vs worst falls of -18.2% (BXM) and -16.0% (PUT); 19 Feb - 8 Apr 2025 S&P -18.9%, BXM -15.5%, PUT -15.0%. PUT's worst month in its whole history: -17.65% (October 2008), worse than the S&P 500's -16.79% that month.
findings.note: All numbers reproduced from the three Cboe files. The original phrase 'the cap stops you taking most of the rebound' overstates it: PUT took 40.6 of 67.9 points (60%), BXM 36.3 (53%). The explanation for March 2020 ('options were re-sold near the low') is the researcher's inference - the roll date was Friday 20 March and the low was Monday 23 March - not something a source states. -17.65% is Bondarenko's minimum monthly return for both 1986-2018 and 2006-2018; the PUT file shows it is October 2008. The S&P comparison in these crash figures is the PRICE index (no dividends).

findings.claim: CORRECTED: the shape is lopsided by design, but the 'one-third of the ups, three-quarters of the downs' line is easy to misread. Those are slopes on top of a head start of about 0.89% a month. In plain averages the put-selling index made about half of what the market made in strong up months, lost about half of what the market lost in strong down months, and made about 1.7% in flat months when the market made nothing. The lopsidedness shows in the extremes: its bad months are rarer but nastier.
findings.numbers: PUT vs S&P 500, monthly, Jul 1986 - Dec 2018 (Bondarenko, Exhibit 28): up-market beta 0.34, down-market beta 0.75 [beta = extra move per extra 1% market move], regression alpha [the starting point when the market is flat] 0.89% a month; with one ordinary beta of 0.56 the alpha is 0.20% a month (2.39% a year). Skew -2.09 vs -0.81 [more negative = rarer but nastier bad months]. Ennis Knupp, 30 Jun 1986 - 31 Oct 2008: strong up months (48.7% of months) PUT +2.11% vs S&P +4.14%; flat months (29.2%) +1.67% vs -0.08%; strong down months (22.1%) -2.93% vs -5.38%. BXM skew -1.55 vs -0.78 (30 Jun 1986 - 31 Jan 2012); BXM in October 1987: -17.5% vs S&P -21.5%.
findings.note: All numbers seen in the PDFs; the Ennis Knupp column mapping is confirmed by the paper's own text ('State 1 ... average monthly return of 4.14%'). The correction is to the wording: the original called 0.89% 'an average fee edge' and the summary section said the index 'caught only about a third of the market's up months while taking about three-quarters of the down months'. 0.89% is a regression intercept, not spendable extra return, and the average capture in both strong-up and strong-down months was about half (2.11/4.14 = 51%; 2.93/5.38 = 54%).

findings.claim: Why it has paid at all: buyers of S&P 500 index options have usually paid for more turbulence than arrived, so the seller collects an insurance-style margin - but collecting a big fee does not mean making money that year.
findings.numbers: VIX [swing size priced into S&P 500 options] averaged 19.3 vs 15.1 actually delivered, 1990-2018 - a gap of 4.2 points; on yearly averages the gap was positive in 28 of 29 years, the exception being 2008 (32.7 priced vs 35.2 delivered). Earlier window Jun 1988 - Mar 2004: 16.5 priced vs 14.9 delivered (Ibbotson). PUT gross fees collected averaged 22.1% of the underlying value per year over 2006-2018 (about 1.85% a month; 2006 covers 11 months), ranging from 11.1% (2017) to 41.9% (2008). In 2008 the index collected that 41.9% and still lost 26.8% for the year.
findings.note: Year-by-year table (Bondarenko Exhibit 11/12) and premium table (Exhibit 22) read directly; I counted 28 of 29 years. These are yearly AVERAGES - individual months inside good years still had delivered swings above the priced level. The -26.8% for 2008 is our arithmetic from the PUT file (reproduced: -26.77%). Bondarenko himself notes 'gross premiums collected are always positive ... net returns can be negative'. This evidence is for S&P 500 INDEX options only.

findings.claim: STRONGEST EVIDENCE AGAINST (2): researchers at AQR took the covered-call strategy apart and found that plain stock-market exposure supplied most of the risk and most of the return; the fee-for-insurance part was well paid for its size but only about a tenth of the risk; and about a quarter of the risk was an unpaid side-bet on timing. A separate AQR paper shows put-selling and covered calls are the same trade - the PUT index's lead over BXM comes from a quirk of about four hours a month.
findings.numbers: Israelov and Nielsen (Financial Analysts Journal vol 71 no 6, Nov 2015), abstract: 'the equity exposure contributed most of the risk and return'; the short-volatility exposure [the fee-for-insurance piece] 'realized a Sharpe ratio of nearly 1.0 but contributed only 10% of the risk'; the equity reversal exposure [the position automatically gets bigger after falls and smaller after rises] 'contributed approximately 25% of the risk but provided little return'. Israelov (AQR white paper, March 2017): PUT beat BXM by about 1.1% a year between 1986 and 2015; the main reason is about four hours a month on option-expiry mornings (9:30 am - 1:30 pm) when PUT holds no stock exposure and BXM holds full exposure. Over 2004-2015 BXM trailed PUT by 2.1% a year, of which about 2.0% came from those expiry-day windows; on all other days BXM was ahead by 0.1% a year.
findings.note: The FAJ abstract was read word for word on the CFA Institute page; the sample period is not given in the abstract and the full article is paywalled. The Israelov 2017 claim is now verified on the PRIMARY paper: SSRN returned 403 and two AQR web pages returned 404, but AQR's own PDF loads and states the 1.1%, 1986-2015 and four-hours figures (the researcher had only a secondary summary). Practical reading: the PUT numbers used as the headline are the more flattering of the two indexes for a reason that is not repeatable skill.

findings.claim: STRONGEST EVIDENCE AGAINST (3): the flattering long-run numbers lean on 1986-2012. Over the last 13 full years the cap cost a bit under half of the market's yearly return, which compounds to roughly a third of the market's total gain; and even the Cboe-funded study shows no risk-adjusted edge in its recent window.
findings.numbers: Calendar 2013-2025 compound yearly return: S&P 500 with dividends about 14.8%, PUT 8.1%, BXM 7.5% ($1 became about $5.99 vs $2.74 vs $2.55 - a gain of $4.99 vs $1.74 vs $1.55). Calendar 2008-2025 (roughly the period since PUT went live): S&P about 11.0%, PUT 6.9%, BXM 5.7%. Bondarenko's own recent window, 31 Jan 2006 - 31 Dec 2018: PUT 5.97% a year vs S&P 7.59%; Sharpe ratio 0.50 vs 0.51; volatility 10.69% vs 14.32%; worst fall -32.7% vs -50.9%. Callan records BXM lagging late in the 1990s bull market (1995-1998). Cboe's own 2021 article says all four of its option-writing indexes had lower annualized returns than the S&P 500 over the 35 years to mid-2021.
findings.note: Recomputed: PUT multiple 2.738 (8.06%), BXM 2.550 (7.46%), Damodaran chain 5.985 (14.76%) for 2013-2025; 6.86% / 5.67% / 10.96% for 2008-2025. Bondarenko figures seen in Exhibits 16 and 19. Callan wording seen ('underperformed the S&P 500 late in the bull equity market (1995-1998)'). The Cboe 2021 sentence was read in the page text. The index returns are our arithmetic from Cboe's files, not published figures.

findings.claim: Practical drag the indexes leave out: taxes, the 100-share lot size, being made to deal early, and fund costs. One addition: the tax treatment of what the indexes do (S&P 500 index options) is gentler than the treatment of options on individual stocks, so the index results understate the tax drag for a stock-picker.
findings.numbers: US tax (IRS Publication 550, 2025 edition): if a sold option lapses, the amount received 'is short-term capital gain'; if a put you wrote is exercised, 'decrease your basis in the stock' by the fee and the 'holding period for the stock begins on the date you buy it'; if a call you wrote is exercised, 'increase your amount realized on the sale' by the fee; a covered call escapes the loss-deferral 'straddle' rules only if 'qualified' (exchange-traded, granted more than 30 days before expiry, not deep in the money, among other tests), and a 'special year-end rule' can still apply. Broad-based stock-index options are 'nonequity options' taxed under the 60/40 rule (60% long-term, 40% short-term) - individual-stock options are not. Size: the industry council's example sets aside $6,000 for one put with a 60 strike (100 shares). Early assignment [being made to carry out the promise before the end date]: possible; for covered calls the classic case is the day before the stock goes ex-dividend. Funds, 31 Dec 2007 - 31 Jan 2012: BXM index +0.47% a year; the ETF tracking it (PBP, 0.75% fee) -1.51% a year; the exchange-traded note tracking it (BWV, also 0.75%) -0.19% a year.
findings.note: IRS text read directly from the page (sections 'Writers of puts and calls', Table 4-3, 'Qualified covered call options and optioned stock', '60/40 rule', 'nonequity options'). OIC pages confirm the $6,000 / 60-strike example and the ex-dividend warning. Hewitt Exhibit 15 confirms the fund figures; the researcher quoted only the worse of the two products (PBP lagged by about 2.0 points a year, BWV by about 0.7), and Hewitt itself reports tracking error of 0.7% and 0.3%. US federal only; not tax advice.

Introduction states: average variance risk premia 'are strongly negative for the S&P 500 and 100 indexes and for the Dow Jones Industrial Average. The variance risk premia for the Nasdaq 100 index and for most individual stocks are also negative, but with a smaller absolute magnitude.' Sample: five indexes and 35 heavily traded stocks over about seven years. The published abstract (https://ideas.repec.org/a/oup/rfinst/v22y2009i3p1311-1341.html, also fetched) confirms title, authors and journal but not this sentence.

sources.title: BIS Quarterly Review, March 2024 - box 'What could explain the recent drop in VIX?'
sources.note: ADDED BY THE FACT-CHECKER. Box text read directly: 'the meteoric rise of yield-enhancing structured products linked to the S&P 500 over the last two years has gone hand in hand with the drop of VIX over the same period'; names the covered call as the classic example. sources.title: Episode 375: Covered Calls: A Devil's Bargain (podcast page)
sources.note: ADDED BY THE FACT-CHECKER, SECONDARY ONLY. Dated 18 Sep 2025. Discusses the paper 'A Devil's Bargain: When Generating Income Undermines Investment Returns' (Roni Israelov and a co-author; SSRN abstract 4580048 returned 403, so the paper itself and the co-author's exact name were not seen). The page's summary: higher distribution yields on covered-call strategies go with lower expected total returns.

missing: The good-looking early record was never lived. Cboe's PUT index was launched in 2007 with history rebuilt back to 1986 'using historical options prices, with the assumption that each put option was sold at the bid price' (Ennis Knupp, a paper Cboe paid for); Bondarenko's Exhibit 1 confirms 'Year Launched 2007'. Since it went live, calendar 2008-2025, PUT made about 6.9% a year against about 11.0% for the S&P 500 with dividends (our arithmetic). Sources fetched: https://cdn.cboe.com/resources/education/research_publications/PUTIndexEnnisKnupp.pdf and https://cdn.cboe.com/resources/education/research_publications/PutWriteCBOE19_v14_by_Prof_Oleg_Bondarenko_as_of_June_14.pdf

The fee edge is smaller on individual stocks than on the index - which is the version a stock-picker would actually run. Carr and Wu (working-paper version of their 2009 Review of Financial Studies article; 5 indexes and 35 heavily traded stocks) found the premium 'strongly negative for the S&P 500 and 100 indexes' but for 'most individual stocks ... with a smaller absolute magnitude'. Driessen, Maenhout and Vilkov's abstract adds that the related premium 'cannot be exploited with realistic trading frictions'. The researcher had this only from memory. Sources fetched: https://engineering.nyu.edu/sites/default/files/2019-01/CarrReviewofFinStudiesMarch2009-a.pdf and https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/jfinan/v64y2009i3p1377-1406.html

The trade may be getting crowded, which would shrink the fee. A Bank for International Settlements box (March 2024) links the 'meteoric rise of yield-enhancing structured products linked to the S&P 500' - covered calls being the classic example - to the fall in the VIX [the swing size option prices charge for] over the same two years. The BIS calls this suggestive, not proven. Source fetched: https://www.bis.org/publ/qtrpdf/r_qt2403a.htm

The index results get a tax break a stock-picker would not. The Cboe indexes sell S&P 500 index options, which IRS Publication 550 treats as 'nonequity options' under the 60/40 rule (60% of gain taxed as long-term whatever the holding time). Fees from options on individual stocks are short-term gains. So the after-tax gap between the paper indexes and a single-stock version is wider than the pre-tax figures suggest (US federal only; not tax advice). Source fetched: https://www.irs.gov/publications/p550

Evidence in the strategy's favour that the researcher underplayed: in a SLOW bear market the cushion was much bigger than in a fast crash. Callan records the S&P 500's worst drawdown as -47.4% (5 Sep 2000 - 9 Oct 2002) against -32.5% for BXM over the same dates, and says BXM 'consistently outperformed the S&P 500 in all periods of declining equity markets' in 1988-2006. 'You take most of the fall' is true of sudden crashes (2020), less true of grinding declines. Source fetched: https://cdn.cboe.com/resources/education/research_publications/Callan_CBOE.pdf

The headline uses the more flattering of the two indexes. AQR's Israelov shows PUT's lead over BXM (about 1.1% a year, 1986-2015) comes from four hours a month when PUT happened to be out of the market; over 2004-2015 that quirk explains about 2.0 of the 2.1 points, and on all other days BXM was slightly ahead. BXM's roughly 8.5% a year since 1986 is therefore the fairer guide to the strategy than PUT's 9.5%. Source fetched: https://images.aqr.com/-/media/AQR/Documents/Insights/White-Papers/AQR-PutWrite-vs-BuyWritevF.pdf

The measured design is the most upside-capping variant. Cboe's own 2021 article says at-the-money selling collects more fee (about 1.7% a month for BXM since May 2006) but 'foregoes participation in the upside', while selling 2% out of the money collects about 0.9% a month and keeps more of a bull market. A strike set at a support or resistance level is an out-of-the-money trade: smaller fee, looser cap - and none of the sources measures it. The same article concedes all four Cboe option-writing indexes returned less than the S&P 500 over the 35 years to mid-2021. Source fetched: https://www.cboe.com/insights/posts/benchmark-indices-series-income-generation-and-smoother-returns-with-cboes-bxm-bxmd-put-and-cmbo-indices

'Income' is the wrong word for the fee. AQR's page for 'Covered Call Strategies: One Fact and Eight Myths' says to drop the stories that covered calls give a downside buffer or generate income, and to see them as stock exposure plus selling volatility. A later paper by Israelov and a co-author ('A Devil's Bargain', 2023) is reported - on a secondary podcast page only; SSRN blocked the paper itself - as finding that the higher the payout a covered-call strategy advertises, the lower its expected total return. Sources fetched: https://www.aqr.com/Insights/Research/Journal-Article/Covered-Call-Strategies-One-Fact-and-Eight-Myths and https://rationalreminder.ca/podcast/375

Interactive Brokers documentation, which the researcher could not open: IBKR's own lesson says its examples leave out commissions, that 'there is also a risk of early assignment when selling options', and that when a cash-secured put finishes below the strike the choices are to take the shares 'at the strike price above where it's trading at in the market', close 'possibly for a loss', or roll to a later date. Its covered-call example shows a $1,500 gain cut to $1,100 when the stock runs past the strike. IBKR's exact cash and permission rules were still not seen (the margin table is loaded by script and did not render). Source fetched: https://www.interactivebrokers.com/campus/trading-lessons/generating-income-through-options/

Who paid for the supportive studies: all five Cboe-hosted studies used here (Ibbotson 2004, Callan 2006, Ennis Knupp 2008, Hewitt EnnisKnupp 2012, Bondarenko 2019) state that Cboe gave financial support or compensation; the researcher flagged this for three and missed Callan and Ennis Knupp. The critical evidence comes from AQR, which runs competing option strategies. Sources fetched: https://cdn.cboe.com/resources/education/research_publications/Callan_CBOE.pdf and https://cdn.cboe.com/resources/education/research_publications/PUTIndexEnnisKnupp.pdf

Limits of this check: the WebSearch tool was unavailable (session budget used up), so I worked by fetching addresses directly. Could NOT be opened: SSRN (403), the two journal pages for Whaley 2002 and Ungar-Moran 2009 (login wall), Morningstar's fund-performance articles (403), Alpha Architect (403), IBKR's knowledge-base article on early assignment (redirects to a search page). Real covered-call fund results after 2012 therefore remain unverified; the only live-fund evidence seen is Hewitt's 2007-2012 table at https://cdn.cboe.com/resources/education/research_publications/HewittEnnisKnupp-BXM-(2012).pdf
failure_modes_checked: Fast crashes: you carry most of the fall. 19 Feb - 23 Mar 2020: S&P 500 price index -33.9%, BXM -30.2%, PUT -28.9% (about 85-90% of the fall); calendar 2008: BXM -28.7%, PUT -26.8% vs S&P -36.55%; October 2008 was PUT's worst month ever at -17.65%, worse than the S&P's -16.79%. All reproduced from Cboe's files and the Bondarenko PDF [S1][S2-BXM][S2-PUT][S2-SPX][S7]

Sharp rebounds (reworded): the cap cost roughly 40-47% of the bounce. 23 Mar - 31 Dec 2020: S&P +67.9% vs PUT +40.6% and BXM +36.3%; the S&P was back to its pre-crash level on 18 Aug 2020, PUT on 7 Jan 2021, BXM on 22 Mar 2021 [S2-BXM][S2-PUT][S2-SPX]

Strong bull years (reworded): about half or more of the gain was given up in 2013 (+13.3% BXM, +12.3% PUT vs +32.15%), 2019 (+15.7%, +13.5% vs +31.21%), 2020 (-2.8%, +2.1% vs +18.02%), 2023 (+11.8%, +14.3% vs +26.06%) and 2025 (+8.9%, +9.2% vs +17.78%); only about a fifth to a quarter in 2021 (+20.5%, +21.8% vs +28.47%) and 2024 (+20.1%, +17.8% vs +24.88%); also late in the 1990s bull market [S2-BXM][S2-PUT][S7][S6]

Whipsaw around the monthly re-sale date: in March 2020 both indexes lost MORE than the S&P 500 price index for the month (BXM -14.9%, PUT -13.4% vs -12.5%). The numbers are verified; the explanation (new options sold on 20 March, one trading day before the low, then capping the bounce) is our inference, not a source statement. AQR separately finds a built-in timing bet is about 25% of a covered call's risk for little return [S2-BXM][S2-PUT][S2-SPX][S9]

A long, steady bull market: 2013-2025 the S&P 500 compounded at about 14.8% a year against 8.1% (PUT) and 7.5% (BXM) - $1 became about $5.99 vs $2.74 vs $2.55; the indexes beat the S&P in only 4-5 of the 18 calendar years 2008-2025 (BXM's 2009 was a near tie) [S2-BXM][S2-PUT][S7]

When markets swing more than option prices assumed, the fee does not cover the damage: 2008 is the one year in 1990-2018 where delivered swings (35.2) exceeded what was priced (32.7) on yearly averages, and PUT lost 26.8% despite collecting 41.9% in gross fees [S1][S2-PUT]

The promise is binding: with a cash-secured put you must buy 100 shares at your price even if the stock has dropped far below it on bad news - worst case is the strike minus the fee if the stock goes to zero; the only exits are taking the shares, buying the option back (possibly at a loss) or rolling it. With a covered call your gain stops at the strike plus the fee if the stock breaks out [S14][S15][S26]

The stock runs away without you: if the price never falls to your level you keep only the fee and own no shares, so the 'missed move' is still missed. The put's own maximum gain is limited to the fee [S14]

Taxes and costs the indexes ignore: in the US, fees from lapsed options are short-term gains; covered calls can trip the straddle loss-deferral rules unless 'qualified'; the indexes exclude trading costs and taxes. The indexes use S&P 500 index options, which get gentler 60/40 tax treatment that individual-stock options do not. Real BXM-tracking products lagged the index by about 0.7 (BWV note) to 2.0 (PBP ETF) points a year over 31 Dec 2007 - 31 Jan 2012 [S13][S1][S4]

Lot size: one contract = 100 shares, so cash set aside = strike x 100 (the industry example ties up $6,000 for a 60 strike; by the same arithmetic a $300 stock ties up $30,000), which forces lumpy position sizes in a personal account [S14]

Scope gap (strengthened): every measured number here is for at-the-money, one-month options on the S&P 500 INDEX. No source measures out-of-the-money puts on individual growth stocks at chart support levels. The one study read on the point (Carr and Wu) found the 'overpriced insurance' effect smaller for most individual stocks than for the S&P indexes [S27][S24]

Back-test risk (added): the PUT index was launched in 2007 and BXM was announced in 2002; their earlier histories are reconstructions, and PUT's assumes every put was sold at the bid. The strongest part of the record (1986-2006) was never lived by an investor [S1][S8][S6]

research.plain_summary: This is the plumbing at Interactive Brokers (IBKR) for selling puts backed by cash (you are paid a fee to promise to buy 100 shares at a set price) and selling calls on shares you already own. IBKR's own pages put covered calls at options Level 1, but selling a put, even one fully backed by cash, at Level 3. One contract is 100 shares, so a SPY put at 780 sets aside about $78,000. The evidence says this pays you while you wait, but does not stop you missing a rally: Cboe's put-selling index returned 9.40% a year against 9.91% for the S&P 500, July 1986 to August 2023.
research.how_it_works: Selling a cash-secured put: you collect a fee (the premium) today and promise to buy 100 shares at a chosen price (the strike) if the put's owner decides to sell them to you (assignment); in an IBKR cash account the broker sets aside the strike times 100 in cash so the purchase is already paid for. Selling a covered call is the mirror image: you own 100 shares, collect a fee, and promise to sell them at the strike if the call's owner asks. Options on shares and ETFs such as SPY are American-style (the owner can exercise on any day up to expiry) and settle in real shares; index options such as Cboe's XSP are European-style (exercise only at expiry) and settle in cash, so no shares change hands. At expiry the clearing house (OCC) automatically exercises any option that is in the money (worth exercising) by one cent or more, so a put seller ends up owning the shares and a call seller's shares are sold; otherwise the option expires and the seller keeps the fee. To keep the position going the seller "rolls" (buys back the expiring option and sells a later-dated one), and IBKR's Trader Workstation (TWS) has Write Options, Rollover Options and Option Chains screens for that. IBKR charges a per-contract commission to open or close, and no IBKR fee for exercise or assignment on US stock options and US index options.
research.sitting_in_cash_relevance: This structure addresses only half of the problem. A cash-secured put turns idle cash into paid waiting: the cash stays set aside (the full strike times 100 in an IBKR cash account), a fee is collected, and there is in effect a standing order to buy at the strike. That fits the stated rule reasonably well on the 'what' side (the put is written only on a company or index the investor would be glad to own on fundamentals) and the strike can be placed at a technical buy or reload level. But it does not put the cash into the market. If the price keeps rising, the investor keeps the fee and still owns nothing, which the OCC's education site names as a principal risk; and Cboe's put-selling index trailed the S&P 500 over July 1986 to August 2023 (9.40% vs 9.91% a year) and lags most in strong up years, exactly when cash hurts. The timing is also handed to the market: shares arrive when the price falls through the strike, not when a technical signal says buy. The covered-call half works against the complaint: it only applies once shares are owned, it caps the upside, and the shares cannot be trimmed while the call is open. Practical limits matter too: about $78,000 per SPY contract, Level 3 permission needed for the put, and no smaller standard contract (XSP is the same size as SPY). In short, the evidence supports this as a way to be paid for patience with a smoother ride, not as a way to stop missing moves.
