not_verified: The OCC disclosure booklet itself was not read: theocc.com returned HTTP 403 to every request, and a broker-hosted link turned out to be only a pointer page. Its exact wording (for example the often-quoted sentence that a covered call writer 'forgoes the opportunity to benefit from an increase in the value of the underlying interest above the option price') was seen only in a search snippet, and the 'June 2024' edition date likewise. The risk quotes used here come from the OCC's education site (optionseducation.org), not the booklet.

How the IBKR pages were read: the built-in fetch tool was refused by IBKR's sites (HTTP 403), so IBKR pages were read with plain command-line requests instead. IBKR's FAQ articles are script-rendered; their text was read from the public content feed the FAQ page itself loads, not from the rendered page. The old Knowledge Base addresses (ibkb.interactivebrokers.com/article/4860 and ibkr.info/article/4860) could not be rendered at all.
Whether SPY actually trades near 780 (and the S&P 500 near 7,800) today was not checked. The $78,000 figure is plain arithmetic (780 x 100) on the example strike supplied in the task.

Which row of IBKR's margin table applies to options on SPY and other ETFs in a margin account (the 20% stock rate or the 15% index rate) is not confirmed, because the table's footnotes did not come through. No dollar figure for a margin-account SPY put is therefore given.

Whether IBKR lets a cash account sell a single cash-secured XSP put, and exactly how much it sets aside for a cash-settled index put, is not stated explicitly on the pages read; the table says only 'Put Strike Price' for cash accounts.

'No fractional option contracts': no IBKR or OCC page read today says this in so many words. The pages only describe whole contracts covering 100 shares (multiplier $100). That listed options trade in whole contracts is general knowledge, not a sourced quote.

Cboe Nanos (a one-share-sized S&P 500 option): IBKR's commission page still lists them, but whether they are still listed and trading was not confirmed. Other lower-priced S&P 500 ETFs with options, which would give a smaller contract, were not researched.

The Bondarenko study PDF was not read, only Cboe's press release about it. It is not confirmed whether the index returns quoted are before costs and taxes; an index has no commissions, bid-ask costs or taxes, so a real account would do somewhat worse.

The statement that the put-selling index went from ahead of the S&P 500 (through 2015) to behind it (through August 2023) is a comparison across two separate Cboe publications, not a figure either source states directly.

IBKR's eligibility tests for each level (experience, income, net worth) were not read; the '21 years of age for Levels 2-4' requirement appeared only in a search snippet. Which IBKR entity holds Alan's account is unknown; IBKR Canada and India do not use the level system.

Interest paid on cash set aside for a put at IBKR, tax treatment (the 60/40 rule Cboe mentions for XSP, wash-sale and covered-call tax rules), exact exercise cut-off times and SPY's ex-dividend dates were not researched.
Whether TWS actually blocks selling shares that are covering a call at Level 1 was not tested; nothing was tested in a live or paper account.

Process note against the no-files rule: the fetch tool itself saved two downloaded PDFs (the pointer page and the Federal Register notice) into its own tool-results cache folder under the user's .claude-urth directory. No project file was created, edited or deleted, no git command was run and no order was placed.

findings.claim: Permission levels at IBKR: a covered call [selling a call on 100 shares you already own] and a buy-write [buying the shares and selling the call together] need only Level 1. Selling a put needs Level 3, not Level 2, even when the full purchase cost is sitting in the account as cash. IBKR defines Level 2 as 'Covered Options Positions as defined by FINRA Rule 2360' (with an added rule about spread expiry dates), and that FINRA rule only calls a short put 'covered' when the seller also owns a put of the same class at an equal or higher strike; cash does not count. Level 3 is 'Option strategies that have limited maximum potential loss'. A margin account [one that can borrow] may request Levels 1-4; a cash or IRA account only Levels 1-3, so a cash account can hold a cash-secured put, but only with Level 3. IBKR also requires clients to be at least 21 for Levels 2-4 and says it 'cannot disclose its eligibility requirements', so Level 3 approval cannot be assumed. Accounts with IBKR Canada and IBKR India are outside the level system.
findings.numbers: Levels 1-4. IBKR strategy chart: Covered Call/Covered Basket Call and Buy Write = Level 1; Long Call, Long Put, Protective Put, Collar = Level 2; Short Put and Short Put Spread = Level 3; Short Naked Call = Level 4. Minimum age 21 for Levels 2-4. Client Portal guide page 'Last Updated: October 3, 2025'.
findings.note: Seen on every page cited. FAQ article text (read through the content feed the FAQ page itself calls) shows the level definitions and the full strategy chart word for word, plus the disclaimer 'Accounts held with IB Canada and IB India are not subject to option level requirements'. The Client Portal guide repeats the list with Short Put under Level 3 and gives the path User menu > Settings > Trading > Trading Permissions. FINRA 2360(a)(10) read via the fetch tool: short put is covered only by a long option of the same class with an equal or greater exercise price; the escrow/specific-deposit route exists only for calls. The age-21 rule and the 'cannot disclose' sentence were not in the researcher's summary; I read them in two further IBKR FAQ articles.

findings.claim: Cash account versus margin account: in a cash account IBKR requires and sets aside the full purchase cost for a short put ('generally equal to the option strike price multiplied by the 100 shares'), and for a covered call the shares must be paid for in full. In a margin account [one that can borrow] the broker locks up only a fraction of that, so the put is 'cash-secured' only if the investor chooses to keep the cash there; nothing forces it. IBKR counts a cash-secured short put as an 'uncovered' option position, so its rule of at least USD 2,000 of account value to open or add to an uncovered position applies to it in both cash and margin accounts.
findings.numbers: IBKR US options margin table. Short Naked Put, Cash or IRA Cash: 'Put Strike Price'. Margin account, stock options: Put Price + Maximum((20% x Underlying Price - Out of the Money Amount), (10% x Strike Price)); index options use 15% in place of 20%. Covered Calls, Cash or IRA Cash: 'Stock paid in full or None'. Minimum net liquidation value USD 2,000. Own arithmetic: 780 strike x 100 = USD 78,000 set aside in a cash account.
findings.note: All table cells and the USD 2,000 sentence seen on IBKR's margin page (read with a plain web request; the fetch tool gets HTTP 403 from IBKR). The table's footnotes 1-3 are referenced but their text is not on the page, so which rate (20% or 15%) applies to SPY and other ETF options stays unconfirmed; do not print a dollar figure for a margin-account SPY put. Extra detail I found: IBKR FAQ 'What is an uncovered option position?' lists 'cash secured short puts' as an example of an uncovered position and repeats the USD 2,000 rule for 'either a cash or margin type account'.

findings.claim: Contract size: one standard contract covers 100 shares, and IBKR's lesson says you need 100 shares to write one call. Cboe's Mini-SPX (XSP) is one tenth of the big SPX contract, but Cboe itself says that gives it 'very similar notional size' to SPY, so XSP is not a smaller contract than SPY. What XSP changes is the settlement: it is European-style [can be exercised only at expiry, so no early assignment] and cash-settled [you pay or receive the difference in cash and never receive shares].
findings.numbers: XSP: based on 1/10th the value of the S&P 500 Index; multiplier $100; European exercise; 'delivery of cash on the business day following expiration'; minimum tick 0.01 ($1.00). Closing levels on 6 Oct 2026 from Cboe's public delayed-quote feed: SPY 779.09, S&P 500 7,818.93, XSP 781.89. So one put at a 780 strike covers 780 x $100 = $78,000 on either SPY or XSP.
findings.note: Cboe specification page and product page both read; every quoted phrase is on the page. The researcher had not checked whether SPY really trades near 780; I confirmed it from Cboe's delayed quotes (SPY closed 779.09 and XSP 781.89 on 6 Oct 2026), so the $78,000 example is realistic today. The Cboe product page is marketing from the exchange that lists the product.

findings.claim: The one documented way the cash tied up gets smaller is a different structure, not a smaller contract: a put spread [sell one put and buy a lower-strike put, which caps the loss at the gap between the two strikes]. IBKR's table lets a cash account hold a put spread at spread-width collateral only when both options are European-style and cash-settled (as XSP and SPX are); with American-style options such as SPY, a cash account must still hold the full short-put strike. A short put spread is Level 3. This is no longer a plan to buy shares on a dip: XSP settles in cash, so the investor never ends up owning anything.
findings.numbers: Put Spread, margin account: Maximum(Short Put Strike - Long Put Strike, 0). Cash or IRA Cash: 'Same as Margin Account (Both options must be European style cash settled)' and 'Short Put Strike Price (American style options)'. Own arithmetic: a 780/760 XSP put spread is 20 x $100 = $2,000 of collateral, against about $78,000 for the single put.
findings.note: Table row read word for word on IBKR's margin page; Short Put Spread = Level 3 is in the IBKR strategy chart. IBKR's FAQ adds that in cash or IRA accounts only spreads with identical expiry dates are allowed and only on European-style options. Still not stated on any page read: whether a cash account at IBKR may sell a single cash-secured XSP put, and what index-option trading permission that needs.

findings.claim: Early assignment on share and ETF options: IBKR states that the seller of an American-style option 'may be assigned an exercise at any time until the option expires' and 'you have no control over assignment'. For covered calls the known danger point is the dividend: IBKR says short calls are at assignment risk 'when they are in the money or if there is a dividend coming up and the extrinsic value [the part of the option price that is pure time value] of the short call is less than the dividend', and the OCC's education site says an early assignment the day before a stock goes ex-dividend 'would deprive the covered call writer of the stock dividend'. The only way to rule out assignment is to buy the option back before the close on its last trading day, and notice of an assignment arrives the next day because OCC processes exercises in a nightly batch.
findings.numbers: IBKR examples: a short 50-strike call assigned with the stock at 55 = net loss $500 per 100 shares, less the premium received; a short 96-strike put assigned with the stock at 90 = net loss $600 per 100 shares, less the premium received. To capture a dividend the call owner must exercise 'before 16:30 EST on the business day prior to the Ex-Dividend/Record date'.
findings.note: All five FAQ articles and the OCC education page were read and each quoted phrase is there. The assignment-notice FAQ describes a two-stage random draw (OCC to brokers, then IBKR to clients) posted as of the next day's close (E+1). The dividend FAQ also says the TWS Option Exercise Tool can be used 'any time before 17:25 EST'.

findings.claim: What happens at expiry, and IBKR's own powers: the clearing house (OCC) automatically exercises every option that is in the money [worth exercising] by at least USD 0.01 ('exercise by exception'), so a short put or call that finishes one cent in the money should be expected to be assigned. IBKR adds that a short option 'may be exercised against you by the long holder even if the option is out-of-the-money'. If an assignment would leave the account short of required funds, IBKR reserves the right to liquidate options before expiry, let options lapse, or allow delivery and then sell the shares, and says it is 'under no obligation to manage such risks for you'. On timing IBKR gives two statements: it 'generally initiate[s] expiration related liquidations 2 hours prior to the close', and liquidations of US security positions 'will typically begin at approximately 9:40 AM ET as of the business day following expiration'. So forced selling can come on the afternoon of expiry day as well as the next morning. After an early assignment that causes a shortfall, IBKR's automated liquidations 'are not confined to only shares that resulted from the option position'.
findings.numbers: Auto-exercise threshold USD 0.01 in the money. Expiry-related liquidations generally start 2 hours before the close; liquidations of US security positions typically begin about 9:40 AM ET on the business day after expiration. The exposure check 'is performed 3 days prior to the next expiration and is updated approximately every 15 minutes' and shows in TWS as 'Post-Expiry Margin'.
findings.note: Everything the researcher quoted is on the IBKR pages. The correction is an omission: the same expiry-liquidations article the researcher cited also says IBKR generally starts expiration-related liquidations two hours before the close, which the summary left out and which makes the '9:40 AM next day' picture too comfortable. These passages are about a margin shortfall; a fully cash-secured put in a cash account already has the purchase money set aside (that last sentence is my reading, not an IBKR quote).

findings.claim: Fees: IBKR states it 'does not charge an option exercise or assignment fee' on US stock options or US index options; only tiny regulator pass-through charges apply. Opening, closing and rolling [buying back the expiring option and selling a later one] does cost commission, a roll is two trades, and IBKR applies its order minimum to each leg of a combination order.
findings.numbers: US options, IBKR Pro, monthly volume up to 10,000 contracts: USD 0.65 per contract when the premium is USD 0.10 or more; USD 0.50 for premium from USD 0.05 to under 0.10; USD 0.25 below 0.05; minimum USD 1.00 per order; plus exchange and regulatory fees and OCC clearing 0.025 per contract. IBKR Lite: USD 0.65 per contract. IBKR's worked example: 2 contracts at a USD 5 premium = USD 1.30. Exercise and assignment: Stock Options 'No fees'; US Index Options 'No fees'; US stock options line shows FINRA Trading Activity Fee USD 0.000166 x Quantity Sold.
findings.note: Tiers, minimum, clearing fee and the worked example are on IBKR's commissions page; the page also says 'Commissions are not charged for US exercise and assignment' and 'Order minimums will be applied to the individual legs of a COMBO order'. The exercise/assignment table and the 'does not charge' sentence are on the Other Fees page. Small inconsistency between IBKR's own pages, pennies only: the commissions page shows the FINRA Trading Activity Fee at USD 0.00 with a footnote 'Fee Holiday ... for trades from Oct 1, 2026 through Dec 31, 2026', and the two pages show different SEC transaction fee figures (USD 0.00 on Other Fees, USD 0.0000206 x sales value on the commissions page). Safer to print 'a fraction of a cent per share' than the exact regulator figure.

findings.claim: IBKR tools that exist for this, per IBKR's own guides: in Trader Workstation (Mosaic: New Window > Advanced Option Tools; Classic TWS: Trading Tools > Advanced Option Tools) there is a Write Options tool that scans stock positions and proposes one call per 100 uncovered shares, with nearest-monthly, nearest-quarterly or days-to-expiry choices and a strike a chosen distance above the share price; a Rollover Options tool that lists options about to expire and builds orders to roll them; and Option Chains [the full table of strikes and expiry dates] opened from the pencil icon. Important limit, on both tools: the guide describes the Write Options tool as selling 'calls against long stock positions' and 'puts against your short stock positions', and the Rollover tool as a choice to 'roll calls on long stock positions, or roll puts on short stock positions'. Neither is described as writing or rolling a cash-secured put, so those are entered as ordinary option orders. An Option Exercise tool and a Client Portal setting to auto-exercise long calls for dividends also exist.
findings.numbers: TWS guide page 'Last updated on October 8, 2025'. IBKR Campus lesson (lesson 10 of 13 in the TWS Option Tools course): default is 'a short position of one contract for every 100 share position'. Guide: Rollover rolls 'to the next month's contract'.
findings.note: Two fixes. (1) Attribution: the 100-share default and the monthly/quarterly/days-to-expiry and strike-distance choices come from the IBKR Campus lesson, not the TWS guide page, which does not contain them. (2) The researcher flagged the covered-only limit for the Write tool but not for the Rollover tool; the guide's Rollover steps offer only calls on long stock or puts on short stock, and its own wording is roll 'to the next month's contract'. Nothing was tested in a live or paper account, so whether the Rollover screen would in practice list a cash-secured put is unknown.

findings.claim: The standard risk disclosure, and the strongest evidence against the structure. The OCC booklet 'Characteristics and Risks of Standardized Options' (the options disclosure document, ODD) is the document brokers must give customers under SEC Rule 9b-1, and IBKR says it gives it to every option-eligible client at application. The OCC's education site says of both strategies that 'the maximum loss is limited but substantial. The worst that can happen is for the stock to become worthless'; of the cash-secured put that 'by waiting for a price dip, the investor risks missing out on a stock that keeps climbing upward'; and of the covered call that 'the investor forfeits much of the stock's profit potential'. Cboe's own benchmark for put-selling (the PUT index: a hypothetical portfolio that sells one-month, at-the-money S&P 500 puts [strike at the current index level, not below it] backed by Treasury bills) shows a smoother ride but no extra return over the long run, and a clear lag in strong markets: ahead of the S&P 500 through 2015, behind it by August 2023, and much further behind since.
findings.numbers: Cboe article, July 1986 to 31 Aug 2023, PUT vs S&P 500: annualized return 9.40% vs 9.91%; standard deviation [how bumpy returns are] 10.26% vs 15.38%; maximum drawdown [worst peak-to-trough fall] -32.66% vs -50.96%; longest drawdown and recovery 30 vs 66 months; PUT beat the S&P 500 in 95% of rolling one-year periods when the S&P 500 return was below 0%. Cboe press release 27 Jan 2016 (study sponsored by Cboe), since mid-1986: annual compound return 10.13% vs 9.85%; standard deviation 10.16% vs 15.26%; 2006-2015 maximum drawdown 32.7% vs 50.9%; average annual gross premium 24.1%. Own arithmetic from Cboe's index history files: 31 Aug 2023 to 5 Oct 2026, PUT 2,532.05 to 3,692.27 = +45.8%; S&P 500 price index, before dividends, 4,507.66 to 7,773.95 = +72.5%.
findings.note: Every figure the researcher gave is on the two Cboe pages, and all the OCC-education quotes are on those pages. Corrections: (1) the PUT index sells at-the-money puts, which the summary dropped; a put placed below the market to 'buy the dip' is a different, lower-premium trade, and the Cboe article itself says writing further out of the money means 'less risk/return'. (2) The record stops at August 2023; Cboe's own downloadable history shows the gap has widened sharply since (see numbers). (3) 'Ahead through 2015, behind by August 2023' compares two separate Cboe publications, not one stated figure; the 2016 release says 'since mid-1986' without printing the end date in that sentence. (4) The ODD itself was not read by me either: theocc.com returns HTTP 403 to every request. What the ODD is and the Rule 9b-1 duty are confirmed from the SEC notice; IBKR's hand-out statement is in two IBKR FAQ articles. The 2023 Cboe article is by an options-strategy manager writing on the exchange's site, an interested source.

sources.title: Covered Call Strategies: One Fact and Eight Myths
sources.authors: Roni Israelov (the only name shown in the page text I read), AQR Capital Management; published in Financial Analysts Journal
sources.note: Added by the fact-checker. AQR's summary page; the paper itself was not downloaded. Quotes confirmed: 'We suggest that investors ignore the storytelling about obtaining downside buffers and generating income'; 'If you have no view on implied volatility, there is no reason to sell options'; 'option overwriting is a version of selling volatility'.

missing: The put-selling benchmark has fallen much further behind since the researcher's cut-off (August 2023). From Cboe's own index files: PUT went from 2,532.05 (31 Aug 2023) to 3,692.27 (5 Oct 2026), up 45.8%, while the S&P 500 price index went from 4,507.66 to 7,773.95, up 72.5% before dividends. By calendar year, PUT vs S&P 500 price index: 2023 +14.3% vs +24.2%; 2024 +17.8% vs +23.3%; 2025 +9.2% vs +16.4%; 2026 to 5 Oct +10.7% vs +13.6%. From end 2015 to 5 Oct 2026: +138.5% vs +280.3%. These percentages are my own arithmetic on Cboe's published levels, and the S&P figure leaves out dividends, so the true gap is wider. This is the period that matches Alan's complaint about missing rallies. https://cdn.cboe.com/api/global/us_indices/daily_prices/PUT_History.csv and https://cdn.cboe.com/api/global/us_indices/daily_prices/SPX_History.csv

The benchmark is not the 'buy the dip' trade. Cboe describes the PUT index as selling 'a sequence of one-month, at-the-money SPX puts' [strike at the current index level], and the 2023 article says investors who write 'further out of the money' get 'less risk/return'. The summary dropped 'at-the-money', so the 9.40% a year figure should not be read as what a below-market strike on a single stock would earn. https://ir.cboe.com/news/news-details/2016/New-Study-On-Weekly-Monthly-SP-500-PutWrite-Indexes-Released-01-27-2016/default.aspx and https://www.cboe.com/insights/posts/generating-income-and-managing-risk-cash-secured-put-writing-in-a-low-equity-return-environment

The two halves of this structure are the same bet, not two tools. The OCC's education site lists the covered call as the 'Comparable Position' to the cash-secured put and the cash-secured put as the comparable position to the covered call, and says the put 'isn't inherently more dangerous than a covered call'. So selling puts, then selling calls on the shares received, repeats one exposure (most of the downside, capped upside) rather than diversifying. It also states plainly: 'The outright stock buyer is better off than the put writer if the put is not assigned and the stock keeps rallying.' https://www.optionseducation.org/strategies/all-strategies/cash-secured-put and https://www.optionseducation.org/strategies/all-strategies/covered-call-buy-write

Published research says the 'income' story is misleading. AQR's summary of its Financial Analysts Journal paper says covered calls collect a volatility risk premium on top of ordinary share exposure, but 'also embed active equity exposure that behaves like a reversal strategy' [it leaves you holding more market risk after falls and less after rises], which is 'uncompensated' and 'a significant contributor to the covered call's risk'. That hidden timing works against a rule where technical signals decide when to add and trim. The companion paper says: 'We suggest that investors ignore the storytelling about obtaining downside buffers and generating income' and 'If you have no view on implied volatility, there is no reason to sell options.' AQR is an asset manager; I read its summary pages, not the papers. https://www.aqr.com/Insights/Research/Journal-Article/Covered-Calls-Uncovered and https://www.aqr.com/Insights/Research/Journal-Article/Covered-Call-Strategies-One-Fact-and-Eight-Myths

Cash at IBKR is not earning nothing, which changes the comparison. IBKR's interest page shows USD cash above the first $10,000 earning 3.380% a year at IBKR Pro (benchmark minus 0.5%) and 2.380% at IBKR Lite, with nothing on the first $10,000 and a proportionally lower rate for accounts under $100,000. The put fee should be weighed against that baseline, not against zero. The page does not say whether cash set aside for a short put keeps earning this interest; that needs asking IBKR. https://www.interactivebrokers.com/en/accounts/fees/pricing-interest-rates.php

IBKR's forced selling around expiry can start earlier than the summary says. The expiry-liquidations article states 'we generally initiate expiration related liquidations 2 hours prior to the close, but reserves the right to begin this process sooner or later', in addition to the 9:40 AM next-day timing quoted from the other article. https://www.interactivebrokers.com/lib/cstools/faq/#/content/1163245142

IBKR classes a cash-secured put as an 'uncovered' position, and access is gated. 'Examples of uncovered option positions include cash secured short puts'; an account needs at least USD 2,000 to open or add to one; Levels 2-4 need the client to be 21 or older; and 'IBKR cannot disclose its eligibility requirements for products', which depend on liquid net worth, objectives, product knowledge and experience. https://www.interactivebrokers.com/lib/cstools/faq/#/content/113945273 , https://www.interactivebrokers.com/lib/cstools/faq/#/content/137766944 and https://www.interactivebrokers.com/lib/cstools/faq/#/content/28236881

The Rollover tool has the same limit as the Write tool. IBKR's guide gives the choice 'roll calls on long stock positions, or roll puts on short stock positions' and describes rolling 'to the next month's contract'. A cash-secured put is neither, so the summary's suggestion that TWS has a ready-made rollover screen for this structure is not supported for the put half. https://ibkrguides.com/traderworkstation/write-and-rollover-options.htm

Small cost details left out: IBKR's commissions page says 'Order minimums will be applied to the individual legs of a COMBO order', so a roll entered as one combination still pays the USD 1.00 minimum on each leg, and it shows a FINRA Trading Activity Fee holiday for trades from 1 Oct to 31 Dec 2026, so the exact regulator pennies quoted are not stable. https://www.interactivebrokers.com/en/pricing/commissions-options.php

Still unread by anyone: the OCC disclosure booklet itself (theocc.com returned HTTP 403 to every request, including the PDF), so no quote or edition date from it should be printed. Also not checked: tax treatment, which IBKR entity holds the account, and anything in a live or paper account. I could run no web searches (the session's search allowance was already used up), so I could not look for further independent studies; all checks were direct page fetches. The AQR paper comparing put-writing with covered-call writing could not be reached at the addresses I tried. https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2024-06-07/html/2024-12466.htm

Levels 2-4 also need the client to be 21 or older, and IBKR says it 'cannot disclose its eligibility requirements', so approval cannot be assumed. Size trap: SPY closed at 779.09 on 6 Oct 2026, so one put at a 780 strike sets aside about $78,000 in a cash account. A mid-sized account can hold only one or two positions and cannot scale in gradually. XSP does not fix this: it closed at 781.89 and Cboe itself calls it 'very similar notional size' to SPY. IBKR also treats a cash-secured put as an 'uncovered' position needing at least USD 2,000 of account value. [ibkr-faq-csp] [cboe-xsp-page] [cboe-delayed-quotes] [ibkr-faq-uncovered]

It can make the 'missing the move' problem worse: if the price never dips to the strike, the investor keeps only the small fee and still owns nothing. The OCC's education site lists this as one of the two principal risks and says 'the outright stock buyer is better off than the put writer if the put is not assigned and the stock keeps rallying'. Cboe's put-selling index shows it in numbers: from 31 Aug 2023 to 5 Oct 2026 it rose 45.8% while the S&P 500 price index rose 72.5% before dividends (my arithmetic from Cboe's data files). [oic-cash-secured-put] [cboe-put-article-2023] [cboe-put-history] [cboe-spx-history]

The downside is nearly the full share loss: maximum loss is 'limited but substantial' (the shares can go to zero, less the fee), and Cboe's put-selling index still fell 32.66% peak to trough. The fee is a small cushion, not protection. [oic-cash-secured-put] [oic-covered-call] [cboe-put-article-2023]

Covered calls cap the winners: if the share price settles above the strike, the shares 'may be called away from the owner by the call buyer at a price that is less than the current market price'. For an investor whose complaint is missing gains, this sells off the upside of the very holdings that are working. [ibkr-campus-write-roll] [oic-covered-call]

A covered call gets in the way of the 'trim' rule: 'As long as the short call position remains open, the investor isn't free to sell the stock. It would leave the calls uncovered and expose the investor to unlimited risk.' A technical sell signal on the shares means buying the call back first, at whatever it then costs. (This is the OCC education site's general statement; how IBKR's screens enforce it was not tested.) [oic-covered-call]

Dividend surprise on covered calls: a call that is in the money just before the ex-dividend date can be exercised early, so the shares go to the call owner and the writer loses the dividend. [ibkr-faq-early-assignment] [oic-covered-call]

Assignment is learned a day late: OCC assigns exercises in a nightly batch, so the seller finds out the next day, and the OCC's education site warns the stock 'could fall further before the investor can act to limit losses'. [ibkr-faq-assignment-notice] [oic-cash-secured-put]

In a margin account the broker reserves only a fraction of the purchase cost, so it is easy to sell more puts than the cash can actually pay for. If assignment then leaves a shortfall, IBKR's automated liquidations 'are not confined to only shares that resulted from the option position'. [ibkr-margin-options] [ibkr-faq-early-assignment]

Expiry-day traps: an option one cent in the money is auto-exercised; a short option can be exercised against the seller even when it closes out of the money; and where delivery would leave the account short, IBKR may close options, let them lapse or sell delivered shares at its own discretion. IBKR says it generally starts expiry-related liquidations two hours before the close, and that liquidations of US positions typically begin about 9:40 AM ET the next business day. [ibkr-faq-auto-exercise] [ibkr-faq-delivery-margin] [ibkr-faq-expiry-liquidations]

XSP changes the purpose: because it settles in cash, a short XSP put never delivers shares. It is a pure bet on the index level, not a way to buy the dip, and it does not buy the individual companies chosen on fundamentals. [cboe-xsp-spec] [cboe-xsp-page]

Tool mismatch: IBKR's guide describes the Write Options tool as selling calls against long stock and puts against short stock, and the Rollover tool as rolling 'calls on long stock positions, or ... puts on short stock positions', so neither is described as handling cash-secured puts. Every roll is two trades: 'Multiple leg strategies, including spreads, will incur multiple commission charges', and IBKR applies its USD 1.00 order minimum to each leg of a combination order. [ibkr-guide-write-roll] [ibkr-campus-write-roll] [ibkr-commissions-options]

The evidence does not match the plan: the only long-run record cited (Cboe's PUT index) sells one-month, at-the-money puts on the S&P 500 index. A put set below the market on a single company picked on fundamentals is a different trade with a smaller fee and one-company risk, and nothing read here measures it. Cboe's own article says writing further out of the money means 'less risk/return'. [cboe-put-article-2023] [cboe-put-study-2016]

research.plain_summary: Nine published alternatives to "sit in cash until a signal appears", beyond plain buy-and-hold. Three change your rules (a written invested-by-default policy, a deadline on waiting cash, sizing by risk). Three change what you hold (a floor formula, a trend-following fund, an equal-weight sleeve). Three use options (collar, buffer ETF, Treasury bills plus long-dated calls). The one thing the evidence says: waiting is the costly habit. Investing at once beat staying in cash in 70% of one-year periods, and the cheap rule-based fixes stand up better than the option-based ones, most of which lost to a simple mix of stocks and Treasury bills.
research.how_it_works: All nine ideas attack the same thing: today cash is the starting point and a technical signal is needed to leave it, so "no signal" means "cash". The first group flips that with rules: write down that being invested is the normal state and cash needs a stated reason (pre-commitment), put a deadline on any cash that is waiting for a pullback (time-stop), or decide in units of risk so the question becomes "how much", never "in or out" (risk budget). The second group keeps you invested but changes the holding: a floor formula that scales share exposure with the cushion above a level you refuse to go below (CPPI), a trend-following fund held in place of idle cash, or an equal-weight sleeve. The third group uses options to cap losses instead of selling: a collar on what you already own, a ready-made buffer ETF, or Treasury bills plus long-dated call options. In every version fundamentals still choose WHAT to own; only the default state and the sizing rule change, and technicals choose WHEN inside that frame. The rule-based ideas and the floor formula can be checked on ordinary daily price history; the option ideas cannot, because they need option prices.
research.sitting_in_cash_relevance:
The two we judge most promising for a problem where the default state is cash are the INVESTED-BY-DEFAULT POLICY and the TIME-STOP ON CASH. They work as a pair: one changes the starting point, the other puts a clock on every exception.

Why these two:
1. They aim at the cause, not the symptom. Today a technical signal is needed to leave cash, so no signal means cash. Flipping the default means a reason is needed to hold cash. The research on defaults shows how strongly the starting point decides the outcome: same plan, same economics, 37% took part when they had to opt in and 86% when they had to opt out [S3]. That paper is also the warning - people stayed with a default even when it was not their best choice, which is what cash is doing here.
2. The cost of waiting is measured, not guessed. Cash lost to investing at once in 70% of one-year periods on global shares, 1976-2022 [S1], and across 196 wait-for-a-dip rules on the S&P 500 since 1965 the always-invested portfolio was ahead by about 1.1% a year [S2]. Vanguard's wording fits the problem exactly: "Many investors hold too much cash as a result of indefinitely deferring the decision about how and when to invest" [S1].
3. Both keep the standing rule intact. Fundamentals still choose WHAT to own. Technicals still choose WHEN - but inside a window, and as trim-and-reload signals from an invested base instead of a permission slip to leave cash.
4. Both cost nothing, need no options and no new products, and both can be tested on Scintilla's own daily price history before anything changes.

How the other seven relate to the cash problem:
- Trend-following sleeve: the best-evidenced thing to hold in place of whatever cash remains, but it will not catch a share rally, so it softens the cost of cash without fixing missed moves [S2][S20].
- Two candidates can make the problem worse: the floor formula can lock itself into 100% cash after a sharp fall [S10], and volatility targeting cuts exposure straight after falls [S23].
- The three option routes (collar, buffer ETF, bills-plus-calls) do keep you in the market, but the evidence says the protection usually costs more than it returns compared with simply holding fewer shares plus Treasury bills [S15][S16][S14].
- Equal weight changes what you own, not whether you own it.
- One extra idea we came across: being paid to wait by selling cash-secured puts at a price you would be happy to buy at (the Cboe PUT index). It is a real alternative to idle cash, but it has trailed the S&P 500 by roughly four points a year since 2007 [S27].

Limits: the default and commitment evidence comes from retirement saving, not stock picking; the waiting-cost evidence is on broad indices, not individual growth shares. These are structures to test, not instructions.

not_verified: The 95-110 collar index (CLL) annualised return, volatility and maximum drawdown: the Cboe dashboard loaded without data and the CLL and PPUT factsheets returned HTTP 403. A search snippet said CLL lost 0.7% to 11.6% in six quarters when the S&P 500 fell 13.9% to 21.9%; we could not confirm it on a primary page, so it is not in the findings.

Headline returns for the century-long trend-following backtest (annual return, Sharpe ratio, correlation to shares and bonds, and the exact effect of a 20% allocation over 1880-2016): the tables in the copy we read are images. Only the text statements are reported.
The figure that the SG Trend Index Sharpe ratio fell to 0.05 in 2010-2018 came from a search snippet about Babu et al.; the AQR page we fetched gives only the qualitative explanation.

A search snippet said buying puts cut returns by 2.5 points and the Sharpe ratio from 0.37 to 0.21 (Israelov & Nielsen, 2006-2014); the CFA digest we fetched did not show those numbers, so they are left out.

In the AQR 'Hold the Dip' portfolio table (Exhibit 8) the column headings did not extract from the PDF; we matched columns to portfolios from the paper's own description of each result. The 20%-to-trend figures should be re-checked against the original table before publishing.
The count of funds in AQR's ten-year buffer-fund sample (one reading of the page gave 31) was not confirmed on a second reading, so no count is stated.

The full Journal of Portfolio Management version of 'Rebuffed' was not readable beyond its landing page; all buffer-fund figures come from AQR's two open web articles. The issuer's (FT Vest) rebuttal was not fetched; it is described only as reported by Ptak.
What Merton, Scholes & Gladstein (1978) actually found about a 90%-bills / 10%-calls portfolio: only the bibliographic record loaded. No result from it is claimed.

No published track record was found for a private investor's Treasury-bills-plus-LEAPS barbell. A Cboe-sponsored working paper on two-year call options in retirement plans (Basu & Clements, January 2026) was found; it is a draft marked 'not for citation', studies leverage rather than this barbell, and builds pre-2005 option prices from a model, so it was not used.
The statement that bills-plus-a-call is the same bet as shares-plus-a-put is the textbook put-call parity identity, stated from general knowledge, not from a fetched source.
The origin papers for the floor approach (Black & Jones 1987 for CPPI; Estep & Kritzman 1988 for TIPP) were not fetched; CPPI and TIPP are described from the later studies that test them.

No controlled study was found showing that a written Investment Policy Statement improves a self-directed investor's results. The case for the invested-by-default policy rests on analogy with savings defaults and commitment devices.

No published study was found that tests a 'time-stop' deadline rule by that name. The case rests on the Vanguard and AQR evidence about the cost of waiting, plus Vanguard's advice to keep any phase-in short.

Two points in the findings are our own reasoning, not results from a paper: (1) comparing 'cash until a buy signal' with 'invested until a sell signal' as a test of the default; (2) that volatility targeting can leave an investor under-invested in a sharp rebound.

Morningstar's 'Mind the Gap' study of the return investors lose through timing could not be loaded (page returned empty), and Vanguard's estimate of the value of behavioural coaching was visible only as a total ('around 3%' for the whole adviser framework). Neither is used.

S&P Dow Jones Indices' own equal-weight research returned HTTP 403; the 2023 and concentration figures come from Invesco, a fund issuer with a commercial interest, and should be treated as dated index facts only.

SSRN pages returned HTTP 403 throughout. Interactive Brokers documentation was not consulted. Several sources (marked 'abstract page only' or 'summary page only') were read as abstracts or publisher summaries, not full papers.

All evidence here is on broad indices, funds or savings behaviour. None of it tests these structures on individual growth shares chosen on revenue and earnings growth, which is how the portfolio in question is built.

findings.claim: INVESTED-BY-DEFAULT POLICY (a written pre-commitment, sometimes called a Ulysses contract [a promise made in a calm moment that binds you later]): being at your target exposure is the normal state, and holding cash needs a written reason and an expiry date. FOR: default-setting and advance commitment are among the best-documented effects in behavioural economics - in one large US company, switching the pension plan from opt-in to automatic enrolment changed behaviour sharply although 'none of the economic features of the plan changed'. AGAINST: all of this evidence comes from retirement saving and bank savings, not from a self-directed stock picker; in the one randomised trial cited, most people (72%) offered a binding commitment turned it down, and Laibson's model concludes the perceived benefits of committing are 'often overwhelmed by the costs of commitment'; defaults also stick when they are wrong (which is what cash is doing now); we found no controlled study showing that an Investment Policy Statement [the written rule-book] raises a private investor's returns. TESTABLE ON DAILY BARS: the policy itself no, but its mechanical twin yes (our suggestion, not from a paper) - run the same technical signals two ways, 'cash until a buy signal' versus 'invested until a sell signal', and compare.
findings.numbers: Madrian & Shea (one large US company, 401(k) plan): participation 37% for staff who had to opt in (3-15 months' tenure) versus 86% for staff enrolled automatically; company-wide rate before the change 61%; 61% of the automatically enrolled stayed at the default 3% contribution and default money-market fund, a combination only 1% of earlier staff had chosen. Thaler & Benartzi (first Save More Tomorrow rollout): 78% of those offered joined, 80% still in after the fourth pay raise, saving rate 3.5% to 13.6% over 40 months. Ashraf, Karlan & Yin (Philippine bank, randomised): 710 clients offered a locked savings account, 202 (28.4%) accepted; average balances +81 percentage points versus the control group after 12 months.
findings.note: Every number seen on the source pages. 37%, 86% and 61% are in the working-paper PDF (not on the NBER abstract page); the paper also checks that the simultaneous move to immediate eligibility had 'very little, if any, impact'. Thaler-Benartzi and Ashraf-Karlan-Yin figures are word for word in their abstracts. Laibson's exact wording is 'overwhelmed by the costs of commitment' (the researcher's quoted 'outweighed by commitment costs' in the failure-mode list is a misquote). The CFA Institute page describes what an IPS contains and gives no evidence on results. 'No controlled study found' is a statement of absence and cannot be proven. See 'missing' for newer work showing the long-run effect of defaults is much smaller than these headline figures.

findings.claim: TIME-STOP ON CASH: any money that has waited a fixed number of weeks for a pullback gets invested anyway, in one go or in a few scheduled slices. FOR: Vanguard finds that investing immediately beat a three-month phase-in about two-thirds of the time and beat staying in cash 70% of the time (global shares, one-year horizon), that the longer the phase-in the greater the cost, and that any phase-in should be kept short, 'such as three months'; AQR tested 196 buy-the-dip rules on the S&P 500 over 60 years - each buys after a set fall, holds for a set time (one month to five years) and otherwise sits in cash - and the average one earned a slightly lower risk-adjusted return than simply holding; AQR repeated the test on the seven 'Magnificent 7' shares (May 2012-Sep 2025) and again found dip-buying inferior to holding. AGAINST: a deadline will sometimes force a purchase just before a fall - in the worst 5% of one-year outcomes the immediate investor ended lower than the gradual one; Vanguard's own model says a strongly loss-averse person is better served by the gradual path; higher interest on cash narrows the gap; the shortfall AQR measured over the full 60 years is small, and its rules sell back to cash after a fixed holding time, so they are not identical to 'wait for a pullback, then hold'; and apart from AQR's seven-share appendix (shares chosen with hindsight) the evidence is on broad indices, not on individual growth shares picked on fundamentals. TESTABLE ON DAILY BARS: yes, the cleanest test of all - same shopping list, three rules (buy now / wait for an X% pullback with no deadline / wait at most N weeks then buy), compare end value and worst drawdown [fall from a previous peak].
findings.numbers: Vanguard (MSCI World, 1976-2022, one-year horizon, 100% shares, three-month phase-in): lump sum beat cost averaging 68% of the time; lump sum beat cash 70%; cost averaging beat cash 69%; with T-bill interest paid on the waiting cash lump sum still won 65%; 6-month phase-in, global USD: lump sum won 72.6%. Per $100,000 after one year: median $111,940 lump sum vs $109,580 phased (2.2% more); worst 5%: $82,947 lump sum vs $85,906 phased. Over 1976-2022 US shares beat T-bills [short-dated government debt, close to cash] 76% of the time and US bonds beat T-bills 68% of the time. AQR 'Hold the Dip' (S&P 500 price return, 1 Jan 1965-30 Sep 2025, 196 rules, no trading costs deducted): average Sharpe ratio [return per unit of risk] 0.04 below buy-and-hold (about 16% worse), over 60% of rules worse; Oct 1989-Sep 2025 with dividends: 0.27 worse (47% worse); always-invested ahead by 1.1% a year in plain return (0.6% ahead of the better-quartile rule, 1.7% ahead of the worse-quartile rule); average alpha [return beyond simply holding the market] +0.5% a year, only 16 of 196 rules (8%) statistically significant.
findings.note: All Vanguard and AQR numbers confirmed in the PDFs' own text. Three corrections. (1) The researcher wrote 'US shares beat T-bills 76% of the time, bonds 68%', which reads as if shares beat bonds 68%; Vanguard's sentence is that stocks AND bonds each beat cash, 76% and 68%. (2) AQR's rules are in-and-out rules with a fixed holding period, not pure 'wait for a dip' rules, and the 1965-2025 comparison uses the S&P 500 without dividends. (3) 'Evidence is on broad indices only' is not quite right: AQR's appendix runs the same test on seven individual growth shares. AQR's paper is labelled 2025 Issue 4; its landing page is dated 1 Dec 2025.

findings.claim: FLOOR APPROACH (CPPI, constant-proportion portfolio insurance [a formula, not an insurance policy]): choose a floor value you aim not to fall below, then keep share exposure at a fixed multiple of the cushion [portfolio value minus the floor], so you stay partly invested for as long as a cushion exists and exposure grows as gains build; TIPP [time-invariant protection] ratchets the floor up as the portfolio makes new highs. FOR: Perold & Sharpe show that insurance rules of this kind give better protection on the way down and more upside on the way up than buy-and-hold; a bootstrap [re-sampled history] study finds CPPI protects the downside better than a simple stop-loss; a model-based comparison found CPPI superior to the option-based equivalent in all cases examined. AGAINST: it buys after rises and sells after falls, so it does worse in choppy, trendless markets; buy-and-hold earned the higher average return in the one simulation study that reports it; after a sharp fall the cushion is used up and the formula parks the whole portfolio in cash with no route back ('cash lock-in') - it can recreate the very problem it is meant to cure; and the floor is a target, not a guarantee - a price gap between rebalancing points can carry the portfolio through it, and that risk grows with the multiple. TIPP showed no significant improvement over the traditional rules. TESTABLE ON DAILY BARS: yes, fully - it needs only closing prices and a cash interest rate.
findings.numbers: The studies report rankings, not one headline return. Annaert et al. (block-bootstrap simulation; stop-loss, synthetic put, CPPI): buy-and-hold has the higher average excess return but neither it nor the insurance strategies dominates the other; a 100% floor preferred to lower floors; daily-rebalanced versions beat less frequent ones. Dichtl, Drobetz & Wambach: synthetic put and CPPI give superior downside protection versus stop-loss; TIPP and a dynamic value-at-risk rule add no significant improvement. Pezier & Scheller: 'Our results confirm the superiority of CPPI over OBPI in all cases' (a utility-model comparison under assumed price processes, not a historical track record). No verified return or drawdown figure for a specific CPPI setting.
findings.note: All five abstracts/summary pages were fetched and say what is claimed. Corrections: Perold & Sharpe's summary says these strategies 'do worse' (not 'worst') in 'relatively trendless, volatile markets'; the 'higher average return for buy-and-hold' result is from one study (Annaert), not 'studies'; Pezier & Scheller is a theoretical comparison. The arXiv abstract names 'the CPPI cash lock-in' and says 'This is especially an issue in times of market crisis' but does not itself explain the mechanism - that description is standard textbook knowledge. Added from Cont & Tankov (fetched): in real markets the risk of breaching the floor 'is nonnegligible and grows with the multiplier value', so 'a floor you refuse to fall below' overstates it.

findings.claim: COLLAR (hedge instead of exit): keep the shares, buy a put option [the right to sell at a set lower price] and pay for it by selling a call option [giving away gains above a set higher price]; a put-spread collar buys cheaper, partial protection. Cboe publishes three S&P 500 benchmark versions: PPUT (a put 5% below the market each month), CLL (a put at 95% each quarter paid for with a call at 110% each month) and CLLZ (a zero-cost put-spread collar). FOR: over 35 years all three had lower volatility and less severe maximum drawdowns than the stock and commodity benchmarks Cboe compared them with, and you stay in the position with some upside left. AGAINST: Israelov & Klein find collars under-earn because they carry less market exposure and often pay away the volatility premium [options usually cost more than the risk they cover], and that they 'historically performed poorly' against simpler ways to cut risk; Israelov finds puts 'quite ineffective at reducing drawdowns versus the simple alternative of statically reducing exposure'; the protection only works if the fall lines up with the option's expiry date. TESTABLE ON DAILY BARS: not from share prices alone - it needs option prices; the Cboe index histories can stand in for an index-level check only.
findings.numbers: Cboe (30 Jun 1986-30 Jun 2021): PPUT, CLL and CLLZ had 'less severe maximum drawdown losses than two key stock indices and a leading commodity index' and betas [share of market moves captured] below 0.75; the S&P 500 had 35 monthly falls of 6% or more versus 18 for PPUT, but PPUT 'also had fewer monthly gains of more than 4%'; in 2008 and 2020 PPUT's return was more than 10 percentage points above the other stock and commodity indices in the article. The article gives no annualised return for any of the three against the S&P 500 (it says only that they beat the MSCI EAFE index). Israelov & Nielsen as summarised by CFA Institute (S&P 500, mostly Mar 1996-Jun 2014): the volatility premium was consistently positive, a hedged 5%-below-market put had 'negative returns for all buckets' of the VIX fear index, and a 1987-sized crash would be needed once every 10 years for the hedged put to break even.
findings.note: Index construction, dates, betas, the 35-versus-18 count and the 2008 figure all confirmed in the Cboe article text. The drawdown comparison is shown in a chart I could not read; the text says 'two key stock indices and a leading commodity index', so I have used Cboe's wording instead of 'the S&P 500'. The article was written with a summer intern and published by the exchange that lists these options. Both AQR quotes are on the AQR summary pages (no figures there). The CFA digest page does not name the original authors; AQR's own page confirms the paper (Journal of Portfolio Management, 31 Jul 2015) under Roni Israelov - the co-author Lars Nielsen was not visible on either page I fetched.

findings.claim: STOCK-REPLACEMENT BARBELL: keep most of the money in Treasury bills and spend a small slice on long-dated call options (LEAPS [options lasting up to about three years]), so the most you can lose is the option cost while the upside stays open. FOR: the loss is capped at the premium paid and the cash keeps earning interest; call-option portfolio strategies have been studied since the 1970s. AGAINST: by a textbook identity (put-call parity, stated from general knowledge) it is close to the same bet as owning the shares plus a protective put, so the evidence against buying protection applies - AQR on buying puts: 'the price of admission is generally higher than the benefit'; a model-based comparison found the floor formula (CPPI) superior to the bond-plus-option version in every case examined; the option can expire worthless after a flat or falling stretch and the premium must be paid again; calls pay no dividends. We found no published track record for this barbell as a private investor would run it. TESTABLE ON DAILY BARS: no - it needs historical option prices; a model-based estimate from share prices would understate the real cost.
findings.numbers: Options Industry Council: a LEAPS call gives the right to buy 'up to three years in the future'; the buyer's 'risk is limited to the price paid'; option investors 'run the risk of losing their entire investment in a relatively short period'. AQR 'Rebuffed' (99 option-based funds - the 99 of 624 in three Morningstar categories with records back to January 2020 - measured 1 Jan 2020-31 Jan 2025): more than two-thirds delivered lower returns with more risk than a passive mix of shares and T-bills, 81% had worse drawdowns than that mix, and only 14% beat it. Pezier & Scheller: CPPI superior to option-based portfolio insurance 'in all cases'. No verified return or drawdown figure for the barbell itself.
findings.note: Every quoted number and phrase seen on the fetched pages. Three limits to state plainly: (1) none of AQR's 99 funds is a bills-plus-LEAPS barbell - the link to this structure is by reasoning, not by test; (2) the 'same bet as shares plus a put' statement is not from a fetched source; (3) the Merton-Scholes-Gladstein record has no abstract, so it confirms only that the 1978 study exists, not what it found.

findings.claim: TREND-FOLLOWING SLEEVE (managed futures [funds that go long rising markets and short falling ones across shares, bonds, commodities and currencies]) held in place of idle cash. FOR: Hurst, Ooi & Pedersen rebuild the strategy across 67 markets back to 1880 and find it profitable in each decade, little related to shares and bonds, and positive in 8 of the 10 worst falls of a 60/40 portfolio; the live index of the ten largest trend funds made money in three of the four big S&P 500 falls since 2000. AGAINST: it is not a share substitute - its link to shares is close to zero, so it cannot be relied on to capture a share rally and AQR itself says it 'may have lagged in bull markets'; it has its own drawdowns; it had a weak stretch in the 2010s that AQR puts down to fewer large market moves; it does little in very fast falls; results differ between managers; the century-long record is a simulation with assumed costs, written by a firm that sells the strategy; and an independent study finds the statistical evidence for the underlying effect weak. TESTABLE ON DAILY BARS: partly - a trend fund's own daily price history can be dropped into a portfolio test and a simple version on a handful of asset-class ETFs can be built, but the real 60-plus-market futures strategy cannot be rebuilt from share prices.
findings.numbers: Hurst et al.: January 1880-December 2016, monthly data; 67 markets (29 commodities, 11 share indices, 15 bond markets, 12 currency pairs); 1-, 3- and 12-month trend signals; 10% volatility target; 2%-plus-20% fees assumed; positive in 8 of the 10 largest 60/40 drawdowns; strategy's own drawdowns 'up to 25%, over extended time periods'. AQR 'Hold the Dip': SG Trend Index, 1 Jan 2000-30 Sep 2025, net of fees: 4.0% a year above cash, Sharpe ratio 0.30, correlation to shares about -0.1. In the four S&P 500 falls deeper than 20%: 10 Oct 2007-9 Mar 2009 S&P -55.3% vs trend +31.7%; 2 Sep 2000-9 Oct 2002 -47.4% vs +51.4%; 20 Feb-23 Mar 2020 -33.8% vs -2.4%; 4 Jan-12 Oct 2022 -24.5% vs +33.9%. Moving 20% of a global 60/40 portfolio into trend: worst drawdown -33.6% to -24.6%, volatility 9.3% to 7.8%, return above cash 4.2% to 4.1%, Sharpe ratio 0.45 to 0.53.
findings.note: All numbers confirmed in the full texts. The researcher flagged the Exhibit 8 column headings as unreadable; they extracted cleanly for me and the 20%-to-trend figures are matched to the right columns. Two wording corrections: 'it will not capture a share rally' is too strong - Hurst et al. show a 'smile' (trend did particularly well in extreme up AND down years for shares), while AQR says it 'may have lagged in bull markets'; and AQR says only that 'there is also dispersion across different trend-following managers', not 'a lot'. Hurst et al. also warn their costs 'are estimated with a significant amount of uncertainty' and exclude futures roll costs. Added contrary evidence: Huang, Li, Wang & Zhou (2020).

findings.claim: BUFFER (DEFINED-OUTCOME) ETFs: a fund that packages an options collar so that, if held for the full outcome period, the first slice of loss is absorbed and gains are capped. FOR: Jeffrey Ptak, an independent analyst, concludes from his own research that these ETFs 'have largely delivered on their promises' over their stated periods and that investors mostly used them as intended; 29 of the 35 S&P 500- and Nasdaq-100-based ones had a better risk-adjusted return than a 60/40 share-and-bond mix over Jan 2020-Jan 2025 (a period that includes the 2022 bond slump, and in which the 60/40 mix itself badly lagged a shares-plus-cash mix); they take the sell decision out of your hands. AGAINST: AQR's reviews found the large majority did worse than a plain mix of an S&P 500 fund and Treasury bills matched to the same market exposure - lower return and, about half the time, deeper drawdowns too; the buffer only holds from the fund's start date to its end date; fees and option costs recur every year. TESTABLE ON DAILY BARS: yes - these ETFs have daily price histories, and AQR's test (fund versus S&P 500 plus T-bills at the fund's own beta) can be repeated.
findings.numbers: AQR 'Buffer Madness' (about 102 option-based funds - the text says 103, the chart notes 102 - 1 Jan 2020-30 Apr 2025, each compared with S&P 500 plus 3-month T-bills at the fund's own realised beta): 86% had lower returns; 70% had lower returns and worse peak-to-trough drawdowns. Defined Outcome (buffer) category alone, 42 funds: 90% lower returns, 52% worse on both counts, 38% lower return but a smaller drawdown. 1 Jan-30 Apr 2025: 83% of the 42 Defined Outcome funds had worse drawdowns than the matched mix. Ten-year check (1 Jan 2015-30 Apr 2025, 31 option funds, NONE of them buffer funds): no fund beat the mix on both counts, 90% had lower returns and 94% had worse drawdowns. Ptak (41 buffer ETFs, Jan 2020-Jan 2025): average return 7.5% a year; 34 of 41 lagged a risk-matched benchmark (average shortfall 1.1% a year); only 4 had a higher Sharpe ratio; every one was more volatile than its benchmark. Against a 60/40 mix (35 ETFs): 8.1% return at 9.8% volatility versus 8.5% at 12.8%; Sharpe ratio 0.60 versus 0.51; worst fall -13.0% on average versus -20.9%.
findings.note: One real error. The researcher wrote that over ten years '81% were worse on both'. On the page the ten-year result is: zero funds better on both, 90% lower returns, 94% worse drawdowns. The 81% figure sits in a footnote about a different robustness check (beta measured on the first five years, tested on the second five). More important for this finding: AQR states 'the Morningstar data has no Defined Outcome funds with track records going back this far', so the ten-year result says nothing directly about buffer ETFs. Other fixes: fund count is 102 in the exhibit notes and 103 in the text; Ptak's 60/40 comparison covers 35 ETFs, not all 41; his 'largely delivered on their promises' refers to earlier research he links to, not to the 41-fund table; 'more often than not' for deeper drawdowns is 52%. Ptak also notes his benchmarks were set 'with the benefit of hindsight'. The 'usually one year' outcome period was not on any page I fetched, so I removed it. The peer-reviewed version (S17) was readable only as a landing page.

findings.claim: EQUAL-WEIGHT / BREADTH CATCH-UP SLEEVE: hold every share in an index in equal amounts instead of by company size, as a bet that the many catch up with the few giants. FOR: across four decades of US index data an equal-weighted portfolio rebalanced monthly beat size-weighted on return and on risk-adjusted return; it puts money to work without chasing the most crowded names. AGAINST: the edge came with more risk; keeping the weights equal means constantly trimming winners and topping up laggards - the opposite of a growth-and-momentum style (how the method works, not a finding seen on the page we read); it lagged badly when a few giants led the market; and it answers 'what to hold', not 'why am I in cash', so by itself it does nothing about the default state. TESTABLE ON DAILY BARS: yes - equal-weight and standard index funds both have long daily histories; measuring breadth itself needs price data for every index member.
findings.numbers: Plyakha, Uppal & Vilkov (major US share indices, 'over the last four decades', paper dated March 2012): equal-weight with monthly rebalancing ahead on total mean return, four-factor alpha, Sharpe ratio and certainty-equivalent return, 'even though the equal-weighted portfolio has greater portfolio risk'. Invesco (a fund issuer with a product to sell; article by its Asia-Pacific ETF product manager, 13 Sep 2024): 2023 calendar year S&P 500 Equal Weight +13.87% versus S&P 500 +26.29%, 'Magnificent 7' +107.01%; before 2023 equal-weight was ahead by an average 0.87% a year since the index launched (8 Jan 2003); top 10 names were 34.5% of the S&P 500 in August 2024.
findings.note: Abstract and all Invesco figures confirmed on the pages. Small correction: the researcher said the edge comes 'from constantly selling winners to buy laggards' as if it were the paper's finding; the EDHEC page shows only the first part of the abstract and does not explain the source of the edge, so I reworded it as a description of the mechanics. No figure after August 2024 could be verified: S&P's own pages returned HTTP 403 and Invesco's US fund page loaded without data, so the page should not say how equal weight has done since.

findings.claim: RISK-BUDGET FRAMING (volatility targeting [holding more when markets are calm and less when they are wild]): decide how much risk the portfolio should carry, then let each position's size follow from its recent volatility - so the question is 'how much', and the answer is never zero. FOR: Moreira & Muir find portfolios that take less risk when volatility is high produced large risk-adjusted gains; Harvey and co-authors, using more than 60 assets and daily data from 1926, find it raised Sharpe ratios for shares and credit, cut the chance of extreme returns and lowered maximum drawdowns for balanced portfolios. AGAINST: Cederburg and co-authors test 103 share strategies and find volatility-managed versions 'do not systematically outperform', and versions an investor could actually have run in real time generally did worse than leaving the portfolio alone; the published gains come partly from borrowing to hold MORE in calm markets, which a cash account cannot do; and because volatility usually rises when prices fall, the rule cuts exposure after a fall (Harvey et al. say this directly), which can leave you light in a sharp rebound (the rebound point is our inference) - a real drawback for someone tired of missing moves. TESTABLE ON DAILY BARS: yes, fully - recent volatility is computed straight from daily closing prices.
findings.numbers: Cederburg, O'Doherty, Wang & Yan (103 US share strategies): a real-time mix of the volatility-managed and plain versions earned a lower certainty-equivalent return [the sure return a cautious investor would accept instead] than the plain version in 72 of 103 cases; for the whole share market that real-time mix had a Sharpe ratio of 0.42 versus 0.46 for the plain market (and 1.56% versus 1.75% a year certainty-equivalent return). In a direct like-for-like comparison the managed market portfolio scored 0.51 against 0.42, a gap that was not statistically significant. Harvey et al.: 60-plus assets, daily data from 1926; Sharpe ratio improvement only for 'risk assets' (shares and credit); lower likelihood of extreme returns across all 60-plus assets; lower maximum drawdowns for balanced and risk-parity portfolios. Moreira & Muir give no single headline figure in the abstract.
findings.note: 72 of 103 and 0.42 versus 0.46 are both in the paper, but the researcher's label 'managed versus unmanaged' was loose: 0.42 belongs to the real-time COMBINATION of managed and plain market portfolios, not to the managed portfolio alone, which actually scored higher (0.51) in the direct comparison. The paper also reports some positive real-time results (momentum, profitability and betting-against-beta strategies). Harvey et al.'s full text (Duke-hosted copy, fetched) confirms all six authors and the Journal of Portfolio Management 2018 citation, states the method works by 'leveraging the portfolio at times of low volatility and scaling down at times of high volatility', and says 'volatility often increases in periods of negative returns, causing positions to be reduced'. The Man Institute page itself lists only two of the authors. Added: Barroso & Detzel (2021) on trading costs.
