missing: The index evidence does not carry over automatically to a hand-picked share list. Bessembinder (2018): the majority of US common stocks since 1926 had lifetime returns below one-month Treasury bills, and the best 4% of companies explain the entire net gain of the market. 'Invested beats cash 70% of the time' is a statement about owning the whole market; for a concentrated list of individual shares the odds per share are worse, which is why the test on Scintilla's own picks matters. https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/jfinec/v129y2018i3p440-457.html

The headline default effect shrinks a lot over time. Choi, Laibson, Cammarota, Lombardo & Beshears (NBER, 2024, 'Smaller than We Thought?'): once job changes, withdrawals and later opt-outs are counted, automatic enrolment raises steady-state saving by only 0.6% of income and auto-escalation by 0.3%; only 40% of people let the first scheduled increase happen. The 37%-to-86% jump the researcher leads with is a first-year participation figure, not a long-run outcome. https://www.nber.org/papers/w32828

A default helps or hurts depending on what it is set to. Choi, Laibson, Madrian & Metrick (NBER, 2001, 'For Better or For Worse'): automatic enrolment lifted participation above 85%, but about 80% initially accepted a low default rate and a conservative default fund and half were still there after three years, so the effects on wealth were 'roughly offsetting on average'. For an invested-by-default policy this means the choice of default level matters as much as having one. https://www.nber.org/papers/w8651

A CPPI floor is not a guarantee. Cont & Tankov (2009): with smoothly moving prices the strategy has no downside risk, but 'in real markets this risk is nonnegligible and grows with the multiplier value' - a gap down between rebalancing points (an earnings shock, an overnight fall) can take the portfolio through the floor. The researcher described the floor as a level 'you refuse to go below'. https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/mathfi/v19y2009i3p379-401.html

Independent challenge to the trend-following evidence, which otherwise comes almost entirely from AQR (a seller of the strategy). Huang, Li, Wang & Zhou (2020): market-by-market tests 'reveal little evidence' of the trend effect in or out of sample, and although the strategy made money it performed about the same as a similar strategy that needs no predictability at all. https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/jfinec/v135y2020i3p774-794.html

Trading costs erase most volatility-targeting gains. Barroso & Detzel (2021): after transaction costs, volatility management of strategies other than the whole market 'generally produces zero abnormal returns and significantly reduces Sharpe ratios'; the whole-market version survives costs but 'only provides superior performance when sentiment is high'. https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/jfinec/v140y2021i3p744-767.html

Volatility targeting as published relies on borrowing. Harvey et al.'s full text says the result is achieved 'by leveraging the portfolio at times of low volatility and scaling down at times of high volatility', and that 'volatility often increases in periods of negative returns, causing positions to be reduced'. A cash account that cannot borrow gets only the cutting half of the rule. https://people.duke.edu/~charvey/Research/Published_Papers/P135_The_impact_of.pdf

AQR's ten-year option-fund result does not cover buffer ETFs at all: 'the Morningstar data has no Defined Outcome funds with track records going back this far'. The 31 funds in that sample are other kinds of option fund. Also, the five-year sample is the 99 funds (of 624 in those categories) old enough to have a record from January 2020, so it describes the early funds, not today's whole shelf. https://www.aqr.com/Insights/Perspectives/Buffer-Madness and https://www.aqr.com/Insights/Perspectives/Rebuffed-A-Closer-Look-at-Options-Based-Strategies

Two caveats from Ptak that cut both ways on buffer ETFs: his risk-matched benchmarks were set 'with the benefit of hindsight' (an investor could not have known the right mix in advance), and the 60/40 mix that buffer ETFs beat on risk-adjusted return itself earned 8.5% a year against 11.5% for a matched 70/30 shares-and-cash mix - so beating 60/40 in 2020-2025 was a low bar. Every one of the 41 buffer ETFs was more volatile than its own benchmark. https://jeffreyptak.substack.com/p/buffer-beef

How big the cost of waiting really is in AQR's study: on the 60-year sample the shortfall is 0.04 of Sharpe ratio, measured against an S&P 500 without dividends and with no trading costs charged to the dip rules; the average rule had a small positive (statistically unreliable) alpha of +0.5% a year. The loss comes mainly from being out of the market, not from picking bad moments - which supports a deadline on cash but also means a dip rule that then stays invested is not what was tested. AQR also notes trend-following 'may have lagged in bull markets' and under-performed again in the March-April 2025 sell-off. https://www.aqr.com/-/media/AQR/Documents/Alternative-Thinking/AQR-Alternative-Thinking---Hold-the-Dip.pdf?sc_lang=en

The Cboe collar article gives no return comparison with the S&P 500 (only that the three indices beat the MSCI EAFE international index), admits PPUT 'also had fewer monthly gains of more than 4% and there is a cost to buying put options', and was produced with a summer intern by the exchange that lists the options. It supports 'smaller falls', not 'similar returns with smaller falls'. https://www.cboe.com/insights/posts/benchmark-indices-series-hedging-downside-exposure-with-pput-cll-and-cllz-indices

The trend-following century study rests on estimated costs: the authors write that transaction costs 'are estimated with a significant amount of uncertainty' and that futures roll costs 'are not accounted for in our simulations'; it also uses monthly, not daily, data. https://fairmodel.econ.yale.edu/ec439/hurst.pdf

Could not be checked, so should not be printed as fact: any equal-weight result after August 2024 (S&P pages returned HTTP 403, Invesco's US fund page loaded without data); any return, volatility or drawdown figure for the CLL collar index (dashboard empty, factsheet HTTP 403); Morningstar's 'Mind the Gap' (page loaded empty). Web search was unavailable for this check (session search budget used up), so all added sources were reached by direct address only and the search for contrary evidence is narrower than it should be.
failure_modes_checked: Waiting for a pullback: across 196 buy-the-dip rules on the S&P 500 (1965-2025; each buys after a set fall, holds for a set time, otherwise sits in cash) the average rule had a slightly lower risk-adjusted return than simply holding (0.04 lower Sharpe ratio; 0.27 lower on 1989-2025 data with dividends), and the always-invested portfolio was ahead by about 1.1% a year in plain return [S2]

Deadline buys at a bad moment: in the worst 5% of one-year outcomes, $100,000 invested at once ended at $82,947 against $85,906 for a three-month phase-in - a time-stop does not remove the risk of buying just before a fall [S1]

Floor formula locks into cash: after a sharp fall the cushion is used up, exposure drops to zero and the portfolio cannot rejoin the recovery - the 'CPPI cash lock-in', described as 'especially an issue in times of market crisis' (the paper names the problem; the mechanism is standard textbook description) [S10]
Floor formula and option insurance are whipsawed: both 'do worse in relatively trendless, volatile markets', buying after rises and selling after falls over and over [S7]

Option protection mis-timed: 'If the duration of the drawdown doesn't align with the maturity of the option, the hoped-for protection won't be there' - for example two 4% monthly falls never trigger a monthly put set 5% below the market [S15]

Buffer and other option funds, 2020-2025: 86% of about 102 funds returned less than a matched mix of shares and Treasury bills, and 70% returned less AND fell further; in the January-April 2025 sell-off 83% of 42 defined-outcome funds had a worse drawdown than the matched mix [S16]
Collars give up return twice: they 'earn less equity-risk premium' because they hold less market exposure, and they often pay away the volatility premium as well [S13]

Protective puts in the typical use case were 'quite ineffective at reducing drawdowns versus the simple alternative of statically reducing exposure'; by the put-call parity identity (general knowledge, not from a fetched page) the same weakness should carry over to Treasury-bills-plus-calls [S14]

Trend-following in a fast crash: 20 Feb-23 Mar 2020 the S&P 500 fell 33.8% and the trend index returned -2.4%, so there was no gain to offset the fall; the long backtest also warns it 'may not perform well in bear markets that occur very rapidly, such as the 1987 stock market crash' [S2][S20]
Trend-following dry spells: the simulated strategy lost 'up to 25%, over extended time periods', and the 2010s were weak because there were 'fewer large moves across markets' [S20][S21]
Equal weight when giants lead: in 2023 the equal-weight S&P 500 returned 13.87% against 26.29% for the standard index [S26]

Volatility targeting in real time: a real-time mix of the managed and plain versions earned a lower certainty-equivalent return than the plain version in 72 of 103 strategies, and for the whole share market that mix had a Sharpe ratio of 0.42 against 0.46 for leaving the market alone [S23]

Commitments people will not make or keep: only 28.4% accepted a binding savings commitment when offered, and Laibson's model finds 'the perceived benefits of commitment are often overwhelmed by the costs of commitment' - a rule that costs nothing to break may not bind [S5][S6]

Defaults are sticky even when wrong: 61% of automatically enrolled staff stayed at the default contribution rate and default fund, a combination only 1% of earlier staff had chosen - the same force that keeps a cash default in place [S3][X8]

Being paid to wait (selling cash-secured puts, the Cboe PUT index): since January 2007 it returned 7.1% a year against 11.0% for the S&P 500 and still fell 32.7% at worst (the S&P 500 fell 50.9%) - upside is capped while much of the downside remains [S27]

tools.plain_summary:
WHAT THE TOOL IS TODAY (branch pa6-20261006, one file: index.html). It is a chain of steps, percent only, never dollars: (1) HEAT - about 21 market readings ("voters"), each scored from -1 (washed out / everything sold down) to +1 (stretched / everything run up), averaged by weight into one number; (2) THE LADDER - that one number picks one of five rungs, and the rung is the percent of the money invested (100 / 80 / 50 / 30 / 15); the rest is cash; (3a) SECTORS - each sector gets one blended reading from five sources; (3b) THE MONEY SPLIT - the invested part is divided across sectors, more to the oversold ones; (4) COHORTS [themed groups of companies] under those sectors; (5) THE KNOCKOUT - inside one cohort, companies in the same business line face off on fundamentals (price, growth, margin, debt), the Geiger [the Hub's own -1..+1 overbought/oversold gauge] only breaks ties; (6) THE PICKS and their percent; (7) THE MOVES - the gap between where Alan is and the target, split into a first clip now and the rest on a named trigger. The EQUALIZER is not a step in this tool: it is the Hub's weighting of chart timeframes inside the Geiger, applied before the tool reads it.

WHY ALAN SITS IN CASH. The ladder is built to hold back when the market is hot. Replayed over the last two years (502 sessions) it never said more than 80% invested and averaged 41% invested (59% cash); on 253 of 502 sessions it said 30%. Today the heat is near zero because hot index readings cancel cold rates/breadth/credit, so the ladder says 50%.

WHAT R4 PROPOSES (study only, nothing on the live tool). Replace the single heat with two dials. REGIME (trend structure of SPY and QQQ against their reviewed breakout line and the 200-day average, plus how many of our own companies are above their 200-day and 50-day averages) sets a base percent invested: 90 / 75 / 60 / 40 / 25. STRETCH (how extended the indexes are against their own last year, RSI and Williams, the VIX against its own baseline, the 10-year yield's own Geiger) moves that base by up to 20 points either way. Weak credit takes 10 off. Bounded 15 to 100. Replayed, that averaged 75% invested (25% cash), ranged 23% to 100%, and today reads 49%. R4 itself says these numbers are "a proposal for Alan, not settled numbers".

R4'S CORE/SATELLITE PROPOSAL. The invested percent is split: SATELLITE (short-term conviction picks) is 25% of invested money in an uptrend, 20% in a range, 10% in a breakdown; CORE is the rest, half index fund and half long-term leaders. A satellite sale goes to the core's index sleeve, not to cash. Today: 49% invested = 19.6 index + 19.6 leaders + 9.8 satellite, 51% cash.

HONEST LIMITS. R4's own history check did not show the two dials separating good breakouts from failed ones (they said "add" on 5 that worked and on all 3 that failed). Everything is a two-year replay, not a record of returns: no portfolio return, drawdown or risk figure has been computed for either method. The tool today has no index sleeve, no list of "long-term leaders", no per-name volatility, no option data and no support/resistance lines on the live page - each of the six structures needs at least one of those added.

Percent only, never dollars.

facts.fact: THE EQUALIZER is the Hub's weighting of chart timeframes inside the Geiger; the allocation page does not recompute it ('The Hub applies the equalizer curve (operator_weights) upstream inside the Geiger this page reads; nothing is re-computed here'). Curve read off the Hub on 19 Jul 2026: 2h 1.2, 3h 3.6, 4h 6.7, 6h 9.3, 12h 9.3, 1d 9.3, 3d 7.6, 1w 2.9; trend 50 / momentum 50; momentum = 60 RSI / 40 Williams.

The Geiger formula as the studies rebuild it: trend = how many of a nine-line fan of averages (EMA 5, 8, 13, 21, 34; SMA 50, 100, 150, 200) are in order; momentum = 0.6 x RSI(14) mapped 23..77 onto -1..+1 plus 0.4 x Williams %R(14) mapped -90..-10; reading = 0.5 trend + 0.5 momentum; blended over the daily, 3-day and weekly bars with Equalizer weights D 3.178477, 3D 2.576738, W 0.987499. The live Hub uses seven rungs; the history uses these three.

STEP 3a SECTORS: one blended reading per sector from five sources at equal default weight 20 each - State Street fund Geiger, Hub sector compare (fund + equal-weight twin), market bow tie over served names, tree close tier, live sector ranking. A missing source is named and the others carry its weight. The 'bow tie' is equal-weight reading minus cap-weight reading (below zero = the giants carry the sector).
facts.evidence: alloc-pa6-20261006/index.html:706-712 (BLEND_SRC, MIX_DEFAULT), :758-766 (blendFrom), :769-779 (bowSides), :815 (sector words use the ladder's thresholds); RETURN-20261005-PA5.md lines 11-21

facts.fact: STEP 3b MONEY SPLIT rule: coldness = the larger of 0.05 and (1 - reading) / 2; multiplied by 'the turn' (improving x1.35, breakdown x0.6, pullback in uptrend x0.85, leading x1); shares normalised to 100% of the invested part; each sector held between 2% and 35% and renormalised; times the rung's % invested. So an oversold sector earns more money, an overbought one less.

STEP 4 COHORTS: the Hub's cohorts are grouped under the sector most of their names sit in, in the bow tie's order (hot to cold). The default cohort for the knockout is the first one in that order with at least 4 names carrying measured fundamentals that is not a whole sector.

STEP 5 KNOCKOUT: only two companies in the same business line may duel; a duel is scored on four fundamentals (price P/E or P/S, growth, margin, leverage), each placed between the first and third quartile of the line's field with price outliers out; the Geiger decides only when two names are within 0.02; a name needs at least two measured readings to enter; seeds by score, first plays last, byes for odd names; line champions never duel, they stand on a podium by score; the podium's first names are the KEEP / DROP picks.
How many names the plan holds: names per sector = 2 + (1 - heat) / 2 x 3 (heat -1 -> 5 names, heat +1 -> 2 names, heat ~0 -> ~4), capped by 'max names per sleeve' 6; hard cap on total names 12.

STEP 6 PICKS: inside a sector the kept names split that sector's share by a weight = washed-out-ness (1 - Geiger)/2 x a regime-fit factor (pullback 1.0, uptrend 0.62, bounce 0.45, breakdown 0.12; regime weight 0.55) x a cheapness-vs-peers tilt (weight 0.22), floor 0.05. There is no volatility term in the sizing.

STEP 7 MOVES: total to deploy = target % invested minus current % invested (current comes from an IBKR state file holding only invested_pct and lc_pct). The first clip = 0.5 + urgency x 0.14 - lagShare x 0.25, held between 20% and 85%; the rest waits on a named trigger ('on the next volatility spike', 'once the lagging sectors turn up', or 'on a -3% pullback or a volatility spike'). R3 found the '% of sectors lagging' factor filters on labels that never occur, so it is always 0%.

tools.plain_summary:
Read-only; nothing was created, edited, fetched or ordered. Scintilla's "what to buy" chain exists and runs, but it is not approved, not live in its newest form, does not yet weight growth the way Alan asked, and keeps no history, so it cannot be backtested today.

WHAT COMPS PRODUCES PER COMPANY. On the Hub, each company gets (a) a peer set [the similar companies it is measured against] of 12 seats, built "business first": a peer is in when at least 15 cents of each revenue dollar sits in a business the two share; (b) a table of 16 measures (6 valuation, 3 growth, 3 margins, net debt/EBITDA, 3 capex); (c) a football field [one bar per measure showing where the company sits against its peers]; (d) an implied price range with upside by ways A, B and C. Outliers [peers priced strangely] are flagged by rule C6b.

HOW THE KNOCKOUT DECIDES. Three generations exist: the K1 workshop (26 Sep: fit, then comps, then timing), A1 (2 Oct: round robin on ten equal-weight comparisons, top 3 advance), and the allocation tool's own (PA5 live; PA6 on a branch). In PA6 only two companies in the same business line may duel. Each name gets one fundamentals score: the plain average of four readings, each 25%: price (P/E, or P/S for a loss-maker), revenue growth, net margin, leverage [debt to equity]. Each reading is the name's position between its field's first and third quartile, clamped 0 to 1; a missing reading counts 0.5. The Geiger [Alan's -1 to +1 overbought/oversold gauge] never scores; it only breaks a tie when two scores are less than 0.02 apart. My reading of the code: because a name's score does not depend on its opponent, the bracket is in effect a ranking by that one score inside each line.

GROWTH'S WEIGHT: 25%, equal to the other three. It is revenue growth only (no earnings growth), and it saturates: 126% and 246% both read 1.00, 18% reads 0.80. Alan's rule "growth ... is the biggest" was said about 13:45 ET on 6 Oct, after PA6 ended at 14:14 UTC (10:14 ET). So the code does not yet follow it.

WHAT COMES OUT. A podium: one champion per business line, in score order (13 names on PA6's live load, 9 on the concept snapshot an hour earlier). The first n are offered as KEEP / DROP cards; n was about three that night. Only a KEEP or DROP press is saved (table comps_decisions, plus the browser). The podium itself is recomputed on every page load and stored nowhere. PA5 reports no real decision recorded.

APPROVAL. Alan: "we never exactly approved the comps knockout yet, but we approved it conceptually." PA6 returned "completed_needs_review", nothing deployed; the local main ref (fetched 14:42 on 6 Oct) is still PA5.

SG1 AND CO1. SG1 adds, per sector, how hot it is against its own last 12 months plus a leader/laggard box. CO1 proposes 63 tighter theme cohorts (57 move together more than their sector). Both are studies; neither is applied.

AS A SATELLITE LIST. The kept podium names are a natural conviction list, and step 6 already turns kept names into % of equity. Missing: approval, growth as the largest weight, a steady data feed (Micron's growth read +146%, then -59%, then +146%), a stored dated history of podiums, a core/satellite split, per-name buy/add/trim/reload levels, and any test that winners outperform.

facts.fact: Hub comps table per company has 16 measures: 6 valuation (P/E trailing, P/E forward, EV/EBITDA, EV/sales, P/S, PEG), 3 growth (Revenue TTM, Revenue next FY, EPS next FY), 3 margins (Gross, Operating, FCF), Net debt / EBITDA, 3 capex (CapEx / revenue, CapEx growth, New revenue per CapEx $).
Comps gives each company an implied price band (lo, mid, hi) and an upside % by four computed 'ways': A range of the medians, B middle-half band, C equal-weight blend, C reliability-weighted blend.

The C5 peer rule is business first: a peer needs at least 15% of revenue in a shared line (SIM_MIN 0.15, LINE_MIN 0.15), size is a small tie-breaker (SIZE_WEIGHT 0.06), default set is 12 names, each business line seats its 2 best peers.
The allocation tool's knockout does NOT read the 16 measures or the A/B/C upside. It reads a slimmer database feed ('comps-feed') and uses four fields: pe or ps, rev_growth, net_m, de.

facts.fact: PA6 scoring formula: score = (sum of the readings present + 0.5 for each missing reading) / 4. Four readings, equal weight, so growth is 1 of 4 = 25%.

facts.fact: Each reading is the name's position between the field's first and third quartile, clamped to 0..1 (1.00 = better than three quarters). Lower is better for price and leverage. So growth above the third quartile earns no extra credit.
facts.evidence: /Users/alanharvey/SCINTILLA 0.5/_worktrees/alloc-pa6-20261006/index.html:521-523 (vsPeers: 't=Math.max(0,Math.min(1,t))'); KNOCKOUT-CONCEPT.html text: SNDK 'growth 126%' = 1.00, LRCX 'growth 246%' = 1.00, NVDA 'growth 18% · field 6% / 13% / 21%' = 0.80

facts.fact: Knockout constants: a name needs 15% of revenue in a line to belong to that line's field; a line needs 5 measured names or the readings use the wider family; two names closer than 0.02 are 'even'.
A duel is won on fundamentals when the two scores are at least 0.02 apart; otherwise the Geiger timing decides and 'the more washed-out name goes through'.
The timing tie-break = ((1 - Geiger)/2) x (0.45 + 0.55 x 2 x regime fit), with regime fit buy 1.0, go 0.62, improve 0.45, avoid 0.12, none 0.5.

Pairing: companies are grouped by the business line carrying most of their revenue; inside a line they are seeded by score, first plays last, an odd name gets a bye, rounds until one champion; a lone name is champion 'unopposed'. A name with fewer than two measured readings sits out.

A name's score is computed once against its line's field and reused in every duel, so (my reading of the code, not a statement in the files) the bracket is equivalent to ranking by that score inside the line, except where two names fall within 0.02.

tools.plain_summary:
Read-only pass. Nothing was written, no order placed, no key printed.

(1) REVIEWED LINES. A reviewed line is a price line Alan approved in the Indicator Lab's Clean Review on TradingView. The Lab owns it; Scintilla holds a read-only copy: 486 lines on 19 names, on a branch, not live yet. Two families. Horizontal lines are flat, set at the exact high or low of a past swing (a "pivot"), ids P1 to P5. Sloped lines are straight channel rails (B), logarithmic rails [rails that rise by a steady percent, not steady dollars] (C and D), and fitted pattern rails such as triangles (T). "P1" is the newest pivot on its timeframe. "2W" means the line was reviewed on two-week bars [one candle = two weeks]; lines also exist on 3D and 1W, none yet on daily. Each line gets one of six states from the last 10 completed daily closes and a 1% "near" band: above, retest from above, broke above, below, retest from below, broke below.
SPY at 780.21 (live price at 14:13 ET): nearest line above is the 1W B2 rail at 788.34 (+1.04%); nearest below is the 1W C2 rail at 779.24 (−0.12%); its 2W P1 is 777.44 (−0.36%). QQQ at 761.30: nearest above is 1W C1 at 776.95 (+2.06%); nearest below is 1W B2 at 755.65 (−0.74%); its 2W P1 is 747.05 (−1.87%), closed above two sessions ago.
One trap for the page: distances use the live price, states use closes. The file tags SPY's P1 "retest from below" (the last close, 774.83, was under it) while LB1's prose says "retest from above after today's break". SPY had not closed above it when the file was made.

(2) GEIGER. A heat reading from −1 (cold) to +1 (hot). Per timeframe it is half trend (are nine moving averages stacked in bullish order) and half momentum (60% RSI scored between 23 and 77, 40% Williams %R scored between −90 and −10), then blended across seven timeframes. It says how extended a name is, not where to buy. SPY read about +0.79 to +0.82 today, QQQ +0.84 to +0.85.

(3) BACKTEST. The reviewed lines themselves cannot be honestly back-tested: they are one snapshot taken in early October 2026 with all history in view. HEAT1 found a mechanical stand-in for one slice only: a pivot high with 2 bars left and 2 right on two-week bars reproduces the reviewed SPY and QQQ 2W pivot dates. The lengths are inferred (2 left, 3 right fits too). It gave 10 breaks in two years, a tiny sample, and tested breakouts, not buying pullbacks to a line. Sloped rails, patterns and the other pivots have no mechanical rule yet.

(4) PLAN. No file defines tranches, a cancel rule or a put strike. The plug-in entries give a proposal built from the states: group lines within 1% into shelves; tranche 1, 2, 3 are the first three shelves below price that price has closed above; a daily close under the third shelf cancels. The put strike would be a horizontal shelf (flat lines do not move before expiry; sloped ones do). One caution from the evidence: SPY is at the 86th percentile of its own year, and the replayed heat was washed out on only 5% of sessions, so a "wait until cold" filter would itself keep Alan in cash.

The six states and their exact rule (N = 10 sessions, near = 0.01, both stated in the snapshot header). All use COMPLETED daily closes. Last close above the line: 'broke_above (k sessions ago)' if any of the last 10 closes was at or below it; else 'retest_from_above (resistance turned support)' if the lowest low of the last 10 sessions was within 1% above the line (min low <= level × 1.01); else 'above'. Last close at or below the line: 'broke_below (k sessions ago)' if any of the last 10 closes was at or above it; else 'retest_from_below (support turned resistance)' if the highest high of the last 10 sessions was within 1% below (max high >= level × 0.99); else 'below'. 'above' means PRICE is above the line, so the line sits underneath as possible support.
State counts across all 486 levels today: above 217, below 148, retest_from_above 36, retest_from_below 31, broke_above 31, broke_below 23.

Distance sign and 'nearest' rule: pct = 100 × (level − price) ÷ price, so plus = line above price, minus = line below. Nearest above = the lowest line strictly above the price; nearest below = the highest line at or below it.

Mismatch to flag on the page: the distance uses the forming daily bar [today's live, unfinished candle] for 15 names, but the state uses completed closes only. So SPY's P1 at 777.439633 is 0.3552% BELOW the live price yet is tagged 'retest_from_below (support turned resistance)', because the last completed close (774.83 on 5 Oct) was under it. Geiger TREND half. A fan of nine moving averages: EMA 5, 8, 13, 21, 34 and SMA 50, 100, 150, 200 (a line joins only when enough bars exist). Count the adjacent pairs where the shorter average is above the longer one; trend = (2 × inOrder − pairs) ÷ pairs. All eight pairs stacked bullish = +1, all stacked bearish = −1.

Geiger MOMENTUM half. 'MOMENTUM = 0.6 × RSI(14) on 23..77 + 0.4 × Williams %R(14) on −90..−10'. RSI 23 scores −1 and RSI 77 scores +1; Williams −90 scores −1 and −10 scores +1; each is clamped to that range. Constants: RSI_OS = 23, RSI_OB = 77, W_OS = -90, W_OB = -10, W_RSI = 0.6, W_WILL = 0.4.

facts.fact: HEAT1's mechanical pivot rule, exact definition. On the provider's two-week bars, bar i is a pivot high when its high is strictly greater than the highs of the 2 bars before it AND greater than or equal to the highs of the 2 bars after it (PL = 2, PR = 2; 'ta.pivothigh(high, 2, 2)'). It counts as confirmed on the last day of the second bar after it: confirmedAt = start of bar i+2, plus 14 days, minus 1 day. A break = 'the first daily close above the pivot high after the bar that confirms it', and before the next pivot is confirmed.

What the rule reproduces and how firmly. 'A pivot high with 2 bars left and 2 right on the provider's two-week bars reproduces every reviewed SPY and QQQ 2W pivot date'. But 'The chart's detector inputs are not in the saved evidence and the source's 10/10 cannot give those dates', and 'The pivot lengths 2/2 are inferred; 2/3 fits the same dates.' The provider's split-adjusted bars read the levels 0.21 to 0.25% higher than TradingView's (SPY 779.37 vs 777.439633; QQQ 748.65 vs 747.04878292). Confirmation comes about six weeks after the high: SPY pivot bar 2026-08-02, confirmed 2026-09-12.

What the rule found. Ten breaks in two years on SPY and QQQ (nine table rows; 15 Apr 2026 was both). 'At the moment of a break the heat barely moves: +0.04 on average from the day before to the day of, never more than +0.17.' '8 of 10 breaks happened with the heat already STRETCHED.' 'twenty sessions on, the heat was higher in 3 and lower in 6 of 9.' SPY's next 20 sessions after the eight rows that have data: −1.2%, +6.0%, +0.3%, +3.6%, +4.5%, −8.3%, −1.6%, +2.6% (5 up, 3 down by my count).

What the rule does NOT cover. It was run on SPY and QQQ only, two-week bars only, pivot HIGHS only, and it measured breakouts upward, not buying a pullback to a line. Several reviewed pivots come from a different detector tagged 'Trendoscope' (SPY 1W P4 and 3D P4; all four QQQ 3D pivots), and no file gives a mechanical rule for the sloped rails (B, C, D) or the patterns (T). R4 reuses the same 2/2 rule on IWM and RSP and notes 'the Lab has reviewed only SPY and QQQ among the indexes'.

SG1 'cold for itself', exact rule. Percentile = the share of the fund's own Geiger readings in the last 365 days that are below today's reading (ties count half). Word: 'HOT FOR ITSELF' if p >= 0.8, 'COLD FOR ITSELF' if p <= 0.2, else 'INSIDE ITS NORMAL'. Case, using the RRG box [a public relative-strength map with four boxes: leading, weakening, lagging, improving]: 'leader on a pullback' if the box is LEADING or WEAKENING and p <= 0.3; 'laggard that is simply low' if LAGGING or IMPROVING and p <= 0.3; 'leader running hot for itself' if LEADING or WEAKENING and p >= 0.8.

plug_in.structure: Level-based scaling in: a ladder of 'shelves' (PROPOSAL built from the files' own definitions; no file defines it). Group a name's lines that sit within 1% of each other (the module's own 'near' band) into one shelf. A shelf counts as a buy level only once price has CLOSED above it (state broke_above, retest_from_above or above). Tranche 1 = the first such shelf under price, tranche 2 = the next one down, tranche 3 = the one after. Illustration, not an order.
